- So the first-level indent is column 0 = line type character (space or `!`) and columns 1 to 2 = two spaces; every further level is exactly three more spaces.
- "Tabs are forbidden in TL-X regions. (One should beware of one's editor's auto-indentation mode.)" (spec §9.1). Tabs in `\SV` regions are only restricted by the HDL tools.
- The 3-space rule applies to SCOPE lines. Assignment CONTINUATION lines are looser: "Assignments continue on subsequent lines with deeper indentation (any number of additional spaces of indentation; not necessarily three spaces)." (spec §15).
- Assignment BLOCKS (`\always_comb`, `\SV_plus` as a block) "begin on a line with a keyword that has a '\' prefix and continue on subsequent lines with a minimum of three spaces of additional indentation" (spec §15); "Lines of the body must be indented at least three additional spaces." (spec §15.3).
- Indentation is the only scope delimiter: "Using specific indentation to convey scope, rather than using begin/end delimiters enforces consistent coding style and avoids inconsistencies between indentation and scope." (spec §9.1). There is no `begin`/`end`, `{`/`}`, or `endpipeline` anywhere in TL-X.
- Comments "are otherwise ignored from the standpoint of indentation" and "may begin anywhere in their line, including at the line-type character" (spec §18). So a comment at column 0 inside a `\TLV` region does NOT end the region.

chunks.heading: TL-X 1d (TL-Verilog) Language Specification: Structured Study Notes > 1. File structure > 1.6 Character set (spec §3)
chunks.text:
### 1.6 Character set (spec §3)
- A TL-X file is UTF-8 text (spec §3). All TL-X characters are in ASCII range 0 to 127 (spec §3).
- Character types: Word `[a-zA-Z_]`; Numeric `[0-9]`; Space `[ ]` (only the space character); Newline (LF, CR, CR+LF); Non-conformant line terminators (VT, FF, NEL, LS, PS and, confusingly, the list repeats LF/CR/CR+LF); Braces `()[]{}`; Symbols (everything else on a standard keyboard: `~`!@#$%^&*-+=\|:;"'<>,.?/`); Unrecognized (all other UTF-8) (spec §3).
- Character classes: Line terminator = newline + non-conformant terminators; Whitespace = space + all terminators; Conformant whitespace = space + newline only; Non-TL-X = non-conformant terminators + unrecognized; TL-X = everything else (spec §3).
- "Non-TL-X characters are only permitted in non-TL-X contexts -- currently, HDL contexts." Non-TL-X contexts are "HDL regions, HDL_plus regions, and assignment statements outside of signal references." (spec §3). So a non-ASCII character in a comment inside an assignment is tolerated, but in a scope line or inside a `$sig` reference it is illegal.
- Note the tab character is not listed in any type; it is neither Space nor a Symbol, so it falls under "Unrecognized"/Non-TL-X, which is consistent with §9.1 forbidding tabs in TL-X regions.

chunks.heading: TL-X 1d (TL-Verilog) Language Specification: Structured Study Notes > 1. File structure > 1.7 Line type character (spec §6)
chunks.text:
### 1.7 Line type character (spec §6)
- "Lines of code in a TLV or SV_plus region begin with a character that defines the line type." (spec §6). Only two are defined:
  - `<space>`: "Pure, safe TLV line (aka, nothing special)."
  - `!`: "Impure line. This is an alert to the use of methods that require caution."
- `!` "may be used on any lines at the designer's discretion, but is required on lines that contain:" (spec §6)
  - "an HDL signal reference (*sig_name) -- because changes to the stage of an assignment statement containing such a line will have an impact on functionality."
  - "an HDL macro instantiation (excluding those contained within the left-hand side of an assignment statement) -- because text macros can be used to do all sorts of strange things."
  - "a pragma or compiler directive -- because these can alter context should be consistent for all TL-X code in the file."
- Verbatim usage (fibonacci_state_example.tlv, incrementer_example.tlv):

```
!  $reset = *reset;
!     $Value <= *reset ? 1'b0    // reset to zero
                       : $Value ^ $carry_in;
!  *passed = ! *reset && *cyc_cnt > 1000 || |fetch/instr>>3$Pc == 12'hfff;
```

- NOT IN SPEC; observed: the tutorials are inconsistent. `default.tlv` writes `   $reset = *reset;` with a space, and `makerchip_tutorial.tlv` uses `*reset`, `*clk`, `` `BOGUS_USE `` and `m4_rand(...)` on lines with no `!`. The spec says `!` is "required"; the tools evidently do not reject its absence. A converter should emit `!` on every line containing `*sig`, a backtick macro, or a pragma to be spec-conformant.
- The `!` occupies column 0 and counts as the first character of the 3-space first-level indent (spec §9.1), so an impure line at level N is `!` followed by 3N-1 spaces.

chunks.heading: TL-X 1d (TL-Verilog) Language Specification: Structured Study Notes > 1. File structure > 1.8 Comments (spec §18)
chunks.text:
### 1.8 Comments (spec §18)
- "Comments use HDL comment syntax." (spec §18), that is `//` and `/* */` in TL-Verilog.
- Comments "may appear within assignment statements and blocks or after scope identifiers (together with their range)" (spec §18). Example from the spec: `$write = $opcode == 5'b11000 /* precise decode */;` and `/inst[3:0]` could be followed by `// Four instructions`.
- "Scope identifiers must begin their line, after indentation, so it is not legal to have a scope identifier after a multi-line-style comment that is terminated on the same line." (spec §18). Illegal: `/* x */ |pipe`.
- A scope line is: identifier, optional range "immediately (no whitespace)", then optionally "(conformant) whitespace and an HDL-style single- or multi-line comment" (spec §9.2). Nothing else may follow a scope identifier on its line.

---

## 2. Identifiers and sigils

### 2.1 General identifier model (spec §7)
- "TL-X defines a rich set of identifier types, each with their own namespace." (spec §7). `$foo`, `/foo`, `|foo`, `*foo` are four different identifiers that do not collide.
- "Identifiers begin with a type prefix containing zero or more symbol characters." What follows decides the kind (spec §7):
  - next char numeric (or `+`/`-` then numeric): numeric identifier (`@1`, `>>2`, `<<-1`);
  - next char alphabetic: named identifier, either delimited or mixed-case depending on the prefix;
  - next char whitespace or brace: an operator, "though no operators are defined in TL-X 1a" (spec §7).
- "There is a single syntax-to-type translation that is consistent in all contexts where identifiers are processed" (spec §7). The same spelling means the same thing everywhere.
- "Some named identifiers types are reserved for keywords ... This way, keywords do not interfere with the namespace of user-defined names." (spec §7). Keywords are `\mixedCase` words and `$UPPER_CASE` words (spec §7.4).
- Identifier types that have NO prefix "don't currently exist" and are "not legal in references"; the same is true of operators (spec §16.1 References, the stray block before §16).

chunks.heading: TL-X 1d (TL-Verilog) Language Specification: Structured Study Notes > 2. Identifiers and sigils > 2.2 Delimited identifier names (spec §7.1)
chunks.text:
### 2.2 Delimited identifier names (spec §7.1)
- "A delimited identifier name is a string comprised of delimited alphanumeric tokens. A token is a caseless string of alphabetic characters optionally followed by any number of numeric characters." (spec §7.1).
- "The first token must begin with a minimum of two alphabetic characters." (spec §7.1). So `$a`, `$x`, `$q1` are NOT valid TL-X names. The tutorials consistently use `$aa`, `$bb`, `$cc` where a Verilog author would write `a`, `b`, `c` (observed in `pythagorean_example.tlv`, `stall_example.tlv`, `div_example.tlv`).
- Because a token is letters THEN digits, digits can only trail a token: `$src1`, `$offset9`, `$err3`, `$data2` are valid (observed). A name like `$x2y` or `$a1_b` has no defined tokenisation for its first token under this grammar; AMBIGUOUS, avoid it. Names such as `$in2out` should be renamed (for example `$in_to_out`).
- "There are four methods of delimitation, distinguished by case of these first two alphabetic characters." (spec §7.1). Verbatim:

```
delimited_identifier    // Lower-case
DelimitedIdentifier     // Camel-case
DELIMITED_IDENTIFIER    // Upper-case
dELIMITEDiDENTIFIER     // Reverse camel-case (Not used)
```

chunks.heading: TL-X 1d (TL-Verilog) Language Specification: Structured Study Notes > 2. Identifiers and sigils > 2.2 Delimited identifier names (spec §7.1)
chunks.text:
- The delimitation style is part of the identifier's TYPE, not just a convention (spec §7, §7.4). For the `$` prefix: `$lower_case` is a pipesignal; `$CamelCase` is a state signal; `$UPPER_CASE` is a keyword (`$RETAIN`, and `$ANY` in practice). The same rule holds for `?$when` (pipesignal condition) versus `?$When` (state-signal condition) and for `$$assigned` versus `$$AssignedState` (reference_card.tlv).
- Lower-case style forbids capitals entirely; a capital anywhere in `$foo_Bar` breaks the token grammar (tokens are caseless strings, and the style is fixed by the first two letters). AMBIGUOUS whether the processor errors or reinterprets; avoid it.
- Underscore is the delimiter in lower-case and upper-case styles; case change is the delimiter in camel-case style. A leading underscore (`$_foo`) does not satisfy "first token must begin with ... two alphabetic characters" and the spec gives it no meaning. Trailing or doubled underscores are likewise undefined. NOT IN SPEC; observed: `\TLV` macro definitions use a leading underscore on PARAMETER names (`/_name`, `#_size`, `_where`, `_in` in `dac_2020_ring.tlv`), which is a macro-layer convention for "substituted text", not a TL-X identifier rule.
- "Most names in TL-X are delimited identifiers, including those that translate to HDL. The restriction on name syntax allows names to carry over directly to HDL with additional available HDL namespace for other generated/derived names." (spec §7.1). This is the spec's only statement about generated-Verilog naming: user names survive into the HDL, and the processor takes the remaining namespace for derived names.

chunks.heading: TL-X 1d (TL-Verilog) Language Specification: Structured Study Notes > 2. Identifiers and sigils > 2.3 Mixed-case identifier names (spec §7.2, §7.4)
chunks.text:
### 2.3 Mixed-case identifier names (spec §7.2, §7.4)
- Prefixes that take mixed-case names: `\`, `*`, `**`, `^` (spec §7.4).
- "Mixed case identifier names can contain any alpha-numeric characters of either case plus '_'. They begin with an alphabetic character (of either case)." (spec §7.2). So `*opcode_u101H`, `*clk`, `**mips_word`, `\SV_plus` are all fine, and any legal Verilog identifier that starts with a letter can be referenced as `*name` unchanged.
- "Mixed case identifiers generally do not transfer into HDL, as doing so would consume the entire HDL namespace." (spec §7.2). `*sig` refers to an existing HDL signal; it does not create one.
- A Verilog identifier that begins with `_` (legal in Verilog) cannot be referenced as `*_name` under this grammar; AMBIGUOUS, the spec does not say what happens. Rename in the SV region first.

### 2.4 Numeric identifiers (spec §7.3)
- "Numeric identifiers are ones whose prefix character(s) (if any) are followed by a numeric string which begins with a decimal digit. However, if that decimal digit is preceded by '+' or '-', the '+'/'-' is taken to be part of the numeric string." (spec §7.3).
- "To avoid ambiguity, numeric identifier prefixes must not end with '+'/'-'." (spec §7.3). This is why 1d moved alignment from `%+3` to `>>3`.
- "Currently the numeric string consists entirely of the optional '+'/'-' followed by decimal digits, to define a decimal number." (spec §7.3). So `@0x1`, `@1'd2`, `>>N` with a symbolic `N` are not numeric identifiers. In practice M4/M5 macro names (`M4_WIDTH`) get textually replaced with digits BEFORE TL-X parsing, which is how `/slice[M4_WIDTH-1:0]` works (observed in `incrementer_example.tlv`; that is a range expression, not a numeric identifier, see §2.6).

chunks.heading: TL-X 1d (TL-Verilog) Language Specification: Structured Study Notes > 2. Identifiers and sigils > 2.5 Complete identifier type table (spec §7.4, verbatim)
chunks.text:
### 2.5 Complete identifier type table (spec §7.4, verbatim)
- Keywords: `\SV_plus` (and `\VHDL_plus`, `\C_plus`), `\source`, `$RETAIN`.
- Scope: `|pipeline`, `/beh_hier`, `?$when`, `?$When`, `@1` (non-negative pipe stage), `@-1` (negative pipe stage), `@++`, `@+=1`, `@+=-1`.
- Signals: `$pipesignal`, `$$produced_signal`, `$StateSignal`, `*HDL_signal` (mixed case), `**HDL_type` (mixed case).
- Other: `>>2` (ahead reference), `<<2` (behind reference), `<>0` (naturally-aligned reference), `^attribute` (mixed case).
- The reference card (NOT IN SPEC; `reference_card.tlv`) adds to this list: `$$AssignedStateSig`, `>>-2` ("permitted"), `\TLV`, `\SV`, `\always_comb`, `\end_source`, `$ANY`, and the Verilog-2005 variants `$$^reg_pipesignal`, `$$^RegStateSignal`, `$$^ANY` for use in `\SV_plus` when an assignment must be of `reg` type. Verbatim from the card:

```
   $$assigned_signal // Assigned pipesignal or state signal in context other than
   $$AssignedStateSig//   left-hand side (i.e. "$sig =", "{$sig, ...} =", and "$$Sig <=".
   ...
   $$^reg_pipesignal   // These explicitly identify an assignment that must be of
   $$^RegStateSignal   //   'reg' type (vs. 'wire') (sequential assignment, vs.
   $$^ANY              //    'assign' and connectivity).
```

- `#index` is NOT in the §7.4 table, but §16.4 uses `/scope[#scope]` and the tutorials use `#slice`, `#port`, `#bank`, `#entry`, `#ring_stop`, `#src` as the integer index of the enclosing replicated hierarchy scope of that name (observed in `incrementer_example.tlv`, `dac_2020_ring.tlv`, `array2d_example.tlv`, `flow_example.tlv`, `mini_cpu_1_cyc.tlv`). Verbatim:

```
      $carry_in = (#slice == 0) ? 1'b1
                                : /slice[(#slice - 1) % M4_WIDTH]$carry_out;
```

- `^attribute` is listed as a type but never defined further in the spec (spec §7.4). The reference card also only says "(mixed case) Attribute". Treat as reserved.
- `%`: appears only as the 1c alignment prefix (spec §1.3) and as a stray allowed first character of an assignment line (spec §15). No 1d meaning.

chunks.heading: TL-X 1d (TL-Verilog) Language Specification: Structured Study Notes > 2. Identifiers and sigils > 2.6 Ranges and indices (spec §8)
chunks.text:
### 2.6 Ranges and indices (spec §8)
- Range/index expressions appear after a behavioral scope identifier or after a signal identifier, in one of exactly four forms (spec §8):

```
[<expr>:<expr>]      Range
[{<expr>:<expr>}]    Subset range
[<expr>]             Index
[*]                  Complete range as defined elsewhere
```

- "<expr> use HDL syntax and may contain HDL constants. They may also contain TL-X signal references in situations where the HDL permits the use of signals." (spec §8). So `$ir[15:12]`, `$value[M4_WIDTH-1:0]`, `/mem[/src[2]$value[4:0]]`, `/reg[$dest_reg]` are all valid (last two observed in `mini_cpu_1_cyc.tlv`).
- "The HDL-context escape character '\' can be used to avoid special parsing of a character. For example, '\:' or '\]'." (spec §8).
- "TL-X processors may provide checking and optimization for the generated HDL if they can evaluate the expressions. For example, if only some bits of a pipesignal are required in a later pipestage, a TL-X processor could stage only those that are required." (spec §8). The processor is allowed, not required, to prune bits.
- A range attached to a scope identifier or an assigned signal must follow it "immediately (no whitespace)" (spec §9.2, §16.3).

---

chunks.heading: TL-X 1d (TL-Verilog) Language Specification: Structured Study Notes > 3. Scope: pipelines, stages, hierarchy, when
chunks.text:
## 3. Scope: pipelines, stages, hierarchy, when

### 3.1 Scope model (spec §9)
- "Every level of scope is introduced by a scope line containing an identifier, sometimes followed immediately (no whitespace) by a range and, optionally, (conformant) whitespace and an HDL-style single- or multi-line comment." (spec §9.2).
- Reentrance: "Scope in TL-X is termed reentrant, in the sense that the flow of the code can define logic in a particular scope, leave that scope, and reenter that scope to define more logic. This is unlike HDLs, where a module is defined contiguously ... For scopes classes that are reentrant we say that multiple lexical scopes can define a single logical scope." (spec §9.3).
- So `|exe` may appear five separate times in the file (it does, in `makerchip_tutorial.tlv`) and `@4` may appear twice under `|exe`; all lexical occurrences are the same logical scope.
- Behavioral scope = behavioral hierarchy (`/x`) + pipelines (`|p`). "The full path to a pipesignal includes all levels of behavioral scope and does not include other scope." (spec §9.4). Stage (`@`) and when (`?`) are NOT part of a signal's path. Hence `/top|exe$rslt` is a complete path, and the stage at which it is referenced is chosen by alignment, not by naming.
- Scope summary table (spec §9.5), transcribed:

| Scope | Range | Nesting requirement | Behavioral scope | Reentrant |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Behavioral hierarchy `/x` | none, `[max:min]`, `[{sub-max:sub-min}]`, `[*]` | Any | Yes | Yes |
| Pipeline `\|p` | none | Exactly one required | Yes | Yes |
| Pipestage `@N` | none | Exactly one required, below pipeline | No | Yes |
| When `?$x` | none | Any | No | Yes |
| Source `\source` | none | Any | No | N/A |

- "Nesting requirement: Exactly one required" for pipeline means every assignment must sit inside exactly one `|pipe`; "Any" for hierarchy and when means zero or more levels, nested in any order relative to each other.

chunks.heading: TL-X 1d (TL-Verilog) Language Specification: Structured Study Notes > 3. Scope: pipelines, stages, hierarchy, when > 3.2 Behavioral hierarchy scope `/name` (spec §10)
chunks.text:
### 3.2 Behavioral hierarchy scope `/name` (spec §10)
- "Behavioral hierarchy is a form of behavioral scope, and therefore provides a level of hierarchy with its own namespace. It also can enables replication of logic." (spec §10).
- Four permitted forms (spec §10, verbatim):

```
/my_hier                    Behavioral hierarchy namespace scope (no replication).
/my_hier[<expr>:<expr>]     Behavioral hierarchy replication scope.
/my_hier[{<expr>:<expr>}]   Behavioral hierarchy replication scope that is a subset of the full scope.
/my_hier[*]                 Wildcarded behavioral hierarchy replication scope.
```

- Range consistency rules across reentered lexical scopes (spec §10): "The lexical range expressions for a logical behavioral scope must define a single range for the logical scope. The lexical scopes must all specify a range, or none of them may. If ranges are provided, one must specify the complete scope (form 1). Others must be identical (by string compare), or be [*], (form 4), or specify a subset range (form 3)."
- AMBIGUOUS: "one must specify the complete scope (form 1)" clearly intends form 2 (`[max:min]`), since form 1 has no range. Read it as: exactly one lexical occurrence carries the full `[max:min]`; every other occurrence is a byte-identical copy of it, or `[*]`, or a `[{sub-max:sub-min}]` subset.
- Consequence: `/inst[3:0]` once and `/inst[*]` elsewhere (spec §2.3 example) is the intended pattern. `/inst[3:0]` and `/inst[0:3]` in two places is illegal (not identical by string compare). `/inst[3:0]` in one place and `/inst` (no range) in another is illegal ("all specify a range, or none").
- NOT IN SPEC; observed in `array_any_example.tlv`: the range declaration must appear before references ("Must be declared before reference (currently)."), and a scope can be declared with nothing under it purely to declare its range:

```
         /M4_ENTRY_HIER
            // Must be declared before reference (currently).
            /trans
```

- "A behavioral hierarchy identifier must be distinct from identifiers of all parent levels of behavioral hierarchy." (spec §10). `/x/y/x` is illegal; sibling reuse (`/a/x` and `/b/x`) is fine. This uniqueness is what makes the up-reference rule in §4.3 work.
- The top level of a module has "an implicit identifier '/top'" (spec §16.4). There is no `/_top`; the spelling is `/top`.

chunks.heading: TL-X 1d (TL-Verilog) Language Specification: Structured Study Notes > 3. Scope: pipelines, stages, hierarchy, when > 3.3 Pipeline scope `|name` (spec §11)
chunks.text:
### 3.3 Pipeline scope `|name` (spec §11)
- "Pipeline scope (|my_pipe) is a form of behavioral scope, and therefore provides a level of hierarchy with its own namespace. Pipeline scope cannot be replicated, so there can be no range expression." (spec §11). `|pipe[3:0]` is illegal; replicate the hierarchy around it instead (`/port[*]` then `|ring` as in `dac_2020_ring.tlv`).
- "All logic in TL-X is defined within a pipeline. Therefore, there must be exactly one pipeline scope for every assignment statement." (spec §11).
- The implicit pipeline: `\SV_plus` regions are "stage 0 (@0) of pipeline 'none' (|none)" (spec §5.2). Every tutorial also places assignments such as `$reset = *reset;` and `*passed = *cyc_cnt > 40;` directly under `\TLV` with no `|` or `@` line, and `makerchip_tutorial.tlv` puts `$Cnt[15:0] <= ...` there (observed). AMBIGUOUS: the spec never says outright that a `\TLV` region's top level is `|none@0`, but §5.2 plus the examples make that the only consistent reading.
- Pipelines nest inside hierarchy and hierarchy nests inside pipelines: `|pipe` then `/inst[3:0]` (spec §2.3) and `/port[*]` then `|ring` (observed). The table's "Exactly one required" for pipeline forbids `|a` inside `|b`.
- Pipeline names are lower-case delimited identifiers (spec §7.4 lists `|pipeline`; the mixed-case set is only `\ * ** ^`). `|Pipeline` as used in the spec's own §16.2 snippet is camel-case; AMBIGUOUS, the spec gives no meaning to a camel-case pipeline name. Tutorials use only lower-case pipeline names.

chunks.heading: TL-X 1d (TL-Verilog) Language Specification: Structured Study Notes > 3. Scope: pipelines, stages, hierarchy, when > 3.4 Pipestage scope `@N` (spec §12)
chunks.text:
### 3.4 Pipestage scope `@N` (spec §12)
- "All logic in TL-X is defined within the context of a pipeline and a pipestage within that pipeline. Therefore, there must be exactly one pipestage scope for every assignment statement, and that pipestage scope must be within a pipeline scope." (spec §12).
- Permitted forms (spec §12, verbatim): `@<number>: Positive pipeline stage. Const-expr is a decimal number.` and `@-<number>: Negative pipeline stage. Const-expr is a decimal number.` (Note "positive" here includes `@0`; §7.4 calls it "non-negative pipe stage".)
- Negative stages are simply stages numbered below zero; the spec attaches no other semantics (spec §12, §7.4). They let logic be placed "before" stage 0 of a pipeline without renumbering.
- Relative stages `@++`, `@+=1`, `@+=-1` are listed as identifier types (spec §7.4) and as 1c features (spec §1.3) but §12 does not list them as permitted forms. The reference card (NOT IN SPEC) documents them: `@+=1 // Subsequent pipestage (or @+=-1 for prior pipestage)` and `@++ // Shorthand for @+=1`. AMBIGUOUS whether a spec-strict processor accepts them; no tutorial file uses them. A converter should emit absolute `@N`.
- Stage lines carry no range and nothing but an optional comment (spec §9.2, §9.5). `@1 // "fetch1"` is fine (observed).
- `@` cannot appear directly under `/hier` without an intervening `|pipe` ("below pipeline", spec §9.5), and `@` cannot nest inside `@`.
- The stage number is the ONLY thing that determines where in time an assignment executes. Two assignments in the same `|pipe` at `@1` and `@3` are two cycles apart; the processor inserts the staging flops for any signal consumed at a later stage than it was assigned. The spec implies this in §8 ("stage only those [bits] that are required") and §16.4 (bit range "may be interpreted by a TL-X processor to determine what bits must be made available in the consuming stage") but never states the flop-insertion rule directly; it is the "timing abstraction" the reader is assumed to know (spec §1.2).

chunks.heading: TL-X 1d (TL-Verilog) Language Specification: Structured Study Notes > 3. Scope: pipelines, stages, hierarchy, when > 3.5 When scope `?$cond` (spec §13)
chunks.text:
### 3.5 When scope `?$cond` (spec §13)
- "A 'when statement' provides a condition under which the contained assignment statements produce valid results." (spec §13).
- Forms (spec §13, verbatim):

```
?$valid_sig     Conditioned on the pipesignal $valid_sig, which must be assigned within the scope of this when statement.
?*HDL_signal    Conditioned on the HDL signal HDL_signal.
```

chunks.heading: TL-X 1d (TL-Verilog) Language Specification: Structured Study Notes > 3. Scope: pipelines, stages, hierarchy, when > 3.5 When scope `?$cond` (spec §13)
chunks.text:
- Plus `?$When` for a state-signal condition (spec §7.4; reference card "When state condition"). The spec body never describes `?$When` beyond listing it.
- AMBIGUOUS: "which must be assigned within the scope of this when statement" reads as if `$valid_sig` must be assigned INSIDE the `?$valid_sig` block, which cannot be intended (the spec's own example assigns `$valid` at `@0` outside the `?$valid` block). The next sentence gives the real constraint: "The condition signal must be a single-bit (boolean) signal in the same behavioral scope as the when statement, which, when asserted, indicates validity." Read "within the scope" as "within the same behavioral scope".
- Condition must be single-bit and in the same behavioral scope (same `/hier` path and same `|pipe`) as the when line (spec §13). `?/other$valid` or `?|p2$valid` is not a listed form; to condition on another scope's signal, first copy it: `$valid = /top|resp<>0$fetch_resp_valid;` then `?$valid` (pattern observed in `makerchip_tutorial.tlv`).
- Invalidity semantics: "When not asserted, the values that would be produced by the assignments under the when scope are 'invalid' and may not be consumed [the definition of consumed is under debate]." (spec §13). The spec does NOT say what value an invalid signal holds in simulation (X, don't-care, or stale); it only says the value is not to be consumed. Makerchip's X-injection for invalid signals is tool behaviour, not spec.
- "An assignment's when scope is defined by all when scope levels within which the assignment is contained." (spec §13). Nested `?$a` then `?$b` means the assignment is valid only when both are asserted.
- "If the condition is a pipesignal, that pipesignal's when scope must be the same, or a subscope of that of the when statement (in addition to being within the same behavioral hierarchy level)." (spec §13). AMBIGUOUS: taken literally this says the condition's own when-scope must be at least as restrictive as the block it guards, which is the reverse of what makes a condition consumable; it may intend the opposite ("the when statement must be within the condition's when scope"). Safe practice from the examples: assign the condition signal in a when-scope that is a SUPERSET (usually none) of where it is used as `?$cond`.
- Stage placement: `?` may sit above `@` (spec §2.3: `?$valid` then `@1`) or below it (`makerchip_tutorial.tlv`: `@4` then `?$instr_valid`). Both are legal ("Nesting Requirements: Any").

chunks.heading: TL-X 1d (TL-Verilog) Language Specification: Structured Study Notes > 3. Scope: pipelines, stages, hierarchy, when > 3.5 When scope `?$cond` (spec §13)
chunks.text:
- A when condition does not gate the ASSIGNMENT itself (there is no enable in the generated combinational logic implied by the spec); it declares that the result is meaningless unless the condition holds. Pipesignals "are invalid when any of their 'when' scopes are not true. This means they cannot be consumed by a valid statement." (spec §16.1).
- State signals interact with when: "These retain their state over invalid transactions, or specifically, when any containing 'when' clauses are not all true." (spec §16.1). So `?$valid` around `$Count <= $Count + 1;` yields a counter that holds when `$valid` is low. This is the one place where the when condition DOES change generated logic (a recirculating enable on the state flop).
- `?*sv_sig` conditions on a raw HDL signal; the line containing it holds a `*` reference and therefore needs `!` under §6.

chunks.heading: TL-X 1d (TL-Verilog) Language Specification: Structured Study Notes > 3. Scope: pipelines, stages, hierarchy, when > 3.6 Source scope `\source` (spec §14)
chunks.text:
### 3.6 Source scope `\source` (spec §14)
- Form: `\source <file> <line>` as a scope line; "this line and its contained TLV code came from the given source file and line number" (spec §14).
- "the line number identifies the source line that produced the '\source' line. These lines are not counted when reporting line numbers in error messages. It is expected that the line that ends this scope is the first that is no longer from the specified source file." (spec §14).
- Multiple nesting levels are allowed for nested macro instantiation (spec §14). The reference card lists `\end_source // Goes with \source` (NOT IN SPEC).
- This exists purely so preprocessors (M4) can map errors back; hand-written code never needs it (spec §14).

---

## 4. Signals, references, alignment, and transaction flow

### 4.1 Signal identifier types (spec §16.1)
- `$my_sig`: pipesignal. "Pipesignals can be thought of as fields of a transaction. The type of a pipesignal can be a single bit (with no range), a vector of bits (with a range), or an HDL type" (spec §16.1).
- `$MyState`: state signal. "State signals hold values between transactions. These retain their state over invalid transactions ... They should generally be assigned a value upon reset. State signals must be assigned with an explicit alignment or by <=." (spec §16.1).
- `*MyHDL_sig`: HDL signal. "A line containing an HDL signal reference must be marked as impure, because it cannot be safely retimed" (spec §16.1).
- `$$dest_sig`: "A pipesignal that is explicitly an assigned signal. Use of these identifiers is not required for common form assignments but is required in other assignments." (spec §16.1).
- `**HDL_type`: an HDL type name used for declaring a pipesignal's type (spec §16.2).

chunks.heading: TL-X 1d (TL-Verilog) Language Specification: Structured Study Notes > 4. Signals, references, alignment, and transaction flow > 4.2 Assigned versus used (spec §16.3)
chunks.text:
### 4.2 Assigned versus used (spec §16.3)
- "A TL-X processor must be able to determine which pipesignals are produced (aka assigned) and which are consumed (aka used). (The distinction is not necessary for HDL signal references (*HDL_sig).)" (spec §16.3).
- "The signal identifier $$sig, explicitly references $sig as assigned. This syntax must be used for all assigned signals in all assignment forms except the common form" (spec §16.3). Observed uses: `casez` branches inside `\always_comb` (`op_add: $$aluop[3:0] = alu_add;`), module instantiation output ports (`.f($$rslt[15:0])`), array writes in `\SV_plus` (`/bank[$bank]/entry[$entry]/trans2$$ANY = /trans$ANY;`).
- "There must generally be exactly one assignment for every pipesignal. In situations where a pipesignal must be used in multiple places as an assignment, one of those places can be chosen to represent the assignment, and the others can safely be treated as uses. Within an assignment block multiple assignments to the same signal may be used, but each must specify the same signal type." (spec §16.3). Observed: `$$aluop[3:0]` on the first `casez` arm, plain `$aluop` on the others (`makerchip_tutorial.tlv`). Note the range `[3:0]` is given only on the `$$` occurrence.
- "Generally, the single assignment (or in rare cases, multiple assignments) specifies the type of the signal." (spec §16.3). Type is declared at the assignment, never at a use.
- "a bit range may be provided immediately following the assigned signal identifier (with no intervening whitespace). If no HDL type or range is specified, the signal is a single bit." (spec §16.3). So `$pc[15:0] = ...;` declares a 16-bit vector and `$valid = ...;` declares 1 bit. A use never carries a declaration range; `$pc[7:0]` in an expression is a bit-select.
- Assigned pipesignals (left-hand side or `$$sig`) "have the scope of the assignment and must have an empty path" (spec §16.4). One cannot write `/other$x = ...;` in TL-X assignment syntax. NOT IN SPEC; observed: `array2d_example.tlv` comments "TLV assignment syntax prohibits assignment outside of it's own scope, but \SV_plus does not." and then writes `/bank[$bank]/entry[$entry]/trans2$$ANY = /trans$ANY;` inside `\SV_plus`; `mini_cpu_1_cyc.tlv` does `/mem[/src[2]$value[4:0]]<<1$$Word[11:0] = /src[1]$value;` inside `\always_comb`.

chunks.heading: TL-X 1d (TL-Verilog) Language Specification: Structured Study Notes > 4. Signals, references, alignment, and transaction flow > 4.3 Pipesignal reference syntax (spec §16.4)
chunks.text:
### 4.3 Pipesignal reference syntax (spec §16.4)
- Simplest: `$sig` "refers to a pipesignal in the same scope" (spec §16.4).
- Full form example (spec §16.4, verbatim):

```
/scope|pipe/instr[2]<<2$addr[12:6]
```

chunks.heading: TL-X 1d (TL-Verilog) Language Specification: Structured Study Notes > 4. Signals, references, alignment, and transaction flow > 4.3 Pipesignal reference syntax (spec §16.4)
chunks.text:
- Grammar as a left-to-right string of identifiers with no separators (spec §16.1 References): `[path][alignment]$signal[bitrange]` where path is a sequence of `/hier[index]` and `|pipe` identifiers and alignment is one of `>>N`, `<<N`, `<>0`.
- Path resolution (spec §16.4): "The first identifier of the path (if the path is not empty) refers to any parent hierarchy level of the assignment's scope (each of which is required to have a unique identifier) or to a child scope. Top level scope has an implicit identifier '/top'. Subsequent path identifiers identify child scope instances."
- So paths are NOT relative in the file-system sense; the first element jumps to ANY ancestor by name (because ancestors have unique names, spec §10) or to a direct child, and everything after that descends. There is no `..`. From inside `/top/bank[*]/entry[*]/trans3` under `|wr`, the reference `|wr/trans$ANY` goes up to the ancestor pipeline `|wr` and down into its child `/trans` (observed `array2d_example.tlv`).
- Ancestor jump for pipelines: the spec's rule says "parent hierarchy level", and observed code jumps to ancestor PIPELINES too (`|wr$wr_en` from within `|wr/bank[*]/entry[*]/trans3`, and `|fetch/instr>>3$Pc` from top level in `mini_cpu_1_cyc.tlv`). Pipeline is a behavioral scope (spec §9.4), so this is consistent.
- `/top` is the universal escape: `/top|exe>>6$valid_br_taken` (observed everywhere). For a signal at the module's implicit top scope, `/top<>0$reset` or `/top>>1$reset` (observed `bp_pipe_example.tlv`).
- Index inheritance (spec §16.4): "A replicated behavioral hierarchy level may be provided an index expression. If none is provided, the corresponding index of a same-named scope on the ancestry of the assignment's scope is assumed. In other words, if /scope is replicated, /scope refers to /scope[#scope]." Inside `/slice[7:0]`, the reference `/slice$carry_out` means this slice; `/slice[(#slice - 1) % M4_WIDTH]$carry_out` means the neighbour (observed `incrementer_example.tlv`).
- Index expressions in a reference may be arbitrary HDL expressions including other pipesignals: `/bank[|rd$bank]/entry[|rd$entry]/trans2<>0$ANY` (observed). The spec permits this via §8 ("may also contain TL-X signal references in situations where the HDL permits the use of signals"). Whether the processor generates a mux or an array index is unspecified.

chunks.heading: TL-X 1d (TL-Verilog) Language Specification: Structured Study Notes > 4. Signals, references, alignment, and transaction flow > 4.3 Pipesignal reference syntax (spec §16.4)
chunks.text:
- Wildcards (spec §16.4): "The right-most scope index(es) may be given as wildcards ([*]). This will reference the concatenation of all instances. This is most useful for bitwise reduction operators (& /inst[*]$bit) or for providing inputs to HDL modules that expect packed bit masks." Only the RIGHT-MOST index or indices may be `[*]`; `/a[*]/b[2]$x` is not permitted. Observed: `$value[M4_WIDTH-1:0] = /slice[*]$Value;` (8 one-bit signals concatenate to 8 bits), `| /src[*]$illegal`, `& /top/tb/ring_stop[*]|passed>>1$passed`.
- A bit range on a reference "may be interpreted by a TL-X processor to determine what bits must be made available in the consuming stage. The TL-X processor may provide more bits than necessary" and this "can be expected when non-numeric HDL expressions are used in the bit range." (spec §16.4).
- After `$object_name` any text is HDL syntax, so `$object_name[..]` is a bit-range and `$object_name\[..\]` must be used to index into an HDL array type (spec §16.2 note). Struct field access `$object_name.field1` is plain HDL text and works (spec §16.2).

chunks.heading: TL-X 1d (TL-Verilog) Language Specification: Structured Study Notes > 4. Signals, references, alignment, and transaction flow > 4.4 Alignment: `>>N`, `<<N`, `<>0` (spec §16.4, §7.4)
chunks.text:
### 4.4 Alignment: `>>N`, `<<N`, `<>0` (spec §16.4, §7.4)
- "<<2, >>3, and <>0 are examples of pipeline alignments. They are used in references to specify the numeric pipestage of the reference relative to the assignment's stage scope." (spec §16.4).
- Within a pipeline: "<< is used to reference a pipesignal of a transaction that is behind the transaction of the assignment statement. Likewise, >> is used to reference ahead." (spec §16.4). "Ahead" = an OLDER transaction that entered the pipeline earlier and is therefore at a HIGHER stage number right now.
- Figure 1 (waterfall, PDF page 18): "illustrates a reference, in stage 2, to >>1, the previous transaction, which is in stage 3." The diagram draws four transactions as rows offset one column each (transaction age down, time right); the highlighted column is one clock; the referencing transaction is at stage 2 in that column and the arrow points up one row to the previous transaction's stage 3 cell.
- Therefore, in the same pipeline, `>>N$x` used at stage S denotes `$x` belonging to the transaction that is now at stage S+N, which is the value `$x` had N cycles ago. It is the TL-X spelling of "N flops of `$x`". Observed: `$val[31:0] = ($reset || ! $run) ? 1 : >>1$val + >>2$val;` (Fibonacci, `sv_tb_example.tlv`), `$mem_resp = >>2$mem_op;` (two-cycle-later response, `makerchip_tutorial.tlv`).
- `<<N$x` used at stage S denotes `$x` of the transaction that is N stages BEHIND, that is the value `$x` will have N cycles in the future. Only meaningful for referring to a signal computed at a LATER stage in another pipeline, or on the LEFT-hand side for state (`<<1$State = next;`, see §4.7). Observed cross-pipeline: `/top|fetch<<4$instr_valid` from `|exe@5` means `|fetch` stage 1 (spec: numeric stage of the reference relative to the assignment's stage, 5-4 = 1, where `$instr_valid` is assigned at `|fetch@1`).
- `<>0` = "Naturally-aligned reference (i.e. >>0)" (reference card; spec §7.4 "Naturally-aligned reference"). Observed: `$instr_valid = /top|resp<>0$fetch_resp_valid;` from `|exe@3` means `|resp` stage 3.
- Default alignment: "A natural or zero alignment is assumed for references within a pipeline (into a pipeline by the same name) if no alignment is specified." (spec §16.4). So `$x` and `<>0$x` are the same thing within one pipeline.

chunks.heading: TL-X 1d (TL-Verilog) Language Specification: Structured Study Notes > 4. Signals, references, alignment, and transaction flow > 4.4 Alignment: `>>N`, `<<N`, `<>0` (spec §16.4, §7.4)
chunks.text:
- Cross-pipeline: "For cross-pipeline references, the terms 'ahead' and 'behind' have less meaning, but the operators are used just the same to indicate a relative numeric stage offset, and an explicit alignment is required." (spec §16.4). Thus `/top|exe$x` with no `>>`/`<<`/`<>` when referenced from `|fetch` is illegal; write `/top|exe<>0$x` at minimum. Observed: every cross-pipeline reference in the tutorials carries an explicit alignment, including `/top<>0$reset` for the implicit top pipeline.
- Same-name pipeline in a different hierarchy counts as "a pipeline by the same name", so `/top|wr$wr_en` referenced from inside `/bank[*]` under `|wr` needs no alignment (observed `array2d_example.tlv` line `$wr_en = /top|wr$wr_en && /top|wr$bank == #bank;`).
- The stage of the referenced signal is `S_ref + N` for `>>N` and `S_ref - N` for `<<N`, where `S_ref` is the stage of the assignment containing the reference. Cross-check from `makerchip_tutorial.tlv`: `$valid_br_taken` assigned `|exe@6`; referenced from `|fetch@0` as `/top|exe>>6$valid_br_taken` (0+6 = 6). `$ld_resp_valid` assigned `|resp@3`; referenced from `|fetch@1` as `/top|resp>>2$ld_resp_valid` (1+2 = 3, after the transaction has been staged, comment says "but better timing").
- Inference, NOT stated in the spec: a signal can only be consumed at or after the stage where it is assigned (for the referenced transaction). The processor inserts flops to carry `$x` from its assignment stage to every later consuming stage; a reference resolving to a stage EARLIER than the assignment stage would require future knowledge and must be an error. Every tutorial reference satisfies `assign_stage <= S_ref + N`.
- `>>-2` is "permitted" per the reference card (NOT IN SPEC) and is the same as `<<2`.
- Alignment sits immediately before the `$` of the signal and after the path: `/top|exe>>6$offset9[8]` (observed). Placing it elsewhere (`>>6/top|exe$x`, or the 1a form `$x#+6`) is not 1d syntax.
- The alignment operators are numeric identifiers (spec §7.3); the number must be literal decimal digits. `>>M4_DEPTH$x` only works if M4 has already substituted digits.

chunks.heading: TL-X 1d (TL-Verilog) Language Specification: Structured Study Notes > 4. Signals, references, alignment, and transaction flow > 4.5 "Alignment" versus "staging"
chunks.text:
### 4.5 "Alignment" versus "staging"
- The spec does not define either word formally. Usage in the text: "alignment" is the `>>N`/`<<N`/`<>0` operator on a REFERENCE (spec §7.4, §16.4, §1.3, §1.4); "staging" is what the processor does to bits to make them "available in the consuming stage" (spec §8, §16.4).
- Working definitions consistent with the spec: staging is implicit and automatic (a signal assigned at `@1` and read at `@3` in the same pipeline is carried by two flops the processor generates); alignment is the explicit operator that says "look at a different transaction than mine" (same pipeline) or "map my stage number onto yours with this offset" (cross-pipeline).
- Corollary for converters: a Verilog `always_ff q <= d;` register becomes EITHER a stage boundary (assign `$d` at `@N`, use `$d` at `@N+1`) OR an explicit `>>1$d` reference at the same stage. Both produce one flop. The first expresses pipeline flow; the second expresses a feedback/history read. A register in a feedback loop (`q <= f(q)`) must use the second form or a state signal (§4.7), because a signal cannot be assigned at a stage after it is consumed within one transaction.

chunks.heading: TL-X 1d (TL-Verilog) Language Specification: Structured Study Notes > 4. Signals, references, alignment, and transaction flow > 4.6 `*HDL_signal` references (spec §6, §16.1, §15.2)
chunks.text:
### 4.6 `*HDL_signal` references (spec §6, §16.1, §15.2)
- `*name` reads or writes an SV signal declared in an `\SV` region (module ports, `logic` declarations) (spec §16.1). It requires `!` on the line (spec §6, §16.1).
- Assigning an SV signal from TL-X: the spec's §2.3 example writes `*arith_err_u104H[inst] = ...;` as a common-form assignment, and §15 says an assignment statement may begin with `*`. Observed: `*passed = *cyc_cnt > 40;`, `*val = $val;`. AMBIGUOUS: §15.2 says a line beginning with `*` is expected to carry an HDL TYPE declaration (`**type $sig = ...`), and never mentions `*sig = ...`; the example in §2.3 shows it works. The processor evidently distinguishes `*` (signal) from `**` (type) by the sigil.
- `*sig[idx]` in the spec example (`*opcode_u101H[inst]`) is an HDL array index in HDL text, where `inst` is presumably an HDL-visible loop/generate index produced for the replicated `/inst` scope. The spec does not explain how `inst` becomes visible in HDL; treat that example as illustrative only. The safe spelling inside TL-X for the replication index is `#inst`.
- A `*sig` reference has no stage semantics: it is the raw SV wire at whatever stage the line sits in. That is exactly why moving the line to another stage "will have an impact on functionality" (spec §6).
- `?*HDL_signal` may be used as a when condition (spec §13).
- `\SV_plus` regions and `*` references are the two directions of SV integration; `$$sig` inside `\SV_plus` is how SV logic drives a pipesignal (spec §15.3, §16.3).

chunks.heading: TL-X 1d (TL-Verilog) Language Specification: Structured Study Notes > 4. Signals, references, alignment, and transaction flow > 4.7 State signals `$Name` and the `<=` / `<<1` idiom (spec §16.1, §7.4; reference card)
chunks.text:
### 4.7 State signals `$Name` and the `<=` / `<<1` idiom (spec §16.1, §7.4; reference card)
- A state signal is any `$`-prefixed CamelCase identifier: `$Val`, `$Cnt`, `$FetchPending`, `$CycCnt` (spec §7.4 `$StateSignal`, §16.1).
- "State signals must be assigned with an explicit alignment or by <=." (spec §16.1). Two equivalent forms, both observed:

```
   $Val[15:0] <= $reset ? 1 : $Val + >>1$Val;            // fibonacci_state_example.tlv
   <<1$StorePending = $next_store_pending;               // makerchip_tutorial.tlv
```

- Concatenated LHS mixing state and pipesignals (observed `makerchip_tutorial.tlv`):

```
         {<<1$FetchPending,
          <<1$LoadPending,
          $next_store_pending} =
            $reset || $mem_resp        ? 3'b000 :
            /top|fetch<>0$instr_valid  ? 3'b100 :
            /top|exe>>4$valid_ld       ? 3'b010 :
            /top|exe>>5$valid_st       ? 3'b001 :
                                         {$FetchPending, $LoadPending, $StorePending};  // $RETAIN
```

- Reading the idiom: on the RHS, `$Val` is the CURRENT value (this cycle); `<<1$Val = expr` or `$Val <= expr` assigns the NEXT value (the transaction one behind, that is next cycle); `>>1$Val` on the RHS is the value one cycle EARLIER than current. In Fibonacci, `$Val + >>1$Val` = current + previous.
- The reference card states the LHS forms exactly: `"$sig ="`, `"{$sig, ...} ="`, and `"$$Sig <="` (NOT IN SPEC; `reference_card.tlv`). The `$$` on the `<=` form is optional in common form (spec §16.1 says `$$` "is not required for common form assignments").
- Inside `\always_comb` or `\SV_plus` blocks the `<=` form is not available; use `<<1$$State = ...;`. Observed comment in `mini_cpu_1_cyc.tlv`: "<<1 because no <= support in this context. (This limitation will be lifted.)".
- State signals "should generally be assigned a value upon reset" (spec §16.1); the tutorials always write `$X <= $reset ? INIT : ...;` or `... *reset ? ... :`.
- State signals hold across invalid transactions: inside `?$valid`, a state assignment only takes effect when valid (spec §16.1). Pipesignals under `?$valid` simply become invalid.
- A pipesignal `$foo` (lower case) assigned with `<=` is not covered by the spec; AMBIGUOUS, do not do it. A state signal assigned with plain `=` and no alignment violates "must be assigned with an explicit alignment or by <=".

chunks.heading: TL-X 1d (TL-Verilog) Language Specification: Structured Study Notes > 4. Signals, references, alignment, and transaction flow > 4.8 `$RETAIN` (spec §16.5)
chunks.text:
### 4.8 `$RETAIN` (spec §16.5)
- "$RETAIN can be used as a used signal in an assignment. It translates to the single destination signal delayed by one cycle. It can be used to retain/recirculate the previous value of the signal." (spec §16.5).
- It is a keyword (upper case `$` identifier, spec §7.4) and requires that the assignment have exactly one destination ("the single destination signal"); a concatenated LHS cannot use `$RETAIN`, which is why the concatenation example above spells the recirculation out by hand and comments `// $RETAIN`.
- `$x = cond ? new : $RETAIN;` is therefore the same as `$x = cond ? new : >>1$x;`. Observed: `$pc[15:0] = $reset ? 16'b0 : (...) ? ... : $RETAIN;` and `$ir[15:0] = $instr_valid ? /top|resp<>0$mem_rdata : $RETAIN;`.
- Note `$RETAIN` on a PIPESIGNAL creates a feedback flop on a pipesignal without making it a state signal. The spec permits this.

chunks.heading: TL-X 1d (TL-Verilog) Language Specification: Structured Study Notes > 4. Signals, references, alignment, and transaction flow > 4.9 `$ANY` and transaction flow (NOT IN SPEC)
chunks.text:
### 4.9 `$ANY` and transaction flow (NOT IN SPEC)
- `$ANY` does not appear anywhere in the spec text. The reference card lists it under keywords: `$ANY // Any signal in the scope; used to create transaction flow`.
- Observed semantics from `stall_example.tlv`, `bp_pipe_example.tlv`, `dac_2020_ring.tlv`, `array2d_example.tlv`: `$ANY = <ref>$ANY;` in scope S at stage N declares that every pipesignal consumed in S that is not assigned in S is pulled, by name, from the referenced scope at the aligned stage. It is a bulk "copy the transaction" statement; a conditional `$ANY = sel ? /a$ANY : /b$ANY;` muxes whole transactions.

```
   |calc2
      @0
         $ANY = /top|calc3>>1$stall ? >>1$ANY : /top|calc1>>1$ANY;
```

- `$$ANY` (in `\SV_plus`, `array2d_example.tlv`) and `$$^ANY` (reference card) are the assigned-side spellings. `/trans$ANY` and `|wr/trans$ANY` show `$ANY` taking a full path and alignment like any signal.
- Because `$ANY` only pulls signals that are USED downstream, tutorials add `` `BOGUS_USE($data1 $data2) `` to force signals through (observed comments "Pull transaction through."). This is a Makerchip macro, not TL-X.

chunks.heading: TL-X 1d (TL-Verilog) Language Specification: Structured Study Notes > 4. Signals, references, alignment, and transaction flow > 4.10 HDL types on pipesignals (spec §16.2)
chunks.text:
### 4.10 HDL types on pipesignals (spec §16.2)
- "Pipesignals can have datatypes from the targeted HDL, either user-defined structure types or built-in HDL types. The type of a pipesignal may be declared in a type declaration statement, or along with an assignment. The HDL type is prefixed with '**'." (spec §16.2).
- "A type declaration statement may be outside of stage scope, but must be within a pipeline." (spec §16.2). It is the one statement kind allowed directly under `|pipe` without `@`.
- "Before declaring an instance with an HDL type within TL-X context, the type must be defined within HDL context." (spec §16.2). Verbatim spec example:

```
\SV
   typedef struct {
      node field1;
      node field2;
   } struct_name;

\TLV
   |Pipeline
      **struct_name $object_name; // type declaration statement
```

- Declaration inside an assignment (spec §16.2):

```
\TLV
   |Pipeline
      @2
         **struct_name $object_name.field1 = ...;  // assignment statement
         $object_name.field2 = ...;  // assignment statement
```

- In common form, `**type` is followed by "a single space, prior to the '$' of the assigned signal" (spec §15.2).
- "HDL types ... cannot be specified within assignment blocks, and can be specified separately." (spec §16.3). So inside `\always_comb` / `\SV_plus` you cannot write `**t $$x = ...`; declare `**t $x;` under the pipeline first.
- Multiple field assignments to one struct-typed pipesignal are the "rare cases" of multiple assignments (spec §16.3); the example shows the type on the first only.

---

chunks.heading: TL-X 1d (TL-Verilog) Language Specification: Structured Study Notes > 5. Assignment statements and blocks
chunks.text:
## 5. Assignment statements and blocks

### 5.1 General (spec §15, §15.1)
- "Assignment statements and assignment blocks (or just 'assignments') are the leaves of the parse tree. They define logic. They utilize HDL syntax for logic expressions, but use TL-X signal references ($sig) in place of HDL signals. A TL-X processor need not parse the HDL expression syntax." (spec §15).
- "All assignment statements begin with a '$', '%', or '*' character." (spec §15). (`%` is vestigial, see §0.3.) Observed additional first characters that the spec does not list: `{` for concatenated LHS (`{<<1$FetchPending, ...} =`), `<` for `<<1$State =`, a module name for instantiation (`regfile rf(...)`), a backtick or `m4_`/`m5_` for macros. AMBIGUOUS; the spec's sentence is narrower than practice.
- Three permitted forms (spec §15, verbatim):

```
1. Common form: "$foo = $bar;" (or "$foo <= $bar;" for TL-VHDL)
2. HDL_plus form:
      \HDL_plus
         <HDL code with pipesignal references>
3. Sequential form (TL-V only):
      \always_comb
         <SystemVerilog always_comb body with pipesignal references>
```

- In TL-Verilog `\HDL_plus` is spelled `\SV_plus` (spec §5.2 names it as a keyword; observed in `div_example.tlv`, `array2d_example.tlv`).
- Escape character (spec §15.1): "'$display' in SystemVerilog context might be undesirably interpreted as a pipesignal, so '\$display' can be used for the SystemVerilog display task and '\%d' for print formatting." Observed: `\$display("Cyc: \%d, \%d / \%d = b0.\%4h (0.\%4h)", $CycCnt, $aa, $bb, ...)`. The `\` "is dropped in translation" (spec §15.2).
- Every SV system task (`$display`, `$random`, `$clog2`, `$bits`, `$signed`, `$size`) and every `%` format inside TL-X context must be escaped. Note `$random()` and `$bits(...)` appear unescaped only in `\SV` regions of the tutorials.

chunks.heading: TL-X 1d (TL-Verilog) Language Specification: Structured Study Notes > 5. Assignment statements and blocks > 5.2 Common form (spec §15.2)
chunks.text:
### 5.2 Common form (spec §15.2)
- "The common assignment form (form 1.) has an explicit left-hand side. Signal references on the left-hand side are recognized as assigned without the need for '$$'." (spec §15.2).
- "'=' ('<=' for TL-VHDL) with conformant whitespace on both sides separates left-hand and right-hand sides." (spec §15.2). `$a=$b;` without spaces is not conformant. Multi-line RHS is fine because continuation lines only need deeper indentation (spec §15).
- "The left-hand and right-hand sides are interpreted as HDL syntax." (spec §15.2). Anything Verilog allows in an expression works: ternaries, concatenation `{{7{...}}, ...}`, reductions `| $rslt[14:0]`, `**`, function calls (`sqrt($cc_sq)`), enum literals (`op_add`), sized literals.
- "For TL-Verilog, 'assign', 'always_comb', 'begin', and 'end' are not required." (spec §15.2). Common form is combinational; the semicolon is kept.
- Concatenated LHS `{$a, $b} = expr;` is listed by the reference card as an LHS form (NOT IN SPEC) and observed with mixed state/pipesignals and ranges declared inline (`{<<1$FetchPending, <<1$LoadPending, $next_store_pending} =`).
- Module instantiation inside a stage is written as plain HDL text with `$` inputs and `$$` outputs (observed `makerchip_tutorial.tlv`); the spec only says instantiations "can be made from within the TL-X code" (spec §2.1):

```
      @4
         regfile rf(.clk(*clk),
                    .load(/top|resp<<1$ld_resp_valid),
                    .in(...),
                    .src_a($src1),
                    .src_b($src2),
                    .dest($dest),
                    .reg_a($$reg_a[15:0]),
                    .reg_b($$reg_b[15:0]));
```

- Per spec §6, that instantiation line contains `*clk` and should carry `!`; the tutorial omits it.

chunks.heading: TL-X 1d (TL-Verilog) Language Specification: Structured Study Notes > 5. Assignment statements and blocks > 5.3 `\SV_plus` block (spec §15.3, §5.2)
chunks.text:
### 5.3 `\SV_plus` block (spec §15.3, §5.2)
- "The HDL_plus assignment form (form 2.) can be used for any HDL expressions. Lines of the body must be indented at least three additional spaces. The body is simply a block of HDL code that can contain TL-X signal references. It does not inherently distinguish produced signals from consumed signals, so produced signals must have a '$$' prefix." (spec §15.3).
- The body is raw SV: `always_ff @(posedge clk)`, `always_comb`, `if`/`begin`/`end`, `$display` (escaped) all appear in observed blocks (`div_example.tlv`, `array2d_example.tlv`).
- As a block under `|pipe@N`, references are resolved relative to that scope (the block "can contain TL-X signal references"); as a top-level REGION, references are relative to `|none@0` (spec §5.2).
- Because it is HDL, `always_ff` inside `\SV_plus` creates a real flop that TL-X does not know about; the pipesignal it writes (`$$x`) appears to TL-X as assigned in that stage. Retiming such a block changes behaviour, which is the §6 rationale for `!`.
- `\SV_plus` is the escape hatch for: array writes (`/mem[idx]<<1$$Word = ...`), non-blocking SV constructs, `$display` monitors, and assignment into another scope (array2d comment).

chunks.heading: TL-X 1d (TL-Verilog) Language Specification: Structured Study Notes > 5. Assignment statements and blocks > 5.4 `\always_comb` block (spec §15.4)
TL-X 1d (TL-Verilog) Language Specification: Structured Study Notes > 6. Macros and preprocessing (brief; the Macros Guide covers detail)
chunks.text:
## 6. Macros and preprocessing (brief; the Macros Guide covers detail)

- The spec says only: many features "can be accomplished with standard macro preprocessors, such as M4", and provides `\source` so errors map back (spec §14). Nothing about `m4_`, `m5_`, `\TLV name(...)`, or `m4+` is in the spec.
- NOT IN SPEC; observed conventions:
  - `\m4_TLV_version 1d: tl-x.org` / `\m5_TLV_version 1d: tl-x.org` selects M4 or M5 preprocessing (every tutorial).
  - `m4_makerchip_module` / `m5_makerchip_module` in an `\SV` region expands to the `module top(...)` header with `clk`, `reset`, `cyc_cnt`, `passed`, `failed`, plus random stimulus support; the file then ends with `endmodule` in `\SV` (`default.tlv`, `sv_template.tlv`).
  - `m4_include_url(['https://...'])`, `m4_define(M4_WIDTH, 8)`, `m4_define_hier(['M4_ENTRY'], 4)` (defines `/M4_ENTRY_HIER`, `M4_ENTRY_RANGE`, `M4_ENTRY_INDEX_MAX`), `m4_rand($sig, hi, lo)` (random stimulus assigning `$sig[hi:lo]`), `m4_eval(expr)`.
  - A TLV macro definition is a `\TLV name(params)` region whose body is the template, with parameters typed by sigil: `/_name` (hierarchy), `#_size` (integer), `|pipe`, `@stage`, `$sig`, plain `_text`. Instantiated with `m4+name(args)` or `m5+name(args)` at the desired scope depth:

```
\TLV ring(/_name, #_size)
   /_name
      /port[*]
         |ring
            @1
               ...
\TLV
   m4+ring(/my_ring, 4)
```

  - `\TLV reference_card()` and `\TLV stall_pipeline()` show zero-arg macros; `stall_example.tlv` instantiates `m4+stall_pipeline()` and then REENTERS `|calc2` and `|calc3` in the same `\TLV` region to add stage-1 logic, which works only because scope is reentrant (spec §9.3).
  - `\viz_js` is a block keyword (like `\SV_plus`) whose indented body is JavaScript for Makerchip's visualisation; it sits under a scope (`/_name` then `\viz_js`, or under `@1`) and can reference `#index` values textually (`dac_2020_ring.tlv`). Ignore for conversion.
  - `` `BOGUS_USE(...) `` is a Makerchip-provided SV macro to mark signals as used; per spec §6 a line with a macro needs `!`, the tutorials omit it.

---

chunks.heading: TL-X 1d (TL-Verilog) Language Specification: Structured Study Notes > 7. SV integration summary (spec §5, §6, §15.3, §16)
chunks.text:
## 7. SV integration summary (spec §5, §6, §15.3, §16)

- Direction SV to TLV: write `$sig = *sv_sig;` on an impure line (spec §6, §16.1). Convention in every tutorial: `$reset = *reset;` as the first TLV line; the spec gives `$reset` no special meaning, it is an ordinary pipesignal.
- Direction TLV to SV: `*sv_sig = $sig;` on an impure line (spec §2.3 example, §15). The SV signal must already be declared in an `\SV` region (module output or `logic`).
- Direction SV logic driving TLV: `\SV_plus` region or block with `$$sig` on the produced side (spec §15.3, §16.3).
- Stage of SV boundary: `\SV_plus` REGIONS are `|none@0` (spec §5.2). A `*sig` reference inside `|p@N` has no staging applied to it; it is the SV wire as-is (spec §6 rationale). To sample an SV input at a specific stage, assign it to a pipesignal in `|p@N` (`$in = *in;` at `|p@0`) and let TL-X stage `$in` from there. This is why the tutorials bind `$reset = *reset;` at the pipeline's first stage (`|fetch@0`, `|resp@1`) and use `$reset` afterwards, or read `/top<>0$reset` / `/top>>1$reset` with explicit alignment.
- Clock: the leading `\SV` region "should provide the main clock" (spec §5.1). TL-X code never names the clock; generated flops use it implicitly. Module instances that need a clock pass `*clk` explicitly (observed `.clk(*clk)`).
- HDL types cross into TL-X via `**type` after a `typedef` in `\SV` (spec §16.2).
- Generated Verilog naming: the spec only promises that delimited names "carry over directly to HDL" and that the processor keeps the rest of the namespace for derived names (spec §7.1), and that mixed-case (`*`) names do not transfer (spec §7.2). `verilog_pyth_example.tlv` shows the hand-copied SandPiper output for the Pythagorean example: pipesignal `$a_sq` at stage 1 becomes `a_sq_a1`, its stage-2 copy `a_sq_a2`, with `always_ff @(posedge clk) a_sq_a2[7:0] <= a_sq_a1[7:0];` as the staging flop and `assign` for combinational lines. That is one observed naming pattern (`<name>_a<stage>`), not a spec rule; empirical naming rules (pipeline prefixes, hierarchy indices, state signals) are documented elsewhere in this reference set.

---

chunks.heading: TL-X 1d (TL-Verilog) Language Specification: Structured Study Notes > 8. Semantics summary and complete rule list
chunks.text:
## 8. Semantics summary and complete rule list

### 8.1 The timing abstraction in one page (spec-grounded where possible)
- A TL-Verilog module body is a set of pipelines (`|p`), each a sequence of integer stages (`@N`), each stage a set of combinational assignments to pipesignals (`$x`) (spec §11, §12, §15). Stage numbers are the only clock-cycle information; there are no `always_ff` blocks, no explicit clock, and no register declarations in TL-X context (spec §15.2 drops `assign`/`always_comb`, §5.1 puts the clock in the SV region).
- A pipesignal is a field of a "transaction" that moves one stage per clock (spec §16.1). It is assigned exactly once, at one stage (spec §16.3), and may be consumed at that stage or any later stage of the same pipeline with no extra syntax; the processor stages (flops) it as needed (spec §8, §16.4).
- A reference with `>>N` looks at the transaction N stages ahead (older, entered N cycles earlier); `<<N` at the transaction N stages behind (newer) (spec §16.4, Figure 1). Within one pipeline `>>1$x` is `$x` one cycle ago. `<>0` is the same transaction (natural alignment) and is the default inside a pipeline (spec §16.4).
- Cross-pipeline references map stage numbers with an explicit offset: from `|a@S`, `/top|b>>N$x` reads `|b` at stage `S+N` (spec §16.4; verified against `makerchip_tutorial.tlv`). Naming a stage in another pipeline that is earlier than where `$x` is assigned has no valid meaning (inference).
- Hierarchy (`/h[N-1:0]`) replicates everything under it N times; `#h` is the instance number; `/h[*]$x` concatenates instances; `/h$x` inside `/h` means this instance (spec §10, §16.4).
- `?$cond` marks assignments as producing valid results only when `$cond` is 1; it changes no combinational logic (spec §13) but makes state signals hold (spec §16.1). Invalid values "may not be consumed" (spec §13); what a simulator shows for them is not specified.
- State signals (`$Name`) are the only construct that carries a value from one transaction to the next by identity; write next-state with `$Name <= ...` or `<<1$Name = ...`, read current with `$Name`, read older with `>>1$Name` (spec §16.1; observed idioms). `$RETAIN` is "this signal, one cycle ago" for any single-destination assignment (spec §16.5).
- Everything else is SystemVerilog text that the processor copies through (spec §1.1, §15, §15.2), so operators, literals, functions and struct fields work unchanged, provided `$`-prefixed system tasks and `%` formats are escaped with `\` (spec §15.1).

chunks.heading: TL-X 1d (TL-Verilog) Language Specification: Structured Study Notes > 8. Semantics summary and complete rule list > 8.2 Every explicit rule, requirement, and prohibition in the spec
chunks.text:
### 8.2 Every explicit rule, requirement, and prohibition in the spec
File and regions:
- The improper syntax "must be reported" by the processor (spec §1.2).
- The first line "must be exactly" the file format line (spec §4).
- The newline on the first line "defines the newline sequence for the remainder of the file" (spec §4).
- Region lines "begin[] with a line that begins exactly as follows" (spec §5.1 to §5.3); only spaces and HDL comments may follow (spec §5.1).
- `\SV_plus` and `\TLV` regions end when indentation returns to the top level (spec §5.2, §5.3).
- HDL and HDL_plus regions "should not alter" the module context; the first HDL region "should provide the main clock" (spec §5.1).
- Non-TL-X characters "are only permitted in non-TL-X contexts" (spec §3).

Line type and indentation:
- `!` is required on lines containing `*sig`, an HDL macro instantiation (except in an LHS), or a pragma/compiler directive (spec §6).
- Scope level = 3 spaces; first level = line type char + 2 spaces (spec §9.1).
- "Tabs are forbidden in TL-X regions." (spec §9.1).
- Assignment continuation lines: deeper indentation, any number of spaces (spec §15).
- Assignment block bodies: at least 3 additional spaces (spec §15, §15.3).
- Scope identifiers "must begin their line, after indentation"; not legal after a same-line-terminated multi-line comment (spec §18).

Identifiers:
- A delimited name's first token "must begin with a minimum of two alphabetic characters" (spec §7.1).
- Tokens are letters optionally followed by digits (spec §7.1).
- Delimitation style is fixed by the case of the first two letters (spec §7.1).
- Mixed-case names begin with an alphabetic character (spec §7.2).
- Numeric identifier prefixes "must not end with '+'/'-'" (spec §7.3).
- Numeric strings are optional sign plus decimal digits only (spec §7.3).
- Identifiers with no prefix, and operators, "are not legal in references" (spec §16.1 References).

chunks.heading: TL-X 1d (TL-Verilog) Language Specification: Structured Study Notes > 8. Semantics summary and complete rule list > 8.2 Every explicit rule, requirement, and prohibition in the spec
chunks.text:
Scope:
- Scope line = identifier, optional range with no whitespace before it, optional whitespace and comment, nothing else (spec §9.2).
- Behavioral hierarchy: lexical ranges "must define a single range"; "must all specify a range, or none of them may"; one must give the complete range; others identical by string compare, `[*]`, or subset (spec §10).
- "A behavioral hierarchy identifier must be distinct from identifiers of all parent levels of behavioral hierarchy." (spec §10).
- Pipeline scope "cannot be replicated, so there can be no range expression" (spec §11).
- "there must be exactly one pipeline scope for every assignment statement" (spec §11).
- "there must be exactly one pipestage scope for every assignment statement, and that pipestage scope must be within a pipeline scope" (spec §12).
- Pipestage forms: `@<number>`, `@-<number>`, decimal (spec §12).
- When condition "must be a single-bit (boolean) signal in the same behavioral scope as the when statement" (spec §13).
- When condition pipesignal's when scope "must be the same, or a subscope of that of the when statement" (spec §13; flagged AMBIGUOUS above).
- Invalid values "may not be consumed" (spec §13).
- `\source` lines "are not counted when reporting line numbers" (spec §14).

chunks.heading: TL-X 1d (TL-Verilog) Language Specification: Structured Study Notes > 8. Semantics summary and complete rule list > 8.2 Every explicit rule, requirement, and prohibition in the spec
chunks.text:
Assignments and signals:
- Assignment statements begin with `$`, `%`, or `*` (spec §15; see caveats).
- `=` must have conformant whitespace on both sides (spec §15.2).
- `**type` in common form is followed by exactly one space then `$sig` (spec §15.2).
- `\` escape is dropped in translation and makes the next character HDL (spec §15.2, §15.1, §8).
- `\always_comb` is TL-Verilog only (spec §15.4).
- Produced signals in `\SV_plus` and `\always_comb` "must have a '$$' prefix" (spec §15.3, §16.3).
- "State signals must be assigned with an explicit alignment or by <=." (spec §16.1). They "should generally be assigned a value upon reset."
- A line with `*sig` "must be marked as impure" (spec §16.1, §6).
- Type must be defined in HDL context before `**type` use in TL-X (spec §16.2).
- Type declaration statement may be outside stage scope "but must be within a pipeline" (spec §16.2).
- "There must generally be exactly one assignment for every pipesignal." Multiple assignments in a block must "specify the same signal type" (spec §16.3).
- HDL types "cannot be specified within assignment blocks" (spec §16.3).
- Bit range on an assigned signal follows "immediately ... (with no intervening whitespace)"; absent range and type means one bit (spec §16.3).
- Assigned pipesignals "must have an empty path" (spec §16.4).
- Only "the right-most scope index(es) may be given as wildcards" (spec §16.4).
- Cross-pipeline references: "an explicit alignment is required" (spec §16.4).
- `$RETAIN` refers to "the single destination signal delayed by one cycle" (spec §16.5).

chunks.heading: TL-X 1d (TL-Verilog) Language Specification: Structured Study Notes > 8. Semantics summary and complete rule list > 8.3 Reserved words and namespaces
chunks.text:
### 8.3 Reserved words and namespaces
- `\`-prefixed keywords: `\TLV_version`, `\SV`, `\SV_plus`, `\TLV`, `\source`, `\always_comb` (spec §4, §5, §7.4, §15), plus observed `\end_source`, `\viz_js`, `\m4`, `\m5`, `\m4_TLV_version`, `\m5_TLV_version`.
- `$UPPER_CASE` keywords: `$RETAIN` (spec §7.4, §16.5); `$ANY` (reference card). All upper-case `$` names are reserved for keywords (spec §7, §7.4), so a user signal may never be `$FOO`.
- `$CamelCase` = state signal, `$lower_case` = pipesignal; these are types, not conventions (spec §7.4).
- `/top` is the implicit top-level hierarchy name (spec §16.4); do not declare a scope named `/top`.
- `|none` is the implicit default pipeline (spec §5.2); do not declare `|none`.
- `^attribute` is reserved with undefined meaning (spec §7.4).
- `#name` is the replication index of scope `/name` (spec §16.4 `/scope[#scope]`).
- Because TL-X drops `assign`, `always_comb`, `begin`, `end` (spec §15.2), those words appearing at the start of a TL-X line are simply not TL-X; in practice they would be parsed as HDL text of an assignment that lacks a `$`/`*` start and therefore violate spec §15.

---

chunks.heading: TL-X 1d (TL-Verilog) Language Specification: Structured Study Notes > 9. Gotchas for Verilog-to-TL-Verilog conversion
chunks.text:
1. Two-letter minimum: `a`, `b`, `q`, `d`, `x` cannot become `$a`, `$b`; rename to `$aa`, `$in_b`, etc. (spec §7.1). Same for hierarchy and pipeline names (`/x`, `|p` are illegal; `/xx`, `|pp` or descriptive names).
2. Letters-then-digits tokens only: `data2out`, `r1w1`, `x2` (single letter) are not delimited identifiers; rewrite as `data_to_out`, `r1_w1`, `xx2` (spec §7.1).
3. No capitals in pipesignal names: `$DataValid` is a STATE signal, `$DATA` is a KEYWORD slot; a Verilog `DataValid` wire must become `$data_valid` (spec §7.1, §7.4).
4. Leading underscore names (`_tmp`) are not valid for `$`, `/`, `|`, or `*` identifiers (spec §7.1, §7.2). Rename in the SV region first.
5. Every Verilog register needs a decision: pipeline stage boundary (assign at `@N`, consume at `@N+1`), history read (`>>1$x`), or state signal (`$X <= ...`). A register in its own feedback loop cannot be a plain stage boundary (spec §16.3 one assignment, §16.4 alignment).
6. State signals must use `<=` or `<<1` on the left; `$Count = $Count + 1;` is illegal, and `$count <= ...` on a lower-case name is undefined (spec §16.1).
7. Reset is ordinary logic: there is no reset port to TL-X; write `$reset = *reset;` (impure) and fold it into each state assignment `$X <= $reset ? INIT : next;` (spec §16.1 "should generally be assigned a value upon reset"; observed idiom).
8. Every line that mentions `*sig` needs `!` in column 0 (spec §6, §16.1). That includes `$reset = *reset;`, `*out = $x;`, `.clk(*clk)`, and any `` `MACRO `` or `` `ifdef `` line.
9. Exactly 3-space indentation for scope, no tabs; a `\TLV` region ends at the first column-0 non-comment line (spec §9.1, §5.3). An editor-inserted tab is a hard error.
10. Every assignment must be under exactly one `|pipe` and one `@N`, or at the implicit `|none@0` top level; `@N` directly under `/hier` without a `|pipe` is illegal (spec §11, §12, §9.5).
11. Cross-pipeline references must carry `>>N`, `<<N`, or `<>0`; `/top|other$x` with no alignment is an error (spec §16.4). Same-pipeline references may omit it.
12. Never write a path on the left-hand side: `/other$x = ...` is illegal in common form; use `\SV_plus` with `$$` if truly needed (spec §16.4, §15.3).

chunks.heading: TL-X 1d (TL-Verilog) Language Specification: Structured Study Notes > 9. Gotchas for Verilog-to-TL-Verilog conversion
chunks.text:
13. Declare width once, at the assignment, glued to the name (`$pc[15:0] =`); never at a use, never with a space (`$pc [15:0]`), never with `logic [15:0]` (spec §16.3, §15.2). Unranged means 1 bit; a Verilog `wire [7:0] w` converted as `$w = ...` silently becomes 1 bit.
14. Exactly one assignment per pipesignal; Verilog `always` blocks that assign the same reg in several places must collapse into one ternary chain, one `\always_comb` block with `$$` on the first write, or a `\SV_plus` block (spec §16.3).
15. `assign`, `always_comb`, `always_ff`, `begin`, `end` must be removed from common-form lines (spec §15.2); `always_ff` has no TL-X form at all and must become staging or `\SV_plus`.
16. Escape system tasks and format specifiers: `\$display`, `\$signed`, `\$clog2`, `\%d` (spec §15.1). Unescaped `$signed(x)` will be parsed as pipesignal `$signed`.
17. Array-typed pipesignals need `\[idx\]` for HDL indexing because `$x[...]` is always a bit range (spec §16.2 note). Verilog memories (`reg [7:0] mem [0:255]`) generally go to `\SV_plus` or a replicated `/mem[255:0]` hierarchy (observed `mini_cpu_1_cyc.tlv`).
18. Struct/enum `typedef`s must be in an `\SV` region BEFORE the `\TLV` region that uses `**type`, and `**type` cannot appear inside `\always_comb`/`\SV_plus` (spec §16.2, §16.3).
19. `=` needs whitespace on both sides (spec §15.2); minified Verilog `assign a=b;` must be respaced.
20. Replicated hierarchy ranges must be written identically everywhere or as `[*]`; `[3:0]` in one place and `[0:3]` or `[N-1:0]` (different text) in another is an error even if equal in value (spec §10, "by string compare").
21. Hierarchy names must be unique along any ancestor chain (`/a/b/a` illegal) (spec §10).
22. Pipelines cannot be replicated (`|p[3:0]` illegal); wrap in `/inst[3:0]` (spec §11).
23. Generate loops with an index variable `i` become `/name[N-1:0]` with `#name` as the index; `i` itself has no TL-X spelling (spec §10, §16.4).
24. `?$valid` does not gate combinational logic; if the Verilog used `if (valid) q <= d;` on a register, the `?$valid` must wrap a STATE signal assignment (holds when invalid), not a pipesignal (spec §13, §16.1).
25. The when condition must be a 1-bit pipesignal in the same `/hier` and `|pipe`; import foreign conditions with a local assignment first (spec §13).
26. Relative stages `@++`/`@+=` are best avoided; emit absolute `@N` (spec §12 lists only absolute forms).
27. Alignment numbers are literal decimal digits; `>>DEPTH` requires M4/M5 substitution before TL-X parsing (spec §7.3).

chunks.heading: TL-X 1d (TL-Verilog) Language Specification: Structured Study Notes > 9. Gotchas for Verilog-to-TL-Verilog conversion
chunks.text:
28. Old-syntax leakage: `$x#+1`, `%+1$x`, `>hier$x` are 1a/1c; 1d requires `>>1$x`, `/hier$x` (spec §1.3, §1.4).
29. The file must start with the format line and end with an `\SV` region containing `endmodule` (no semicolon) (spec §2.1, §4, §5.1; the spec's own example has a stray `endmodule;`).
30. Non-ASCII characters (smart quotes, non-breaking spaces from copy-paste) are illegal anywhere in TL-X context, including scope lines and signal references (spec §3).
31. Comments after a scope identifier are fine, but a scope identifier after a `/* */` on the same line is illegal (spec §18).
32. Reading a signal at a stage earlier than it is assigned (for the same transaction) has no valid meaning; check every `<<N` and every cross-pipeline `>>N` against the target's assignment stage (inference from spec §16.4 and Figure 1).
33. `$RETAIN` only works with a single LHS destination; concatenated LHS must spell out the recirculation (spec §16.5; observed).
34. Do not declare `/top` or `|none`; they are implicit (spec §16.4, §5.2).
35. Module instantiation ports: inputs take `$sig`, outputs take `$$sig[range]` with the width declared there; the instance line is HDL text inside a stage (spec §16.3; observed).

chunks.heading: TL-Verilog Macro-Preprocessor User Guide: study notes
chunks.text:
# TL-Verilog Macro-Preprocessor User Guide: study notes

Source: `tlv_reference/text/Macros_Guide.txt` (pdftotext of "TL-Verilog Macro-Preprocessor User Guide (Draft)", RW-PP-UG v0.0.0, November 8, 2022, Redwood EDA). The document is an unversioned draft and says so: "backward compatibility and robustness may take a back seat to experimentation" (Why M5 / The Utility of Macro Preprocessing). Section names below are the guide's own headings. Where a fact comes from real code rather than the guide, it is marked **[observed]** with the file it came from. Where the guide itself is unsure it says so, and those spots are marked **[guide unsure]**.

Companion file: `03_m5_spec.md` covers the M5 language itself (quotes, `m5_var`, `m5_fn`, conditionals, loops, strings). This file covers only the TL-Verilog integration.

---

## 1. What M5 does for TL-Verilog (Introduction, Why M5?)

- TL-Verilog macro preprocessing is provided by M5, which is implemented on top of GNU M4, and is shipped with Redwood EDA's SandPiper compiler (Introduction).
- M5 "goes beyond simple text substitutions and is capable of parsing arbitrary inline syntax" (Introduction). The Verilog macro preprocessor can also be used from TL-Verilog, but the guide says M5 integration is "far more capable".
- The three stated goals are parameterization, modularity and reuse, and code construction (Introduction).
- The guide positions M5 between a traditional macro preprocessor and a programming language: the default behavior is still "echo the source code to the output", but M5 adds procedural features for the rare cases that need them (Language Tradeoffs, Best of Both).
