chunks.heading: TL-Verilog Macro-Preprocessor User Guide: study notes > 6. Procedural TLV Code Generation: m5_TLV_fn(...)
chunks.text:
## 6. Procedural TLV Code Generation: m5_TLV_fn(...)

- "Infrequently, it is convenient to generate multiline macros procedurally. This can be done to avoid the overhead of line tracking using \source and \end_source."
- "Such macros can be defined using the m5_TLV_fn macro, which follows the same protocol as m5_fn." Parameters, `...`, named args, code-block bodies all follow `m5_fn` (see `03_m5_spec.md`, Functions).
- "The resulting output text is a block of TL-Verilog code. The output text should begin with a new line. Indentation will be added such that output lines with no indentation will align with the call."
- "Functions defined in this manner are called just like \TLV-style macros, using m5+ notation. The arguments are passed into the function as for m5_fn."
- **[observed]** Real definitions (`warp-v.tlv`), all inside `\m5` regions, written without the `m5_` prefix:

```
TLV_fn(redirect_conditions, ['m5_redirect_pc_conditions'])

TLV_fn(riscv_decode_expr, {
   ~decode_expr
})

TLV_fn(instr_types_decode, ..., {
   ~(\SV_plus)
   ~types_decode(m5_instr_types_args())
})

TLV_fn(riscv_cnt10_prog, {
   ~assemble(['
      # /==================\
      ...
   '])
})
```

  The comment above `riscv_decode_expr` (`warp-v.tlv` line 1909) states the motivation: "These are expanded in a separate TLV macro because multi-line expansion is a no-no for line tracking. This keeps the implications contained."
- The generated text of a `TLV_fn` has no `\source`/`\end_source` wrapper, so Makerchip NAV-TLV cannot trace those lines back to a source line. That is the trade-off the guide is describing.

---

chunks.heading: TL-Verilog Macro-Preprocessor User Guide: study notes > 7. TLV Macro Block Conventions (reproduced in full)
TL-Verilog Macro-Preprocessor User Guide: study notes > 7. TLV Macro Block Conventions (reproduced in full)
chunks.text:
"The inputs and outputs of the logic defined by a TLV macro block can be parameters or hardcoded. It is generally best to parameterize inputs. Outputs may be parameterized or not. If parameterized, they may be assigned in the calling scope. If not parameterized, they should be assigned within the macro's scope, e.g. /_name, to avoid conflicts."

"Macros may be written to be instantiated within a pipestage, within a pipeline, but not within a pipestage, or not within a pipeline. Header comments should specify the use model."

Notes on the conventions from real code:

- **[observed]** In the `wire` example, `/_top` is passed `|pipe`, a pipeline, not a hierarchy. The `/_top` parameter is a "path" placeholder; the call site decides what scope prefix it resolves to. `pipeflow_lib.tlv` calls use `/_top` with a hierarchy (`/flop_fifo_test`) and refer to `/_top|_out_pipe>>...$blocked` inside the body.
- **[observed]** Additional sigils in use beyond the guide's list: `>>_data_delay` (`\TLV ring(... >>_data_delay, ...)`, `pipeflow_lib.tlv` line 1307) for an alignment offset. The guide's parameter grammar permits `>` as a leading symbol.
- **[observed]** Header comment style that follows the guide's rule ("Header comments should specify the use model"): `pipeflow_lib.tlv` documents each macro with `// Args:` and per-parameter lines, and the serv pilot documents `serv_rf_ram_if(/_top)` with a `// The guts of module serv_rf_ram_if.` header.
- **[observed]** The serv pilot `serv_rf_ram_if_macro.tlv` takes only `/_top` and hardcodes all signal names inside `|default @0`, matching the guide's "outputs ... not parameterized ... assigned within the macro's scope" pattern.

---

chunks.heading: TL-Verilog Macro-Preprocessor User Guide: study notes > 8. Library Inclusion
chunks.text:
## 8. Library Inclusion

General rules (Library Inclusion):

- Libraries are included by URI: local files or URLs. Applies to both (System)Verilog and TL-Verilog libraries.
- "Since these mechanisms require access to system commands and the internet, their availability depends upon the SandPiper installation and may be limited for security reasons."
- "To ensure reproducible results, it is important to only reference URLs that are trusted to contain immutable content", such as CDN links or "version control host links with specific commit IDs". **[observed]** Every real include uses a raw GitHub URL pinned to a commit hash, e.g. `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/TL-X-org/tlv_lib/3543cfd9d7ef9ae3b1e5750614583959a672084d/fundamentals_lib.tlv`; some tutorials use `/master/`, which is the non-reproducible form the guide warns against.

### 8.1 Verilog/SystemVerilog Library Inclusion

- "Some library inclusion mechanisms for M5 are under development. For now, some mechanisms utilize macros with m4_ names." The `m5_include` name asked about in the task does not appear in either PDF and was not found in any local `.tlv` file; only `m4_`-named inclusion macros exist as of these documents.
- Local header inclusion is plain Verilog `` `include ``. URL inclusion of header files uses `m4_sv_include_url(...)`, "within \SV regions and the included content should be structured to define global content."
- Protocol (verbatim):

```
\SV
      m4_sv_include_url(<URL> [, <name>])
```

- `<URL>` is "the complete URL to a raw immutable Verilog header file"; `<name>` is "an optional name to give the local file (within sv_url_inc/) which defaults to the file name from the URL."
- Behavior: "The file is downloaded into a folder in the SandPiper object directory called sv_url_inc/, and it outputs a `include line that includes this file, assuming the Verilator include path includes this directory."

chunks.heading: TL-Verilog Macro-Preprocessor User Guide: study notes > 8. Library Inclusion > 8.2 TL-Verilog Library Inclusion
chunks.text:
### 8.2 TL-Verilog Library Inclusion

- "All TL-Verilog files can be included as libraries. Library inclusion results in the inline elaboration of the included file. The resulting text from the elaboration is generally discarded, but definitions established in the elaboration persist."
- What survives: macro definitions from `\m5` regions and `\TLV` macro blocks. What is discarded: "the main \TLV region is discarded, as are \SV and \SV_plus regions. These regions however are elaborated, so they may define macros." So a library's own testbench `\TLV` and its `\SV` module wrapper do not leak into the includer (this is what makes `macro_library_template.tlv` work: it has a self-test `\TLV` plus `\SV endmodule` that vanish on include).
- `m5_show(<text>)` forces text through to the includer's output; "this is generally reserved for one specific scenario: the use of m4_sv_include_url. m4_sv_include_url outputs `includes using m5_show such that the `includes are passed along to the caller."
- Because of that: "file inclusion should be done within an \SV code region. There may be multiple lines of output, so line tracking will not be properly preserved. The impact should be minimized by beginning a new code region immediately following library inclusion calls."
- Protocol (verbatim):

```
\SV
      m4_include_lib(<URL>)
```

- `<URL>` is "the complete URL to a raw immutable .tlv library file. The file is downloaded into a file in the SandPiper object directory called m4_include_url_file.#, where # is replaced by an incrementing count, and the contents of this file are elaborated inline, possibly producing `include statements."
- **[observed]** Two names exist for the same job: `m4_include_lib(['...'])` (guide, `warp-v.tlv`, `macro_library_template.tlv`, MYTH workshop) and the older `m4_include_url(['...'])` (`tutorial/*.tlv`, `grid_network.tlv`, `flop_fifo_v2_test.tlv`). Both take one quoted URL argument. `warp-v.tlv` line 1162 also references `m4_include_url_depth` and `m4_show` internally.
- **[observed]** Local file form: `m4_include_lib(['this_file.tlv'])` in `macro_library_template.tlv` line 28 (commented usage instructions).
- **[observed]** `m4_include_makerchip_hidden(['myth_workshop_solutions.private.tlv'])` (`RISC-V_MYTH_Workshop/reference_solutions.tlv` line 33): a Makerchip-specific variant, not documented in the guide.
- **[observed]** Conditional inclusion is written within-line in an `\SV` region: `m5_if(m5_NUM_CORES > 1, ['m4_include_lib(['https://...pipeflow_lib.tlv'])'])` (`warp-v.tlv` line 1211). Inclusion from inside a `\m5` region, discarding output: `nullify(m4_include_lib(m5_warpv_includes['risc-v_defs.tlv']))` (`warp-v.tlv` line 533), where `m5_warpv_includes` is a URL prefix variable concatenated with a quoted filename.
- **[observed]** The `\SV` region containing includes typically also contains `m5_makerchip_module` (the guide's example and `warp-v.tlv` line 1213 `m5_eval(m5_sv_content())`), and the file then opens a fresh `\TLV` region, following the guide's "begin a new code region immediately following library inclusion calls".

---

chunks.heading: TL-Verilog Macro-Preprocessor User Guide: study notes > 9. Quoting rules inside TLV files (collected from every section)
chunks.text:
## 9. Quoting rules inside TLV files (collected from every section)

The M5 quotes are `['` and `']`. Full semantics are in `03_m5_spec.md`; these are the rules that matter at the TLV level.

1. Quote any `m5+`/`m5_` argument that contains a comma or unbalanced parenthesis, otherwise the comma splits the argument (`m5+` args "follow the rules of M5 argument lists"). **[observed]** `m4+flow_interface(/_top, [' |_in_pipe, @_in_at'], [' |_out_pipe, @_out_at'], $_reset)` passes a two-item list as one argument (`pipeflow_lib.tlv` line 626).
2. When a `\TLV` macro forwards a parameter that itself holds a list, re-quote it: `m4+flow_inputs(/_top, ['_ins'], $_reset1)` (`pipeflow_lib.tlv` line 116). The substitution happens inside the quotes, and the quotes keep the list from being split at the inner call.
3. Use `['']` (empty quotes) as a word delimiter so parameter substitution finds a parameter that is glued to other word characters: `full_mark_['']m4_plus_inst_id`, `$csr_['']csr_name['']_hw_wr`.
4. `\TLV` blocks passed as arguments are implicitly quoted; do not wrap them in `['...']`.
5. To place an `m5+` call within a line, hide it in a quoted body of a conditional: `m5_if(cond, ['m5+it()'])`. Unquoted, `m5+it()` would be expanded while the `m5_if` arguments are elaborated, before the condition is tested.
6. Multi-line quoted text inside a `\TLV` region: `m5_if_eq_block(m5_cond, 1, ['` newline, body lines at the same indentation as the call, newline `'])`. This is the pattern the serv conversions use (see 10.2). The opening `['` ends the call line; the closing `'])` begins a line.
7. Quoted single-line snippets inside expressions: `m5_if(m5_REG_BYPASS_STAGES >= 3, ['(bypassAmount == 3) ? '/instr$bypass_avail3' :'])` (`warp-v.tlv` line 5342). Verilog `'` characters inside `['...']` are fine; M5 only recognizes the two-character sequences `['` and `']`.
8. A quote that is not balanced within a line but balanced across the file will pass the M5 checker but misbehave; keep quotes balanced per line unless deliberately building a text block (see `03_m5_spec.md`, Quote and Parenthesis Matching).
9. Breaking M5 sugar in a URL: `m4_include_url(['https:/']['/raw.githubusercontent.com/...'])` (`flop_fifo_v2_test.tlv` line 10) splits `//` with `']['` so the `//` is not taken as a comment by an older `\m4_TLV_version` flow. **[observed, reason inferred]** Other files write `//` inside quotes without this trick, so treat it as a legacy defensive habit, not a requirement.
10. Verilog `` `define `` and string literals are pass-through text to M5; only `['`, `']`, `m5_`, `m4_`, `///`, `/**`, `**/`, and line-ending `[`/`{` matter (see `03_m5_spec.md`, Ensure No Impact).

---

chunks.heading: TL-Verilog Macro-Preprocessor User Guide: study notes > 10. Library-defined TLV helpers seen in real code but absent from both PDFs
chunks.text:
## 10. Library-defined TLV helpers seen in real code but absent from both PDFs

These come from `use(m5-1.0)` and from `fundamentals_lib.tlv` / SandPiper built-ins. Their exact definitions were not available locally (no `fundamentals_lib.tlv` in `tlv_reference/raw/`), so signatures are inferred from usage. Flagged **[observed]** throughout.

### 10.1 default_var(Name, Value [, Name, Value ...])

- `warp-v.tlv` line 317 comment: "default_var(..) allows external definition to take precedence." So `default_var(X, v)` defines `X` only if it is not already defined (for example by a SandPiper `--m5def` command-line definition). The serv pilot uses it for exactly this: `/Configuration knobs normally supplied by fev.sh (--m5def); defaults for standalone compilation.` then `default_var(cond_width_32, 0)`.
- Multi-pair form with interleaved quoted comment strings (`warp-v.tlv` line 334):

```
default_var(
  ['# ISA (MINI, RISCV, MIPSI, [TODO: POWER,] DUMMY, etc.)'],
  ISA, RISCV,
  ['# A standard configuration ...'],
  STANDARD_CONFIG, 4-stage,
  ['# Number of words in the data memory.'],
  DMEM_SIZE, 32)
```

  Arguments beginning with `#` inside quotes are treated as comments by `default_var`. This is the "macro specifically accepts comment arguments" exception the guide mentions for multi-line calls.
- Also callable within a `\TLV` body with the prefix: `m5_default_var(IMEM_SIZE, 1024)` (`warp-v.tlv` line 1698).
- Contrast: `var` (spec) always (re)declares in the current scope; `set` (spec) reassigns an existing variable; `default_var` declares only if undefined. See `03_m5_spec.md` for `var`/`set`.

chunks.heading: TL-Verilog Macro-Preprocessor User Guide: study notes > 10. Library-defined TLV helpers seen in real code but absent from both PDFs > 10.2 m5_if_eq_block(String1, String2, TrueBlock [, String1b, String2b, TrueBlockb ...] [, ElseBlock])
chunks.text:
### 10.2 m5_if_eq_block(String1, String2, TrueBlock [, String1b, String2b, TrueBlockb ...] [, ElseBlock])

- Not in the M5 spec or the Macros Guide. Usage (`warp-v.tlv` 19 call sites, serv pilot 7 call sites) shows it takes the same argument pattern as `if_eq`: pairs of strings followed by a block, chained, with an optional trailing else block. Blocks are quoted multi-line text that begins with a newline and ends with a newline.
- Exact syntax as used by the serv conversion (`/Users/hale/atlas_run/hier_exp/serv_rf_ram_if_macro.tlv`):

```
         m5_if_eq_block(m5_cond_ratio_2, 1, ['
         $wtrig1 = $wcnt[0];
         '], ['
         $wtrig1 = $wtrig0_r;
         '])
```

  with the condition variable defined in the `\m5` region as `default_var(cond_ratio_2, 0)`. An empty true branch is `[''] `:

```
         m5_if_eq_block(m5_cond_ratio_2, 1, [''], ['
         <<1$wtrig0_r = $wtrig0;
         '])
```

- Chained form with two conditions and a final else (`warp-v.tlv` line 5668):

```
m5_if_eq_block(m5_FORMAL, 1, [''], m5_IMEM_STYLE, EXTERN, [''], ['
...
'])
```

- String arguments may be quoted (`m5_if_eq_block(m5_ISA, ['RISCV'], ['...'])`) or bare (`m5_if_eq_block(m5_EXT_F, 1, ['...'])`). A computed condition works too: `m5_if_eq_block(m5_if_defined_as(RETIMING_EXPERIMENT_ALWAYS_COMMIT, 1, 1, 0), 0, ['...'])` (line 4068).
- Indentation convention: the body lines are written at the same indentation as the `m5_if_eq_block(` line itself (serv pilot, `warp-v.tlv` line 4068 onward). The `_block` suffix presumably removes the leading and trailing newline so the call line collapses cleanly; this whitespace handling is inferred, not documented. **[ambiguity]** If the output has stray blank lines, that is the reason.
- Nested `m5_if_eq_block` inside another `m5_if_eq_block` body is used (`warp-v.tlv` lines 6602-6606). Calls can be chained back-to-back on the closing line: `'])m5_if_eq_block(m5_EXT_F, 1, ['` (line 1931) so that no blank line separates the branches of a ternary chain.
- Inside a `\TLV` region, `m5_if_eq_block` bodies can contain `m5+` calls (`m5+formal()` at line 6615) and TLV hierarchy (`/fpu` at line 4082).

chunks.heading: TL-Verilog Macro-Preprocessor User Guide: study notes > 10. Library-defined TLV helpers seen in real code but absent from both PDFs > 10.3 Other observed helpers
chunks.text:
### 10.3 Other observed helpers

- `m5_makerchip_module`: expands within-line (in `\SV`) to the Makerchip top-module header with `clk`, `reset`, `cyc_cnt`, `passed`, `failed` (guide example; `macro_library_template.tlv`). The M4-era name is `m4_makerchip_module`.
- `m5+ifelse(...)`: see 5.4.
- `m5+call(m5_name)`: call a `\TLV` block by computed name (`warp-v.tlv` line 6575).
- `m5_if_def_tlv(name, then, else)`: tests whether a `\TLV` block named `name` exists (`warp-v.tlv` lines 6573-6574).
- `m5_define_hier(NAME, count, min)`: defines `m5_NAME_CNT`, `m5_NAME_RANGE`, `m5_NAME_MAX` and friends (`makerchip_examples/frog_maze.tlv` line 16 used with `m5_YY_RANGE`, `m5_YY_MAX`). The `_RANGE` / `_CNT` / `_MAX` / `_HIGH` suffix family appears throughout `warp-v.tlv` (`m5_WORD_RANGE`, `m5_WORD_CNT`, `m5_CSR_PKTINFO_HIGH`).
- `m5_align(@a, @b)` / `m4_align`: stage alignment arithmetic used inside `\TLV` bodies (`pipeflow_lib.tlv` line 629, `warp-v.tlv` 12 uses).
- `m5_repeat(N, ['...m5_LoopCnt...'])` in a `\TLV`/`\SV_plus` body (`warp-v.tlv` line 1752); `m5_LoopCnt` is the spec's implicit loop counter.
- `m4_pushdef`, `m4_ifelse`, `m4_eval`, `m4_stage_eval`, `m4_plus_inst_id`: raw M4 forms used by the older `pipeflow_lib.tlv`; the M5 spec discourages direct `m4_` use.
- `m5_asm(...)`, `m5_define_csr(...)`, `m5_binary_width(...)`, `m5_hop_param(...)`: warp-v-specific.

---

chunks.heading: TL-Verilog Macro-Preprocessor User Guide: study notes > 11. Issues (verbatim)
chunks.text:
## 11. Issues (verbatim)

"Errors or omissions with this guide as well as bugs or issues with Redwood EDA, LLC tools can be emailed to help@redwoodeda.com or filed publicly at https://gitlab.com/rweda/support/-/issues."

---

## 12. Gotchas (things that silently do the wrong thing)

chunks.heading: TL-Verilog Macro-Preprocessor User Guide: study notes > 11. Issues (verbatim)
chunks.text:
1. A within-line macro or variable whose value contains a newline breaks line tracking; the guide says "must produce no carriage returns" and gives no error. Use `\TLV` blocks or `m5_TLV_fn` for multi-line output.
2. Continuation lines of a multi-line `m5+` call must be indented exactly three spaces; other indentation is parsed as a new TLV statement, and the call sees a truncated argument list.
3. Putting the closing `)` of an `m5+` call on its own line appends a newline plus spaces to the last argument. Same for the closing `'])` of a quoted body: the newline before `'])` is part of the string unless the macro strips it (`m5_if_eq_block` appears to).
4. A `\TLV` block argument, its following `,`, and the final `)` all need exactly three spaces of indentation past the `m5+` line; the body inside the block goes three more.
5. `m5+name(...)` written inside an unquoted `m5_if(...)` argument expands before the condition is evaluated. Always `m5_if(cond, ['m5+name()'])`.
6. Parameter substitution in `\TLV` bodies is textual and word-bounded. `#_depth` inside `#_depth_plus` does not match; `csr_name` inside `csr_csr_name` does not match because `_` is a word character. Insert `['']` to delimit. Conversely, a parameter named `_in` will match every standalone `_in` token in the body, including in comments.
7. Parameter names must start with `_` after the sigil so they cannot collide with real TL-Verilog identifiers (which cannot start with `_`). A parameter named `$in` would substitute into every `$in` in the body.
8. `\m5` regions produce no output; any text a statement emits there is discarded without warning. If a `\TLV` block seems to be missing, check whether it was accidentally generated inside `\m5`.
9. Macro processing is sequential: a `\TLV` block or `\m5` variable must be defined earlier in elaboration order than its first `m5+`/`m5_` use, including across included libraries. Include libraries before the `\TLV` regions that use them.
10. Library inclusion elaborates the whole library, but only definitions persist; the library's `\TLV`, `\SV`, and `\SV_plus` text is dropped. If you rely on a library's `\SV` module header, it will not be there.
11. `m4_include_lib` / `m4_sv_include_url` can emit several lines through `m5_show`, so line numbers after the include drift. Start a new region (`\SV`, `\TLV`) right after the includes to resynchronize.

chunks.heading: TL-Verilog Macro-Preprocessor User Guide: study notes > 11. Issues (verbatim)
chunks.text:
12. `//` is not a comment to M5. A `\TLV` body line such as `// m5+old_call()` or `// m5_var(X, 1)` still executes. Use `///` (M5 line comment) to disable macro code, or `/` at statement start inside `\m5`.
13. Comments are not allowed inside `m5+` argument lists (and M5 argument lists generally) unless the macro accepts comment arguments (`default_var` does, via `['# ...']` strings).
14. Unpinned library URLs (`/master/`) make builds non-reproducible; the guide requires immutable URLs (commit IDs or CDN).
15. `m5_TLV_fn` output is not wrapped in `\source`/`\end_source`, so Makerchip cannot trace its lines to source; the output must start with a newline or the first line lands on the call line.
16. `m5_include` and `m5_include_lib` do not exist in either document or in any local `.tlv`; the inclusion macros are `m4_include_lib`, `m4_include_url`, `m4_sv_include_url`. `use(m5-1.0)` loads the M5 standard library, and is not a TLV library include.
17. `use(m5-0.1)` in the guide's example is stale; real files use `use(m5-1.0)`.
18. `m5_if_eq_block`, `default_var`, `m5+ifelse`, `m5_if_def_tlv`, `m5_makerchip_module`, `m5_define_hier` are library or tool built-ins not documented in either PDF; their whitespace and argument semantics above are inferred from usage.
19. Commas inside TL-Verilog expressions passed as arguments (`{a, b}` concatenations, `$sig[7:0]` is fine but `{x, y}` is not) split the argument. Quote them: `['{x, y}']`.
20. Verilog `'` inside quoted M5 text is fine (`['1'b0']`), but `']` inside Verilog text (for example `mem['1']`) closes the M5 quote early. Watch array indexing with `'` in TLV code inside `['...']`.

chunks.heading: M5 Text Processing Language: study notes
chunks.text:
# M5 Text Processing Language: study notes

Source: `tlv_reference/text/M5_Spec.txt` (pdftotext of "M5 Text Processing Language User's Guide", M5 version 2.0, document subversion 1, 2024, Steve Hoover, Redwood EDA, CC0). Section numbers below are the spec's own (1.x Background through 8 Reference Card). Facts from real TLV code are marked **[observed]** with the file. Constructs the serv conversions use that are NOT in the spec (notably `m5_if_eq_block` and `default_var`) are collected in section 18 and flagged.

Companion file: `02_tlv_macros_guide.md` covers `\m5` regions, `\TLV` macro blocks, `m5+` calls, and library inclusion.

---

## 1. Background (spec 1.1 to 1.5)

- M5 "is built on the simple principle of text substitution but provides features and syntax on par with other simple programming languages" (1.1).
- Version scheme (1.2): the document's major version is the language version, the minor version is the library version, and there is a document subversion. This is v2.0 of the language with the "M5 1.0 library" (section 7 heading).
- Origin (1.3): created as the TL-Verilog preprocessor, later decoupled. It is implemented as M4 plus Perl sugar processing; "Though M5 would benefit from a fresh non-M4/Perl-based implementation, I had to draw the line somewhere."
- Beyond M4, M5 adds (1.4): programming-language feel, literal string variables, functions with named arguments, variable/macro scope, minimal syntactic sugar, document generation assistance, stack traces, safer parsing and string manipulation, a richer core library, and "a future plan for modular libraries".
- "This document is intended to stand on its own, independent of the M4 documentation. The M4 documentation can, in fact, be confusing due to M5's philosophical differences with M4." (1.4)

chunks.heading: M5 Text Processing Language: study notes > 1. Background (spec 1.1 to 1.5) > 1.5 Limitations of M5 (M4 differences and limitations, all inherited from M4)
chunks.text:
### 1.5 Limitations of M5 (M4 differences and limitations, all inherited from M4)

- **Security (1.5.1):** M4 "has full access to its host environment"; third-party M5 code should be vetted or run in a container. Library inclusion by URL "enables easy execution of public third-party code, so use it with extreme caution."
- **Modularity (1.5.2):** "M4 does not provide any library, namespace, and version management facilities. Though M5 does not currently address these needs, plans have been sketched in code comments."
- **String processing (1.5.3):** M4's `m4_regexp`, `m4_patsubst`, `m4_substr` "return unquoted strings that will necessarily be elaborated, potentially altering the string." M5 provides `regex(...)` and `substr(...)` that return quoted text "for strings of limited length", but "m4_patsubst cannot be fixed (though for_each_regex(...) is similar)". There is no `m5_patsubst`; to get its effect you quote the input or ensure all text is matched and quote the substitutions. The M4 regex engine "does not support lookahead, lazy matches, and character codes."
- **Introspection (1.5.4):** "essentially impossible"; the only way to see definitions is to dump them to a file.
- **Recursion (1.5.5):** "fixed (command-line) depth limit, and this limit is not applied reliably." See `$recursion_limit` and tail recursion (section 12.9 below).
- **Unicode (1.5.6):** M4 is byte-oriented. `length(...)` returns bytes, and `substr(...)` and regexes operate on bytes, so UTF-8 characters can be split.
- **Debugging (1.5.7):** M4 maps output lines only to top-level call line numbers; no call stack with line numbers, no debugger. "Printing (see DEBUG(...)) is the debugging mechanism of choice."
- **Performance (1.5.8):** text processing only, not compute.
- **Graphics (1.5.9):** none.
- **Status (1.5.10):** next steps are "a better library system" and "Some syntactic sugar (quotes, code blocks) should not be recognized in source context."

---

chunks.heading: M5 Text Processing Language: study notes > 2. Tool (spec 2.1 to 2.4)
chunks.text:
## 2. Tool (spec 2.1 to 2.4)

- Run: `m5 in-file > out-file` (2.2). Depends on M4 and Perl; no installer.
- No configuration mechanism exists yet for the reserved syntax (2.1).
- **Ensure No Impact (2.3):** M5 passes a file through unaltered as long as the file contains no: quotes `['` `']`; `m5_` or `m4_`; M5 comments `///`, `/**`, `**/`; code blocks, meaning `[` or `{` followed by a newline, or `]` or `}` beginning a line after optional whitespace. The spec notes the quote and code-block restrictions in source context are "being removed".
- **Tool flow (2.4):** two steps, "Interpret syntactic sugar" then "Run M4", plus a minor third step that undoes some sugaring. Object files (`m5 -h`) expose the sugar interpretation; in them, quotes and commas are replaced by control characters, so they look binary.
- **Processing steps (3.10), in order:** substitute quotes for single control characters; process syntactic sugar in a single pass (strip M5 comments; process block and label syntax; process pragmas and check indentation and quote/parenthesis matching); write the file; run M4 on it.

---

chunks.heading: M5 Text Processing Language: study notes > 3. Concepts overview (spec 3.1 to 3.9)
chunks.text:
## 3. Concepts overview (spec 3.1 to 3.9)

- A macro preprocessor "processes a text file sequentially with a default behavior of passing the input text through as output text" (3.1).
- Define a static macro: `m5_macro(hello, Hello World!)`; the definition line substitutes with an empty string. Call: `m5_hello()` produces `Hello World!` (3.2).
- Parameterized: `m5_macro(hello, Hello $1!)` then `m5_hello(World)` gives `Hello World!` (3.2).
- Quotes protect commas (3.3): `m5_macro(hello, ['Hello, $1!'])`. A second level is needed if the result is elaborated again: `m5_macro(hello, ['['Hello, $1!']'])` then `m5_hello(World)` substitutes with `['Hello, World!']` ("actually `['Hello, World!']['']`") which elaborates to `Hello, World!`.
- Variables (3.4): `m5_var(Hello, ['Hello, World!'])`, `m5_var(Age, 23)`, used as `m5_Hello I am m5_Age years old.` giving `Hello, World! I am 23 years old.` "Variables are always returned as literal strings, so a second level of quoting is not required for the definition of Hello." Scoped variables are named in Pascal case by convention.
- Macro stacks (3.5): every macro and variable is a stack of definitions; the top is active; pushing and popping is normally done through scoped declarations, not explicitly.
- Code syntax (3.6): source-context syntax gets "clunky" with heavy `m5_` prefixing and single-line nesting. Code context fixes this. The two forms are equivalent (the code-block form has "a slight performance impact"):

```
m5_macro(assert, ['m5_if(['$1'], ['m5_error(['Failed assertion: $1.'])'])'])
```

```
m5_macro(assert, {
   if(['$1'], [
      error(['Failed assertion: $1.'])
   ])
})
```

  "m5_macro( enters "argument list context", where parentheses and brackets have special meaning. { at the end of its line enters code context, where, most notably, text does not implicitly pass through to the output and m5_ is implied at the beginning of each code statement (beginning its line). On the final line, } and ) exit these contexts."
- Functions (3.7): `fn(assert, Expr, { if(m5_Expr, [ error(Failed assertion: m5_Expr.) ]) })`; `Expr` is local. Functions produce result text and side effects (variable declarations, STDERR output).
- Output from code blocks (3.8): statements that produce output are prefixed with `~`: `~(Failed assertion: m5_Expr.)`.
- Libraries (3.9): "a macro library file is simply imported by its URI (URL or local file). Libraries can be imported into their own namespace (though this mechanism is not yet implemented)." The spec gives no import macro name; in TL-Verilog the mechanism is `m4_include_lib` (see `02_tlv_macros_guide.md`).

---

chunks.heading: M5 Text Processing Language: study notes > 4. Quotes (spec 4.2)
chunks.text:
## 4. Quotes (spec 4.2)

- Quotes are `['` and `']`; "a configuration mechanism is not yet available to change this". They "are recognized only when they appear in a source file and cannot be constructed from their component characters" (so `[` followed by `'` built by concatenation is not a quote). "Quotes, however, are an essential part of M5, not a syntactic convenience."
- Semantics: "Quoted text begins with ['. The quoted text is parsed only for [' and '] and ends at the corresponding ']. The quoted text passes through to the resulting text, including internal matching quotes, without any substitutions. The outer quotes themselves are discarded. The end quote acts as a word boundary for subsequent text processing."
- Inside quotes, commas, parentheses, and `m5_`-prefixed words "have no special treatment" (after sugar processing).
- Quotes as word delimiters: `Index['']m5_Index` and `['Index']m5_Index` both let `m5_Index` substitute. Shorthand: `Index\m5_Index` (section 6.4).
- Quotes also stop `m5_foo` from being recognized as sugar.
- Newlines in quoted text: "Outside of those constructs [text blocks], quoted text should not contain newlines since newlines are used to format code. Instead, the nl() variable (or macro) provides a literal newline character", e.g. `m5_DEBUG(['Line:']m5_nl['      ']m5_Line)`.
- **[observed]** TLV code violates the "no newlines in quotes" advice routinely: `m5_if_eq_block(cond, 1, ['<newline>...<newline>'])` and `macro(module_def, ['<newline>...'])` (`warp-v.tlv` line 1116). It works because quotes are just control characters by the time M4 runs; the advice is about code formatting, not a hard rule.
- One level of quotes is consumed per elaboration. A macro body that must return literal text with a comma needs two levels (`['['Args:$1,$2']']`); a variable value needs one (variables are returned literally).

---

chunks.heading: M5 Text Processing Language: study notes > 5. Variables (spec 4.3, 7.2.1)
chunks.text:
## 5. Variables (spec 4.3, 7.2.1)

- "A variable holds a literal text string." Declared with `var(...)`, reassigned with `set(...)`, read with `get(...)`:

```
m5_var(Foo, 5)
m5_set(Foo, m5_calc(m5_Foo + 1))
m5_get(Foo)
```

- Sugar: `m5_Foo` (no following `(`) means `m5_get(Foo)` (5.3).
- `var(Name, Value)`: "Declare a scoped variable." Value is optional, empty by default. Redeclaring in the same scope overrides; both definitions are popped at scope end (5.5.4 NOTE).
- `vars(Name, Value, ...)`: declare several; "values are required". Example `vars(Foo, 5, Bar, NULL)`.
- `set(Name, Value)`: set an existing scoped variable. The spec does not say what `set` does on an undefined variable. **[unspecified]**
- `push_var(Name, Value)` / `pop(Name)`: explicit stack push and pop; `pop` also pops `push_macro`.
- `null_vars(...)`: declare variables with empty values.
- `get(Name)`: "the value of a variable without $ substitution (even if not assigned as a string)". Example: `var(OneDollar, ['$1.00'])` then `get(OneDollar)` outputs `$1.00`. This is the reason variables are safe holders for text containing `$`.
- `must_exist(Name)` / `var_must_exist(Name)`: assert a macro or variable exists.
- `default_var` is NOT in the spec. See section 18.
- Naming: scoped variables and macros use Pascal case (`MyVar`); TLV libraries also use ALL_CAPS for configuration knobs (`m5_EXT_M`, `m5_WORD_RANGE`) and lower case for lib-level names (`m5_isa`). **[observed]**

---

chunks.heading: M5 Text Processing Language: study notes > 6. Declaring macros (spec 4.4, 7.2.2)
chunks.text:
## 6. Declaring macros (spec 4.4, 7.2.2) - `m5_macro(echo, ['['$1']'])`: `m5_echo(['Hello, World!'])` substitutes with `['Hello, World!']`, elaborating to `Hello, World!`. - `m5_macro(foo, ['['Args:$1,$2']'])` defines the body `['Args:$1,$2']`; `m5_foo(A,B)` yields `Args:A,B`. - Mechanics: "A macro call returns the body of the macro definition with numbered parameters substituted with the corresponding arguments. Dollar parameter substitutions are made throughout the entire body string regardless of the use of quotes and adjacent text. The result is then evaluated." - Special dollar parameters: - `$1`, `$2`, ...: arguments. - `$#`: number of arguments. - `$@`: comma-delimited list of the arguments, each quoted. `m5_macro(foo, ['m5_bar($@)'])` makes `foo` behave like `bar`. - `$*`: like `$@` but unquoted; "rarely useful". - `$0`: the macro's own name (for recursion, though `recurse(...)` is preferred). `$0__` is a prefix to localize names to this macro (discouraged; see Variable Masking). For functions, `$0` is the internal body name and must not be used for recursion, but works as a unique prefix. - CAUTION (verbatim sense): a macro declared inside another macro's body has its `$n` substituted by the OUTER macro's arguments. Do not use numbered parameters in nested declarations; use functions with named parameters or block labels. - `macro(Name, Body)` / `null_macro(Name, Body)`: declare a scoped macro; a null macro must produce no output. Example with a label: `m5_macro(ParseError,

[ error(['Failed to parse $

1.']) ])`. - `set_macro(Name, Body)`: set a macro's value ("scoped(?)" in the spec; rare). - `push_macro(Name, Body)` / `pop(Name)`: explicit push; rare. - `append_macro` / `prepend_macro` (7.4.2): append text to a macro body. `append_var` / `prepend_var` do the same for variables. "A macro evaluates its context; a variable does not." Example: `m5_var(Hi, ['Hello'])`, `m5_append_var([', ']m5_Name['!'])`, `m5_Hi` gives `Hello, Joe!` (the example as printed omits the variable name argument; correct usage is `append_var(Hi, ...)` per the signature). **[spec typo]** - **[observed]** Multi-line `macro` bodies with a code block: `macro(process_redirect_conditions, [ ... ])` (`warp-v.tlv` line 864) using `$@`, `$1`, `m5_shift($@)` for recursion over an argument list. ---

chunks.heading: M5 Text Processing Language: study notes > 7. Calling macros (spec 4.5)
chunks.text:
## 7. Calling macros (spec 4.5)

- Call form `m5_foo(hello, 5)`. In source files this is sugar that also verifies the macro exists (5.2).
- "A well-formed M5 macro name is comprised of one or more word characters (a-z, A-Z, 0-9, and _)."
- Recognition rule: in unquoted text, "without a preceding word character or immediately following another macro call", the sequence `m5_` + defined name + `(` triggers a call. Argument list is processed, `$` substitutions are applied to the body, "the resulting text replaces the macro name and argument list followed by an implicit [''] to create a word boundary, and elaboration is resumed from the start of this substituted text."
- Zero-argument calls: "Macro names should not be encountered without an argument list" (confusing with variables). Use `m5_call(macro_name)`. `m5_foo()` passes ONE empty argument, not zero.
- Names with non-word characters can only be called indirectly: `m5_call(b@d, args)`.
- `m4_` macros are available but discouraged; "Elaboration of the string m4_ should by avoided."

---

chunks.heading: M5 Text Processing Language: study notes > 8. Macro arguments (spec 4.6)
chunks.text:
## 8. Macro arguments (spec 4.6)

- Arguments are inside `(` `)`, comma-separated. "For each argument, preceding whitespace is not part of the argument, while postceding whitespace is."
- Text after `(` is elaborated sequentially (macros invoked, quotes interpreted); an argument starts at the first elaborated non-whitespace character; unquoted `(` are counted; an argument ends at "the first unquoted and non-parenthetical , or )". Whitespace includes spaces, newlines, tabs.
- Examples (verbatim; `m5_foo(A,B)` echoes `{A;B}`):

```
m5_foo( A, B)            ==> Yields: "{A;B}"
m5_foo(    [''] A,B)     ==> Yields: "{ A;B}"
m5_foo( A , B )          ==> Yields: "{A ;B }"
m5_foo(m5_foo(A, B), C)   ==> Yields: "{{A;B};C}"
m5_foo(m5_foo([')'],B),C)==> Yields: "{{);B};C}" (with a warning about unbalanced parentheses)
```

- Empty arguments: `()` is one empty argument, `(,)` is two. Prefer `([''])` and `([''], [''])` for clarity.
- Multi-line argument lists: put newlines BEFORE arguments, not after:

```
m5_foo(long-arg1,
       long-arg2)
```

  "Notably, the closing parenthesis should not be on a the next line by itself. This would include the newline and spaces in the second argument." (In TLV `m5+` calls the continuation indentation must additionally be exactly 3 spaces; see `02_tlv_macros_guide.md`.)
- Arguments are elaborated BEFORE the macro runs (call-by-value of elaborated text). To pass code unevaluated, quote it.

---

chunks.heading: M5 Text Processing Language: study notes > 9. Syntactic sugar (spec 5.1 to 5.4)
chunks.text:
## 9. Syntactic sugar (spec 5.1 to 5.4)

### 9.1 Comments

- M5 line comment `///` (to end of line) and block comment `/** ... **/` are stripped before anything else (5.1.1). Consequences: commented-out parentheses and quotes are invisible to matching checks; an M5 comment may follow the `[` or `{` that opens a code block, or follow a comma before an argument on the next line, without affecting them.
- "Whitespace preceding a line comment is also stripped. Newlines from block comments are preserved." Text right after `**/` may begin the line, and comments are stripped before indentation checking, so "multi-line block comments end with a newline" is recommended.
- To emit a literal `///` or `/**`, split it with quotes: `['//']['/']`.
- Target-language comments (`//`) are NOT comments to M5 (5.1.2): "To disable M5 code, it is important to use M5 comments, not target-language comments."
- Statement comments `/` apply only in code blocks (5.1.3, 9.6 below): a line beginning with `/` inside code context is a comment.

chunks.heading: M5 Text Processing Language: study notes > 9. Syntactic sugar (spec 5.1 to 5.4) > 9.2 Macro call sugar (5.2)
chunks.text:
### 9.2 Macro call sugar (5.2)

- `m5_foo(` is sugar for `m5_call(foo,`; the only effect is verifying `foo` exists. It also enters argument list context. Do not leave `m5_foo(` in literal text that is never evaluated. M5 "may avoid applying this sugar for common macros from the M5 core library".

### 9.3 Variable sugar (5.3)

- `m5_Foo` without `(` is sugar for `m5_get(Foo)`. Same warning about literal text.

### 9.4 Backslash word boundary (5.4)

- `m5_\foo` yields the literal text `m5_foo` without sugaring; use it in quoted text that will not be evaluated when you want the literal string.
- `\m5_foo` is shorthand for `['']m5_foo`, providing a word boundary "enabling M5 processing of m5_foo when preceded by a word". **[observed]** `m5_WORD_CNT'b0\m5_eval(m5_rslt_mux_expr)` (`warp-v.tlv` line 1943); `m5_pre\m5_if_eq(...)` (line 1757); `my_fn\m5_comma_args()` (spec 6.3.9).

---

## 10. Bodies and blocks (spec 5.5)

### 10.1 Bodies

- "Body" arguments are code to be evaluated later. Immediate bodies: `m5_if(m5_A > m5_B, ['m5_A'], ['m5_B'])` where `if` returns one to be evaluated in the caller's context. Indirect bodies: the final argument of `fn(...)` or `macro(...)`, captured for evaluation when the declared macro is called.
- A body as a quoted string: `m5_if(m5_A > m5_B, ['['Yes, ']m5_A[' > ']m5_B'])`; the inner `['Yes, ']` keeps the comma from splitting when the body is evaluated.

chunks.heading: M5 Text Processing Language: study notes > 10. Bodies and blocks (spec 5.5) > 10.2 Code blocks `[` ... `]` (5.5.3)
chunks.text:
### 10.2 Code blocks `[` ... `]` (5.5.3)

Equivalent to the above, in a code body:

```
/Might result in "Yes, 4 > 2".
~if(m5_A > m5_B, [
   ~(['Yes, '])
   ~A
   ~([' > '])
   ~B
])
```

Rules:

- "The block begins with [, followed immediately by a newline. It ends with a line that begins with ], indented consistently with the beginning line." This is an unscoped block. Scoped blocks use `{` `}`.
- "The first non-blank line of the block determines the indentation of the block. Indentation uses spaces; tabs are discouraged, but must be used consistently if they are used. All non-blank lines at this level of indentation (after stripping M5 comments) begin a "statement". Lines with deeper indentation would continue a statement. A continuation line either begins a macro argument or is part of its own (nested) code block argument."
- Statements can be: macro calls (`~if(...)`), variable elaborations (`~A`), output statements (`~(['Yes, '])`), comments (`/A comment.`).
- "Statements that produce output ... must be preceded by ~ (and others may be)." `~(...)` outputs the given text. `m5_` is implicit on statements. To call an `m4_` macro as a statement use `~out(m4_...)`.
- Equivalent sugar-free form (so you can reason about it):

```
m5_out(m5_if(m5_A > m5_B, m5__block(['
   m5_out(['Yes, '])
   m5_out(m5_get(A))
   m5_out([' > '])
   m5_out(m5_get(B))
'])))
```

  "The (internal) m5__block macro evaluates its argument and results in any text captured by m5_out." So a code block's output is whatever `out` captured, not the raw substitution text. A statement without `~` still runs; its output text (if any) is dropped.

chunks.heading: M5 Text Processing Language: study notes > 10. Bodies and blocks (spec 5.5) > 10.3 Scoped code blocks `{` ... `}` (5.5.4)
chunks.text:
### 10.3 Scoped code blocks `{` ... `}` (5.5.4)

- Within `{ }`, variable declarations (`var(...)`) are pushed at declaration and popped at block end.
- "It is recommended that all indirect body arguments ... such as those of fn(...) be scoped. Immediate body arguments ... such as those of if(...), are most often unscoped, but scope may be used to isolate the side effects of the block to explicit out_eval(...) calls."
- Example: `fn(check, Cond, { if(m5_Cond, [ warning(Check failed.) ]) })`.
- "Declarations from outer scopes are visible in inner scopes. Similarly, declarations from calling scopes are visible in callee scopes, though functions should generally be written without any assumptions about the calling scope." (Dynamic scoping.)
- Redeclaring a variable in the same scope is fine; conditional declaration is fine.

### 10.4 Text blocks `['` ... `']` (5.5.5)

- Multi-line quoted text "indented with its surroundings". The opening `['` must be followed by a newline, the closing `']` must begin a line indented consistently with the line that opened the block. Indentation is set by the first non-blank line; "All lines must contain at least this indentation (except the last). This fixed level of indentation and the beginning and ending newline are removed."

```
macro(copyright, ['['
   Copyright (c) 20xx
   All rights reserved.
']'])
```

  equals `macro(copyright, ['['Copyright (c) 20xx']m5_nl['All rights reserved.']'])`.
- "The text of the block is in source context, thus syntactic sugar is interpretted under the assumption that the text is to be evaluated." Literal text inside should avoid `m5_...(` (argument-list context), and M5 comments inside it vanish.
- **[observed]** The `m5_if_eq_block(..., ['` + newline + body + newline + `'])` idiom in TLV is a text block whose body lines are at the same indentation as the call line rather than deeper. Whether SandPiper's TLV parser treats it exactly as a spec text block (stripping the fixed indentation) is not documented; the observed effect in serv and warp-v is that the body lines come out at their written indentation. **[ambiguity]**

chunks.heading: M5 Text Processing Language: study notes > 10. Bodies and blocks (spec 5.5) > 10.5 Evaluate blocks `*{` / `*[` / `*['` (5.5.6)
chunks.text:
### 10.5 Evaluate blocks `*{` / `*[` / `*['` (5.5.6)

- A `*` before the opening quote makes the block's evaluated output the (non-body) argument. Example building an error message:

```
error(*{
   ~(['Arguments include negative values: '])
   var(Comma, [''])
   ~for(Value, ['$@'], [
      ~if(m5_Value < 0, [
         ~Comma
         set(Comma, [', '])
         ~Value
      ])
   ])
   ~(['.'])
})
```

### 10.6 Block labels `<name>{` and `$<name>1` (5.5.7)

- Syntax: `macro(my_macro, ..., <sf>{ })`. Two uses: escape out of a block to generate text, and bind numbered parameters to a specific block.
- Problem case (verbatim idea): a `macro(ParseError, { error(['Parsing of ']m5_What[' failed with: "$1"']) })` nested inside `macro(my_parser, {...})` has two bugs: `m5_What` is read at ParseError call time (masking risk if `What` is reused), and `$1` is substituted when `my_parser` is called, "with a null string".
- Fix:

```
macro(ParseError, <err>{
   error(['Parsing of ']<err>m5_What[' failed with: "$<err>1"'])             /// 2 Fixes!
})
```

- `']<err>m5_What['` acts as `']']m5_nquote(1,m5_get(What))['['`, escaping enough quote levels to evaluate `m5_What` at definition time. `$<err>1` binds `$1` to the `err` block, equivalent to `']']m5_nquote_dollar(1,1)['['`.
- The need for labels "is rare and is mostly replaced by mechanisms provided by Functions" (named parameters, `fn_arg`, `fn_args`).

---

chunks.heading: M5 Text Processing Language: study notes > 11. Contexts (spec 5.6)
chunks.text:
## 11. Contexts (spec 5.6)

Illustrative file (verbatim):

```
Copyright (c) Joe Cool           /// source context
m5_do([                          /// enter argument list context then code context
   var(Ver, 1.0)                 ///     code context
   var(Banner, ['                /']['//     code context, enters source context
       Zap™ (v']m5_Ver[')        /']['//       text (escaping to code) context
       Author: Joe Cool          /']['//       text context
   '])                           ///     exits source context
])                               /// exit code context then argument list context
File version: m5_Ver             /// source context
```

- **Source context (5.6.1):** default; passes text through. Recognizes vanishing comments, macro calls, variable instantiation, pragmas. Also the context of text blocks. "Features supported in source context are supported in all contexts."
- **Text context (5.6.2):** entered by `['` (block or inline). Adds quote parsing and matching.
- **Argument list context, called "M5 context" (5.6.3):** entered by `m5_foo(`, exited by the matching `)`. Adds code and text blocks, and parenthesis matching.
- **Code context (5.6.4):** entered by `[` or `{` ending a line (after comment stripping), exited by `]` or `}` beginning a line at matching indentation. Adds implicit `m5_` at line starts, `~` output (`~(hi)`, `~MyVar`, `~nl()`), and `/` comments.
- In TL-Verilog, a `\m5` region behaves as code context (statements without `m5_`, `/` comments) and `\TLV`/`\SV` regions are source context. **[observed]** The `m5_do([` shown above is not documented in the library section; `warp-v.tlv` does not use it. Treat `do` as an evaluate-a-block helper of unknown status. **[ambiguity]**

---

chunks.heading: M5 Text Processing Language: study notes > 12. Syntax checks, pragmas, literal commas (spec 5.7, 5.8)
chunks.text:
## 12. Syntax checks, pragmas, literal commas (spec 5.7, 5.8)

- Indentation of code and text blocks is checked (5.7.1).
- Quote and parenthesis matching (5.7.2): after comment stripping, quotes (including `[ ]` and `{ }` block quotes) must balance. Within each quote level, parentheses must balance, except parentheses in source and text context are excluded. "Within a line, '] / [' quotes may be used (including nesting) to escape from and return to the same quoted context ... thus parenthesis matching happens across the escaping":

```
~hello(']<top>m5_Name[')
m5_var(Expr, ['m5_calc(6 * (1 +']m5_Val['))'])   /// OK - both match
/// Similar, across two lines:
m5_var(Expr, ['m5_calc(6 * (1 +'])    /// Bad
m5_append_var(Expr, m5_Val['))'])     /// Bad
m5_var(Open, ['('])   /// OK - paren in text context
```

- Pragmas (5.7.3), recognized as strings after comment stripping: `where_am_i` (print quote context to STDERR); `[enable/disable]_[paren/quote]_checks`; `[enable/disable]_sugar`; `[enable/disable]_debug` (readable sugar output, continue after fatal errors); `[enable/disable]_verbose_checks`. Since bare strings would pass through, use the macro forms that elaborate to nothing: `m5_pragma_where_am_i()`, `m5_pragma_[enable/disable]_{check}()`. **[observed]** `~pragma_enable_verbose_checks()` / `~pragma_disable_verbose_checks()` bracket a function in `warp-v.tlv` line 1154.
- Literal commas (5.8): a comma in source or text context is literal and "can never have special meaning as an argument separator even if used to construct a string that is evaluated as a macro call." A comma in argument-list or code context is a separator if evaluated. Examples:
  - `m5_macro(MyList, ['A, B, C'])`: `m5_foo(m5_MyList)` receives ONE argument.
  - `m5_macro(MyList, A\m5_arg_comma B\m5_arg_comma C)`: `m5_foo(m5_MyList)` receives THREE (`$arg_comma` is a universal variable producing a separator comma).
  - `m5_macro(MyExpr, ['m5_foo(A, B, C)'])`: `m5_MyExpr()` calls `foo` with three arguments (commas are in argument-list context inside the recognized call).
  - `m5_macro(MyExpr, ['m5_\foo(A, B, C)'])`: `m5_\foo` is not recognized as a call at sugar time (the `\` disappears), so the commas are literal and `foo` gets ONE argument; same as `['m5_foo(['A, B, C'])']`.

---

chunks.heading: M5 Text Processing Language: study notes > 13. Status (spec 6.2, 7.3.1)
chunks.text:
## 13. Status (spec 6.2, 7.3.1)

- `$status` (universal variable `m5_status`): set by some macros as a side effect; "A non-empty value indicates that the macro did not perform its duties to the fullest." Several `m5_if*` macros set non-empty status when they evaluate no body. Empty means no special condition.
- "Well-behaved macros set $status always or never (and never is the assumption if no side effect is listed in a macro's documentation). Thus $status is more like a return value than a sticky flag." Check it immediately after the call.
- `else(Body)` / `if_so(Body)` act on `$status`: `else` evaluates when non-empty, `if_so` when empty. Both then set status.
- No try/catch. In `macro(...)` bodies you may need to save and restore status manually; `fn(...)` does this automatically.
- `sticky_status()`: copies `$status` into `$sticky_status` if the latter is empty and the former is not. `reset_sticky_status()`: outputs 0/1 for the original nullness of `$sticky_status` and clears it. Example:

```
if(m5_A >= m5_Min, [''])
sticky_status()
if(m5_A <= m5_Max, [''])
sticky_status()
if(m5_reset_sticky_status(), ['m5_error(m5_A is out of range.)'])
```

---

chunks.heading: M5 Text Processing Language: study notes > 14. Functions (spec 6.3)
chunks.text:
## 14. Functions (spec 6.3)

- Declaration: `m5_fn(<name>, [<param-list>,] ['<body>'])`. One-liner: `m5_fn(mul, val1, val2, ['m5_calc(m5_val1 * m5_val2)'])`. Code-block form:

```
fn(mul, val1, val2, {
   ~calc(m5_val1 * m5_val2)
})
```

  Called as `m5_mul(3, 5)` giving `15`.
- `fn` vs `lazy_fn` (7.2.2): functionally equivalent; lazy functions define themselves on first use, do not support inherited `^` parameters, and "are generally preferred in libraries except for the most commonly-used functions."
- "Unlike typical programming languages, functions, like all macros, evaluate to text that substitutes for the calls. There is no mechanism to explicitly print to the standard output stream ... Only a top-level call from the source code will implicitly echo to standard output."

### 14.1 Parameter types (6.3.1)

- Numbered: `$1`, `$2` as in `macro`, but must be listed in the parameter list. `m5_fn_arg(3)` also reads the literal third argument.
- Special: `$@`, `$*`, `$#` reflect only numbered parameters. `$0` "will not have the expected value" but `$0__` still works as a prefix. `fn_args()` gives a quoted list of numbered args; `fn_arg_cnt()` their count.
- Named: local variables in the body; "not available to the Aftermath of the function."

chunks.heading: M5 Text Processing Language: study notes > 14. Functions (spec 6.3) > 14.2 The parameter list (6.3.1.2)
chunks.text:
### 14.2 The parameter list (6.3.1.2)

Each `<param-spec>` is `[?][[<number>]][[^]<name>][: <comment>]` in that order, e.g. `?[2]^Name: the name of something`:

- `<name>`: named parameter.
- `?`: optional. "Non-optional parameters may not follow optional ones." Calls are checked for all non-optional, non-inherited parameters.
- `[<number>]`: numbered parameter; the first must be `[1]`; numbering is verified sequential; a numbered parameter may also be named and accessed either way.
- `^`: inherited; must be named; its value comes from the context of the function DEFINITION. If undefined, `['']` is used and an error is reported unless optional (`?^Name`). No call argument corresponds to it; conventionally listed last. "`$`s are problematic in inherited parameter values."
- `<comment>`: description, extractable for docs.
- `...` after the last numbered parameter allows extra numbered arguments; without it "extra arguments result in an error (except for the single empty argument of e.g. m5_foo()".

### 14.3 Which parameter type to use (6.3.2)

- Numbered/special: substitute everywhere regardless of quotes, but are awkward in nested definitions (they bind to the OUTER body) and hurt readability.
- Named: act like normal function args, readable, "work perfectly well in functions defined within other functions/macros", but do not substitute inside quotes, so text must be unquoted around them: `['Arg1: ']m5_arg1['.']` versus `['Arg1: $1.']`.
- Inherited: customize a function to its definition context (a function defining a function tailored to the outer parameters).

chunks.heading: M5 Text Processing Language: study notes > 14. Functions (spec 6.3) > 14.4 Call arguments (6.3.3)
chunks.text:
### 14.4 Call arguments (6.3.3)

- Positional; "misaligning arguments is a common source of errors." Required-argument and extra-argument checking exists. `m5_foo()` is allowed for a no-parameter function but passes one empty argument; `m5_call(foo)` is cleaner.

### 14.5 Example (6.3.4, verbatim)

```
/Context:
var(Inherit2, two)
/Define foo:
fn(foo, Param1, ?[1]Param2: an optional parameter,
        ?^Inherit1, [2]^Inherit2, ..., {
   ~nl(Param1: m5_Param1)
   ~nl(Param2: m5_Param2)
   ~nl(Inherit1: m5_Inherit1)
   ~nl(Inherit2: m5_Inherit2)
   ~nl(['numbered args: $@'])
})
/Call foo:
foo(arg1, arg2, extra1, extra2)
```

Output:

```
Param1: arg1
Param2: arg2
Inherit1:
Inherit2: two
numbered args: ['arg2'],['two'],['extra1'],['extra2']
```

Note `$@` contains only the numbered parameters (`[1]Param2`, `[2]^Inherit2`, and the `...` extras), not `Param1`. Also note `~nl(text)` here is used as "output text plus newline"; the library entry for `nl()` documents only the zero-argument newline form. **[spec inconsistency]**

### 14.6 Aftermath, by-reference, status, body args, tail recursion (6.3.5 to 6.3.9)

- "Aftermath": code a function schedules to run in the CALLER's scope after its own parameters are popped, via `on_return(...)` or `return_status(...)`. Needed for passing by reference, returning status, evaluating body arguments, and tail recursion.
- By reference:

```
fn(update, FooRef, {
   var(Value, ['updated value'])
   on_return(set, m5_FooRef, m5_Value)
}
set(Foo, ['xxx'])
update(Foo)
~Foo
```

  (The spec's example is missing the closing `)` of `fn(`; that is a typo in the document.) `on_return` avoids the masking that `update(Value)` would cause if the function assigned directly.
- Returning status: `fn(my_fn, Val, { if(m5_Val > 10, ['']) return_status(m5_status) })`. "Functions automatically restore $status after body evaluation to its value prior to body evaluation, so the evaluation of the body has no impact on $status. Aftermath is evaluated after this. It is fine to call return_status(...) multiple times. Only the last call will have a visible effect."
- Body arguments (6.3.8): evaluate the body via `on_return(Body)` so its side effects (variable sets, `return_status`) land in the caller, not in the function:

```
 1: // Evaluate a body if a value is negative.
 2: fn(if_neg, Value, Body, {
 3:    var(Neg, m5_calc(Value < 0))
 4:    ~if(Neg, [
 5:        /~eval(m5_Body)
 6:        on_return(Body)
 7:    ])
 8:    return_status(if(Neg, [''], else))
 9: })
10:
11: fn(my_fn, {
12:    var(Neg, [''])
13:    return_status(['pos'])
14:    ~if_neg(1, [
15:        return_status(['neg'])
16:        set(Neg, ['-'])
17:    ])
18:    ...
19: })
```

chunks.heading: M5 Text Processing Language: study notes > 14. Functions (spec 6.3) > 14.4 Call arguments (6.3.3)
chunks.text:
"Since macro(...) does not support Aftermath, it is not recommended to use macro(...) with a body argument." (Line 3's `m5_calc(Value < 0)` without `m5_` on `Value` is as printed.)
- Tail recursion (6.3.9): recurse in aftermath to avoid growing the stack: `on_return(my_fn\m5_comma_args())` inside `~unless(m5_Done, [...])`.

chunks.heading: M5 Text Processing Language: study notes > 14. Functions (spec 6.3) > 14.7 Variable masking (6.4.1)
chunks.text:
### 14.7 Variable masking (6.4.1)

A macro that sets a variable named by an argument, or evaluates a body that sets variables, can accidentally update its OWN local variable of the same name. Fixes by declaration style:

- Functions: set variables through Aftermath (`on_return(set, ...)`); preferred.
- Macros with code-block bodies: set variables with `out_eval(...)`.
- Macros with string bodies: push/pop locals named with the `$0__` prefix.

---

## 15. Library reference, by category (spec 7)

Conventions (7.1): integers are decimal strings; booleans are `0`/`1`; "Resulting output text is, by default, literal (quoted). Macros named with a _eval suffix generally result in text that gets evaluated." Behavior for unspecified argument values is undefined. In this list "sets status" means the macro sets `$status` empty iff a body was evaluated.

### 15.1 Conditionals (7.3.2)

- `if(Cond, TrueBody, ...)`, `unless(Cond, TrueBody, FalseBody)`, `else_if(Cond, TrueBody, ...)`: `Cond` is evaluated with `calc(...)`; non-0 is true for `if`/`else_if`, 0 for `unless`. Extra args are either a FalseBody or (for `if` only) more `Cond, TrueBody` pairs; a single trailing arg is the else. `unless` cannot chain. The spec sentence "if_else does nothing if m5_status is initially empty" appears to describe `else_if` (it only runs when the preceding conditional set non-empty status). **[spec wording]** Sets status.

```
~if(m5_eq(m5_Ten, 10) && m5_Val > 3, [
   ~do_something(...)
], m5_Val > m5_Ten, [
   ~do_something_else(...)
], [
   ~default_case(...)
])
```

- `if_eq(String1, String2, TrueBody, ...)`, `if_neq(...)`: string comparison; chains as `S1, S2, Body, S1, S2, Body, ..., Else`. Sets status.

```
~if_eq(m5_Zero, 0, [
   ~zero_is_zero(...)
], m5_calc(m5_Zero < 0), 1, [
   ~zero_is_negative(...)
], [
   ~zero_is_positive(...)
])
```

chunks.heading: M5 Text Processing Language: study notes > 14. Functions (spec 6.3) > 14.7 Variable masking (6.4.1)
chunks.text:
**[observed]** One-line source-context form is the most common in TLV: `m5_if_eq(m5_BRANCH_PRED, ['fallthrough'], [''], ['$pred_taken_branch = $pred_taken && $branch;'])`; also `m5_if_eq(['$@'], ['['']'], [''], [...])` to test for an empty argument list (`warp-v.tlv` line 865), and `m5_if_eq(['$2'],,,[...])` with empty positional args (line 642).
- `if_null(Var, Body, ElseBody)`, `if_var_def(Var, Body, ElseBody)`, `if_var_ndef(Var, Body, ElseBody)`, `if_defined_as(Var, Value, Body, ElseBody)`: test a variable's emptiness, existence, non-existence, or definition-equals-value. `Var` is the NAME (no `m5_`). The spec's `if_defined_as` text reads "not defined and equal to the given value", which is a typo for "defined and equal". Sets status. **[observed]** `m5_if_var_def(VIZ_ASM_COLS, ['m5_VIZ_ASM_COLS'], 0)`, `m5_if_defined_as(RETIMING_EXPERIMENT_ALWAYS_COMMIT, 1, 1, 0)` (`warp-v.tlv`).
- `else(Body)`, `if_so(Body)`: on `$status` non-empty / empty. Sets status.
- `else_if_def(Name, Body)`: body iff variable `Name` is defined (and presumably prior status non-empty). Example: `m5_set(Either, if_var_def(First, m5_First)m5_else_if_def(Second, m5_Second))`.
- `case(Name, Value, TrueBody, ...)`: like `if_eq` but the first arg is a variable NAME whose value is compared to each `Value`; trailing single arg is else. Sets status.

```
~case(Response, ok, [
   ~ok_response(...)
], bad, [
   ~bad_response(...)
], [
   error(Unrecognized response: m5_Response)
])
```

  **[observed]** `case(ISA, ['MINI'], [...], ['RISCV'], [...])` and `case(STANDARD_CONFIG, ['1-stage'], [...], ...)` in `warp-v.tlv` `\m5` regions.
- `if_regex` / `else_if_regex` / `var_regex`: see 15.5.

chunks.heading: M5 Text Processing Language: study notes > 15. Library reference, by category (spec 7) > 15.2 Loops (7.3.3) and recursion (7.3.4)
chunks.text:
### 15.2 Loops (7.3.3) and recursion (7.3.4)

- `loop(InitList, DoBody, WhileCond, WhileBody)`: general loop. `InitList` is a parenthesized `(Var, Init, ...)` list (at least one pair) or `['']`; `DoBody` runs first each iteration; `WhileCond` is quoted so loop variables are in scope, evaluated via `calc`; `WhileBody` (optional) runs when true. Implicit `m5_LoopCnt` starts at 0 and increments after both bodies.

```
~loop((MyVar, 0), [
   ~do_stuff(...)
], ['m5_LoopCnt < 10'], [
   ~do_more_stuff(...)
])
```

- `repeat(Cnt, Body)`: evaluate `Body` `Cnt` times, `m5_LoopCnt` 0..Cnt-1. **[observed]** `m5_repeat(m5_NUM_INSTRS, ['assign instrs[m5_LoopCnt] = m5_eval(m5_eval(m5_get(['instr']m5_LoopCnt))); '])` (`warp-v.tlv` line 1752).
- `for(Var, List, Body)`: `Var` is set to each item of the comma-separated `List` ("the last of which will be skipped if empty", so a trailing comma is harmless); maintains `m5_LoopCnt`. Example `~for(fruit, ['apple, orange, '], [ ~do_stuff(...) ])`.
- There is no `while` macro in the library; `loop` with an empty `InitList` and an empty `DoBody` is the while form.
- `recurse(max_depth, macro, ...)`: call a macro recursively with a depth cap; "Functions have a built-in recursion limit, so this is only useful for macros." Example `m5_recurse(20, myself, args)`.
- `$recursion_limit` (7.6.2): universal variable; exceeding it in the function call stack is a fatal error.

chunks.heading: M5 Text Processing Language: study notes > 15. Library reference, by category (spec 7) > 15.3 Special characters (7.4.1)
chunks.text:
### 15.3 Special characters (7.4.1)

- `nl()`: produce a newline. "Programmatically-generated output should always use this macro ... rather than using an actual new-line in the source file." Also usable as variable `m5_nl`.
- `open_quote()`, `close_quote()`: literal quote characters; "should rarely (never?) be needed" since they create undetected imbalance.
- `$arg_comma`: an argument-separator comma (see Literal Commas).
- `orig_open_quote()`, `orig_close_quote()`: produce the two-character `['` / `']` text. In the file these are translated to control characters internally; in STDOUT/STDERR they appear as single-unicode "printable quotes" (`printable_open_quote()`, `printable_close_quote()`).
- `UNDEFINED()`: a unique untypeable sentinel. `m5_var(Foo, m5_UNDEFINED)` then `m5_if_eq(Foo, m5_UNDEFINED, ['['Foo is undefined.']'])` (note the example compares the NAME `Foo`, not `m5_Foo`, as printed; likely a typo for `m5_Foo`). **[spec typo]**

### 15.4 Strings (7.4.2 to 7.4.5)

- `append_var(Name, String)`, `prepend_var`, `append_macro`, `prepend_macro`.
- `substr(String, From, Length)` / `substr_eval`: 0-based byte index; `Length` optional (to end). Empty result on parse error, `From` past end, or negative `Length`. If the result would contain quotes, an error is reported (use `dequote`/`requote`) and quotes become control characters. `substr` is slow relative to `substr_eval`. Example `m5_substr(['Hello World!'], 3, 5)` gives `lo Wo`.
- `join(Delimiter, ...)`: `m5_join([', '], ['one'], ['two'], ['three'])` gives `one, two, three`.
- `translit(String, InChars, OutChars)` / `translit_eval`: byte-for-byte substitution. Quotes can be substituted only with `translit_eval`. Example `m5_translit(['Testing: 1, 2, 3.'], ['123'], ['ABC'])` gives `Testing: A, B, C.` **[observed]** `var(isa, m5_translit(m5_ISA, ['A-Z'], ['a-z']))` for lowercasing with ranges (`warp-v.tlv` line 728).
- `uppercase(String)`, `lowercase(String)`: ASCII only.
- `replicate(Cnt, String)`: non-evaluating repeat; `m5_replicate(3, ['.'])` gives `...`.
- `strip_trailing_whitespace_from(Var)`: modifies the variable.
- `format_eval(string, ...)`: printf-style; supports `c s d o x X u a A e E f F g G %`, widths/precisions, flags `+ - space 0 # '`, modifiers `hh h l`. Not supported: positional args, `n p S C`, `z t j L ll`, escape sequences. Examples: `m5_format_eval(`String "%s" uses %d chars.', Foo, m5_length(Foo))` gives `String "Hello" uses 5 chars.`; `m5_format_eval(`%.0f', `56789.9876')` gives `56790`. (The examples use M4-style backtick quotes; that is as printed.)
- `length(String)`: bytes. `index_of(String, Substring)`: 0-based or -1. `num_lines(String)`: count of newlines.
- `for_each_line(Text, Body)`: `m5_Line` holds each line without newline.
- `dequote(String)` / `requote(String)`: swap real quotes for inert "surrogate quotes" so the string can be sliced safely, then restore. `output_with_restored_quotes(String)`: replace quotes, surrogate quotes and printable quotes with `['`/`']`. `no_quotes(String)`: assert no quotes.

chunks.heading: M5 Text Processing Language: study notes > 15. Library reference, by category (spec 7) > 15.5 Regular expressions (7.4.6)
chunks.text:
### 15.5 Regular expressions (7.4.6)

- Syntax is GNU Emacs regex (BRE-like): groups are `\( \)`, alternation `\|`, `\w`, `\s` work; no lookahead, no lazy matches, no ERE. `[` and `]` are special inside regexes even though `['` `']` are quotes.
- `regex(String, Regex, Replacement)` / `regex_eval`: without `Replacement`, outputs the 0-based index of the first match or -1. With it, outputs the replacement (`\1`..`\9` for groups, `\&` for the whole match, `\c` for literal `c`); empty if no match. Literal result for `regex`, evaluated for `regex_eval`. Example: `m5_regex_eval(['Hello there'], ['\w+'], ['First word: m5_translit(['\&']).'])` gives `First word: Hello.` (the printed example splits the replacement across a line; treat it as one line).
- `var_regex(String, Regex, VarList)`: declare variables from groups; `VarList` is a parenthesized list `(Operation, Src1, Src2)`; status non-empty iff no match:

```
m5_var_regex(['mul A, B'], ['^\(\w+\)\s+\(w+\),\s*\(w+\)$'], (Operation, Src1, Src2))
m5_if_so(['m5_DEBUG(Matched: m5_Src1[','] m5_Src2)'])
m5_else(['m5_error(['Match failed.'])'])
```

  (The spec's regex writes `\(w+\)` where `\(\w+\)` is clearly intended.)
- `if_regex(String, Regex, VarList, Body, ...)` / `else_if_regex`: chain of pattern matches, each in its own scope; more `Regex, VarList, Body` triples or a final else. Status non-null if nothing matched.

```
~if_regex(m5_Instruction, ['^mul\s+\(w+\),\s*\(w+\)$'], (Src1, Src2), [
   ~calc(m5_Src1 * m5_Src2)
], ['^incr\s+\(w+\)$'], (Src1), [
   ~calc(m5_Src1 + 1)
])
```

- `for_each_regex(String, Regex, VarList, Body)`: evaluate Body for every match "in the first line of String"; regex must contain at least one group and no `$`; `$status` unassigned. `m5_for_each_regex(H1dd3n D1git5, ['\([0-9]\)'], (Digit), ['Found m5_Digit. '])` gives `Found 1. Found 3. Found 1. Found 5.` **[observed]** Used in `warp-v.tlv` line 1757 to escape `%` in strings.

chunks.heading: M5 Text Processing Language: study notes > 15. Library reference, by category (spec 7) > 15.6 Fundamental utilities (7.5.1, 7.5.2)
chunks.text:
### 15.6 Fundamental utilities (7.5.1, 7.5.2)

- `defn(Name)`: the M4 definition (slightly different from the M5 definition).
- `call(Name, ...)`: indirect call; zero-arg calls and computed names. `m5_call(error, ['Fail!'])`.
- `quote(...)`: `$@`, i.e. each arg quoted, comma-separated: `m5_quote(A, ['B'])` gives `['A'],['B']`.
- `nquote(Num, ...)`: args inside `Num` levels of quotes, innermost per argument; `Num` 0 inlines `$@`. Examples: `m5_nquote(3, A, ['m5_nl'])` gives `['['['A'],['m5_\nl']']']`.
- `eval(Expr)`: evaluate the argument. `m5_eval(['m5_calc(1 + 1)'])` gives `2`; `m5_eval(['m5'])_calc(1 + 1)` gives `m5_calc(1 + 1)` (the boundary after `eval` prevents joining). **[observed]** `m5_eval(['m5_get(['CSR_']m5_uppercase(csr_name)['_RANGE'])'])` reads a variable whose name is computed (`warp-v.tlv` line 1783); `m5_eval(m5_sv_content())` emits a function's captured text into an `\SV` region (line 1213).
- `comment(...)`, `nullify(...)`: output nothing; discard an evaluation's result. **[observed]** `nullify(m4_include_lib(...))` (`warp-v.tlv` line 533).
- `get_ago(Name, Ago)`: read an older stack entry (0 current, 1 previous). `depth_of(Name)`: stack depth (0 before any `push_var`).

### 15.7 Argument processing (7.5.3)

- `shift(...)`: drop the first argument; result `['']` if fewer than two. `comma_shift(...)`: same but with a leading `,` if any remain. Examples `m5_foo(m5_shift($@))`, `m5_call(foo['']m5_comma_shift($@))`.
- `nargs(...)`: count. `m5_set(ExampleList, ['hi, there'])`; `m5_nargs(m5_ExampleList)` is 1; `m5_nargs(m5_eval(m5_ExampleList))` is 2 (evaluation makes the literal comma a separator).
- `argn(ArgNum, ...)`: nth argument or `['']`. `m5_argn(2, a, b, c)` gives `b`.
- `comma_args(...)`: quoted argument list to arguments with a leading comma; needed for possibly-empty lists: `m5_call(foo['']m5_comma_args(['$@']), last)`.
- `echo_args(...)`: outputs `$@`; pathological example `m5_macro(append_to_paren_list, ['m5_echo_args$1, ${empty}2'])`, `m5_append_to_paren_list((one, two), three)` gives `(one,two,three)`.

chunks.heading: M5 Text Processing Language: study notes > 15. Library reference, by category (spec 7) > 15.8 Arithmetic (7.5.4)
chunks.text:
### 15.8 Arithmetic (7.5.4)

- `calc(Expr, Radix, Width)`: 32-bit signed integer math, silent wraparound, warning on divide-by-zero or parse failure (output empty if invalid). Operators by decreasing precedence: `()`; unary `+ - ~ !`; `**` (right-assoc, non-negative exponent); `* / %`; `+ -`; `<< >>` (shift amounts > 32 masked with 0x1f); `> >= < <=`; `== !=`; `&`; `^`; `|`; `&&`; `||`. Radix prefixes: none decimal, `0` octal, `0x` hex, `0b` binary, `0r#` radix `#` (1 to 36). Output radix (default 10) and zero-pad `Width` (excluding sign), lowercase digits, no prefix. Examples: `m5_calc(2**3 <= 4)` gives `0`; `m5_calc(-0xf, 2, 8)` gives `-00001111`.
- `equate(Name, Expr)`: `Name = calc(Expr)`. `operate_on(Name, Expr)`: `Name = calc(Name Expr)`, e.g. `m5_operate_on(Foo, * (3-1))`. Example sequence `m5_equate(Foo, 1+2)`, `m5_operate_on(Foo, * (3-1))`, `m5_Foo` gives `6`.
- `increment(Name, Amount)`, `decrement(Name, Amount)`: by 1 or by `Amount` (the spec says the default is zero in one place and one in another; behavior in examples is by one). **[spec inconsistency]**

chunks.heading: M5 Text Processing Language: study notes > 15. Library reference, by category (spec 7) > 15.9 Boolean (7.5.5)
chunks.text:
### 15.9 Boolean (7.5.5)

- `is_null(Name)`, `isnt_null(Name)`: 0/1 for a variable that must exist.
- `eq(String1, String2, ...)`, `neq(...)`: 0/1; `eq` is true if String1 equals ANY of the rest; `neq` true if it equals none. `m5_if(m5_neq(m5_Response, ok, bad), ['m5_error(Unknown response: m5_Response.)'])`.

### 15.10 Within functions or code blocks (7.5.6)

- `fn_args()`, `comma_fn_args()`: the numbered arguments of the current function, each quoted; `comma_` form has a leading comma if non-empty. As variables (`m5_fn_args`) they give quoted versions. `m5_foo(1, m5_fn_args())` (needs 1+ args) versus `m5_foo(1['']m5_comma_fn_args())` (0+ args).
- `fn_arg(Num)`, `fn_arg_cnt()`.
- `out(String)`, `out_eval(String)`: append to the enclosing code block's output; `out_eval` evaluates its argument (used for side effects). `~(...)` is effectively `~out(...)`. Not recommended inside function blocks; use Aftermath.
- `return_status(Value)`: shorthand for `m5_on_return(set, status, m5_Value)`; last call wins; `Value` defaults to current status.
- `on_return(MacroName, ...)`: call a macro after the function returns (arguments as for `call`):

```
fn(set_to_five, VarName, {
   on_return(set, m5_VarName, 5)
})
fn(set2, VarName1, Val1, VarName2, Val2, {
   ...
   on_return(eval, {
       set(VarName1, m5_Val1)
       set(VarName2, m5_Val2)
   })
})
```

  (In `set2` the `set(VarName1, ...)` inside the evaluated block sets a variable literally named `VarName1`; that is how the spec prints it.)

chunks.heading: M5 Text Processing Language: study notes > 15. Library reference, by category (spec 7) > 15.11 Checking and debugging (7.6)
chunks.text:
### 15.11 Checking and debugging (7.6)

- `debug_level(level)`: get (no args) or set `min`/`default`/`max`. Example `debug_level(max)` before `use(m5-1.0)`. **[observed]** `warp-v.tlv` line 34 has `/debug_level(max)` commented out above `use(m5-1.0)`.
- `errprint(text)`, `errprint_nl(text)`: raw STDERR output.
- `warning(msg)`, `error(msg)`, `fatal_error(msg)`, `DEBUG(msg)`: report with a stack trace (no trace for DEBUG); `fatal_error` exits non-zero. Conditional forms `warning_if(cond, msg)`, `error_if`, `fatal_error_if`, `DEBUG_if` with `cond` as for `if`.
- `assert(cond)`, `fatal_assert(cond)`: e.g. `Error: Failed assertion: -1 < 0`.
- `verify_min_args(Name, Min, Actual)`, `verify_num_args(Name, Min, Actual)`, `verify_min_max_args(Name, Min, Max, Actual)`: for traditional macros, e.g. `m5_verify_min_args(my_fn, 2, $#)`.
- `abbreviate_args(max_args, max_arg_length, ...)`: shorten an argument list for messages; output is "a quoted string of quoted args with a comma preceding every arg".

---

## 16. Reference Card (spec 8, compact)

Table 1, Core Syntax (Feature: syntax; contexts; must be evaluated?):

- M5 comments: `///`, `/**`, `**/`; all contexts; N/A.
- Quotes: `['`, `']`; all; yes.
- Macro calls: `m5_my_fn(arg1, arg2)`; all except as a code statement; yes.
- Numbered/special parameters: `$3`, `$@`, `$#`, `$*`; within the outermost macro/function (not var) definition body; N/A.
- Escapes: `\m5_foo` (yes, must be evaluated), `m5_\foo` (must NOT be evaluated); all.

"Yes" means the syntax must not reach the output unevaluated. Block syntax is recognized only when the special quote opens at the end of a line or closes at the beginning of a line, e.g.:

```
/Report error.
error(*<blk>{
   ~(['Something went wrong!'])
})
```

Table 2, Block Syntax (all must be evaluated):

- Code block quotes: `[`, `]`, `{`, `}` ending/beginning a line; M5 and code contexts.
- Text block quotes: `['`, `']` ending/beginning a line; M5 and code.
- Evaluate blocks: `*[` ... `]`, `*{` ... `}`, `*['` ... `']`; M5 and code.
- Statement comment: `/Blah blah`; code.
- Statement with no output: `Foo`, `bar(...)` (`m5_` implied); code.
- Statement with output: `~Foo`, `~bar(...)`; code.
- Code block output: `~(...)`; code.

Table 3, Block Label Syntax:

- Named blocks: `<foo>` before the open quote, after an optional `*`, e.g. `*<bar>{` or `<baz>['`; M5 and code; must be evaluated.
- Quote escape: `']<foo>m5_Bar['`; anywhere within any M5 quotes; `<foo>m5_Bar` must be evaluated.
- Labeled parameter: `$<foo>2`, `$<bar>#`; within the corresponding block; N/A.
