chunks.heading: 05. The two foundational TL-Verilog papers (Makerchip LEARN menu) > Paper 1: Timing-Abstract Circuit Design in Transaction-Level Verilog
chunks.text:
## Paper 1: Timing-Abstract Circuit Design in Transaction-Level Verilog

### Citation (as printed)
- Title: "Timing-Abstract Circuit Design in Transaction-Level Verilog".
- Author: Steven Hoover, Redwood EDA, Shrewsbury, MA, USA (p525).
- Venue and year, as printed in the copyright block on p525: S. F. Hoover, "Timing-Abstract
  Circuit Design in Transaction-Level Verilog," 2017 IEEE International Conference on Computer
  Design (ICCD), Boston, MA, 2017, pp. 525-532. DOI 10.1109/ICCD.2017.91.

### Thesis in two sentences
- Cycle-level detail can be kept in the source while being made cheap and safe to change, by
  writing behavior inside pipelines and treating the assignment of logic to pipeline stages as
  a physical implementation attribute that tools turn into flip-flops (p525, abstract).
- The primary payoff claimed is IP reuse across different timing constraints with fewer bugs;
  smaller source code is explicitly called a "secondary benefit" (p525, abstract; p530).

### Problem framing
- Design effort per chip has grown "by nearly a factor of five" over the past decade despite EDA
  advances, and the author calls a continuation of that trend "unsustainable" (p525, citing [4]).
- Transistor counts have grown 25,000x and clock frequencies 100x since RTL was adopted in the
  mid-1980s, yet RTL remains the predominant design methodology (p525).
- SoC methodology (assembling IP blocks) is the biggest productivity gain of the decade, but RTL
  IP bakes in assumptions, "most-significantly" the depth of logic that fits in one clock period,
  which differs between implementations (p525).
- Retargeting RTL IP to a different clock or technology "requires retiming, repipelining, and
  microarchitectural changes" and "significant rewriting" (p525, abstract).
- C/C++ HLS (SystemC, OpenCL) is judged good for optimized computational pipelines (DSP, GPU) and
  timing-insensitive channels, but not for "control-intensive designs" with complex cycle-level
  interactions such as a CPU with hazards, bypass paths, and misprediction recovery (p526).
- "Designers make tradeoffs with workloads in mind, and this information is not available to HLS
  tools" and "generalized fully-automated optimizations are not in sight" (p526).
- The stated goal is to resolve "the conflicting goals of having explicit cycle-level detail in
  the source code and having the ability to change details without disruptive rewrites" (p526).

chunks.heading: 05. The two foundational TL-Verilog papers (Makerchip LEARN menu) > Paper 1: Timing-Abstract Circuit Design in Transaction-Level Verilog > Key concepts with the paper's definitions
chunks.text:
### Key concepts with the paper's definitions
- Timing-abstract modeling: "A timing-abstract modeling approach is presented that separates the
  concerns of behavior and timing. Timing-abstract behavior is specified within the context of
  pipelines, and logic within pipelines is assigned to pipeline stages as a matter of
  implementation detail. Sequential elements are generated by tools from the pipelined
  specification." (p525, abstract)
- TL-Verilog: "a language extension of SystemVerilog, called Transaction-Level Verilog, or
  TL-Verilog. TL-Verilog was developed originally at Intel Corporation, driven in large part by
  the author, and is now an evolving open language standard." (p526 to p527)
- Pipesignal: "Identifiers such as $aa in Fig. 3, are termed pipesignals. A pipesignal represent
  a signal and all staged versions of that signal." The SystemVerilog equivalent needs two
  signals for $aa_sq, one per stage (p527; the singular "represent" is the paper's typo).
- Pipeline: "TL-Verilog introduces a scope construct for pipelines -- |calc in Fig. 3. These
  pipelines are free-flowing without back-pressure. They provide a mechanism for abstracting
  time." (p527)
- Pipestage: "TL-Verilog also introduces a scope construct for pipeline stages, or pipestages,
  within pipelines, such as @1." (p527)
- Implied flip-flops: "Flip-flops are implied where pipesignals cross pipestage boundaries."
  (p527, Fig. 4)
- Behavior excludes staging: "Strictly speaking, the timing-abstract behavioral model does not
  include the pipestage specifications. These have no impact on the overall behavior of the
  model. A timed signal, such as the pipeline output $cc at stage @3, exhibits an identical
  waveform regardless of the staging of the logic that produces it." (p527)
- Augmentation and timing-augmented model: "Pipeline staging is considered to be a physical
  attribute, or augmentation, describing an implementation of the behavioral model. A
  timing-abstract model, together with timing augmentation is termed a timing-augmented model."
  (p527)
- Retiming freedom: "Logic retiming (described in [13]) at a statement level is a simple matter
  of changing timing augmentation and does not carry the risk of introducing bugs." and "In
  TL-Verilog, every logic statement belongs to a pipeline and can therefore be retimed." (p527)
- Consumed-before-produced is not a behavioral error: "Even if a pipesignal is consumed in an
  earlier stage than it is produced, this is a reflection of an infeasible physical
  implementation and does not reflect upon the validity of the timing-abstract behavioral
  model." (p527)
- Syntax conveniences: a pipesignal's type such as [31:0] is written in its assignment, no

chunks.heading: 05. The two foundational TL-Verilog papers (Makerchip LEARN menu) > Paper 1: Timing-Abstract Circuit Design in Transaction-Level Verilog > Key concepts with the paper's definitions
chunks.text:
separate declaration; assign and always_comb keywords are not required (p527).
- Pipeline alignment: "The >> (ahead) or << (behind) syntax, or pipeline alignment specifier,
  provides the stage of a referenced pipesignal relative to the stage of the assignment
  statement." (p527 to p528)
- Relative alignment is the safety mechanism: "the use of relative alignments is key to enabling
  safe retiming of logic where transactions do interact. It also clarifies the nature of the
  interaction." (p528)
- Naturally-aligned reference: an offset of zero, reflecting "the natural flow of the pipeline";
  all references in the Pythagorean example are naturally aligned (p528).
- Cross-pipeline reference: /top|mem>>5$mem_data gives the pipeline scope of a pipesignal in
  another pipeline, with its stage computed from the alignment (3 + 5 = 8 in the example) (p528).
- Retiming worked example: moving the operand mux from @3 to @4 in TL-Verilog changes one stage
  scope; in RTL "Two (64-bit-wide) flip-flops must be added and one removed; one signal must be
  added and one removed" and mux signal names change, which the author calls "non-trivial and
  rather bug prone" (p528).
- Timing precision is a dial: an "approximately-timed model can provide a good balance" and
  "eliminates the need to break up single logic statements that would physically span cycle
  boundaries"; precise timing is needed when flows manipulate sequentials after synthesis (scan
  insertion, clock network generation) or to correlate physical timing paths back to source
  (p528).
- When condition: "?$valid ... applies to all the logic of the pipeline, across all stages. It
  indicates that the pipeline logic is valid only when $valid ... is correspondingly asserted."
  Staged versions of $valid become enable or gating conditions for sequentials, and it is "up to
  the tools processing TL-Verilog code" to derive the clock-gating network (p529).
- Validity also enables checking and debug: invalid values can be modeled as X (don't care) or
  produce assertions, which makes "inadvertent consumption of invalid signal values" detectable
  and pipeline traces readable (p529).
- Control over sequentials: synchronous reset is plain combinational logic (AND NOT reset);
  asynchronous reset is "outside the scope of timing-abstract modeling"; scan is auto-inserted
  and "not an obstacle"; enable flops are inferred by synthesis; TL-Verilog "does provide an
  explicit construct for recirculation" (p529).
- "Clock-gating logic, which is typically a disruptive afterthought, can be in place in a design
  from the start." (p529)

chunks.heading: 05. The two foundational TL-Verilog papers (Makerchip LEARN menu) > Paper 1: Timing-Abstract Circuit Design in Transaction-Level Verilog > Methodology (Section VI, p529 to p531)
chunks.text:
### Methodology (Section VI, p529 to p531)
- Two kinds of evidence are used: a contrived long-division example analyzed completely, and code
  size statistics from three industry examples converted by hand from Verilog/SystemVerilog to
  TL-Verilog (p529 to p530).
- In all cases Redwood EDA's SandPiper code generator translated the TL-Verilog into
  SystemVerilog; the generated SystemVerilog is the comparison basis for the divider (p530).
- The author argues that generated code "reasonably approximates hand-generated code, following
  the chosen industry-recommended coding conventions", and that "industry data will provide
  evidence" of this (p530). This is asserted, not demonstrated in the paper.
- Code was categorized (Table I, p530) into Clock Gating, Validity, Code Structure, Staging,
  Declarations, and Logic. Declarations and Code Structure are treated as "syntactic benefits";
  the other categories are attributed to timing abstraction (p530).
- Counts exclude comments and whitespace; the unit is characters (Fig. 11) and both lines and
  characters (Table II) (p530 to p531).
- For the real-world designs, "source lines left as Verilog or SystemVerilog were not included
  in the data. Most notably, this includes module interfaces." (p531)

chunks.heading: 05. The two foundational TL-Verilog papers (Makerchip LEARN menu) > Paper 1: Timing-Abstract Circuit Design in Transaction-Level Verilog > Quantitative claims (exact numbers as printed)
chunks.text:
### Quantitative claims (exact numbers as printed)
- Long-division example (A/B to four hex digits, one quotient digit per cycle, control in stage
  0 and calculation in stage 1): TL-Verilog is smaller than the generated SystemVerilog "by a
  factor of 3.4" excluding comments and whitespace (p530).
- Same example, excluding the syntactic categories (Declarations, Code Structure): "the estimated
  reduction from timing abstraction for this example is 3.0" (p530).
- Fig. 11 (chart reading, approximate): TL-Verilog total roughly 400 characters, almost all
  Logic; generated SystemVerilog roughly 1,900 characters split across Logic, Declarations,
  Staging, Structure, Validity, and Gating (p530).
- Repipelining the divider to two cycles per iteration with even/odd interleaving (Fig. 12):
  Table II reports lines changed/added of 7 in TL-Verilog versus 34 in SystemVerilog, and
  characters changed/added of 30 versus 1122 (p531).
- After that change the SystemVerilog is "6.4 times the size of the TL-Verilog code" (p531).
- Fig. 13, three real-world hand conversions, y axis in kCharacters, three bars each (Orig SV,
  TLV, Gen SV). Chart reading, approximate, no ratios are printed in the paper (p531):
  - 3.2GHz ASIC Encryp: Orig SV about 17k, TLV about 7k, Gen SV about 21k.
  - 3.1GHz ASIC Cache Ctl: Orig SV about 18k, TLV about 6k, Gen SV about 19k.
  - 250MHz FPGA Eth Pkt: Orig SV about 28k, TLV about 16k, Gen SV about 37k.
- Qualitative results on the real-world designs: "Logic synthesis was run for two of the
  designs, and results demonstrated consistency with the original code." (p531)
- "For the third case, the designer was able to easily remove one of three stages from the main
  pipeline after conversion, which was reportedly a valuable improvement that would have been
  impractical to implement in the Verilog source code." (p531)
- "One conceptual bug was known to be eliminated in the course of the conversions as a natural
  outcome of cleaner pipeline expression, though it is unknown whether this bug could manifest
  in the context of its full-chip model." (p531)

chunks.heading: 05. The two foundational TL-Verilog papers (Makerchip LEARN menu) > Paper 1: Timing-Abstract Circuit Design in Transaction-Level Verilog > Comparisons to other languages and flows
chunks.text:
### Comparisons to other languages and flows
- SystemC and OpenCL (C/C++ HLS): momentum comes from the role of software modeling; synthesis
  from software must bridge sequential software to parallel hardware; "the use of C++ language
  semantics presents complications for both designers and tools" (p526).
- HLS fit: good for DSP/GPU-style computational pipelines and timing-insensitive channels, not
  for control-intensive designs whose microarchitecture changes with constraints (p526).
- Bluespec SystemVerilog [10][11] and Chisel [12]: "provide incremental improvements in
  abstraction" but "remain explicit about sequential elements (flip-flops and latches) and
  therefore do not provide sufficient abstraction to avoid redesign" (p526).
- SystemVerilog RTL: the Fig. 2 style (sequentials separate from combinational logic, signals
  named by stage) is the comparison style throughout; the third real-world case used a denser
  hand-coding style "common of FPGA designs" and showed less reduction (p526, p531).

### Limitations the author states
- "No data is currently available to analyze real-world IP block modifications" so the reuse
  benefit (the primary goal) is only shown on the contrived divider (p531).
- The divider comparison is against machine-generated SystemVerilog, not hand-written code (p530).
- Module interfaces and any lines left in Verilog/SystemVerilog were excluded from the
  real-world counts (p531).
- Reduction is smaller for dense FPGA coding styles and at lower clock frequencies "as there are
  fewer sequentials to manage" (p531).
- Some code growth in the generated SystemVerilog comes from clock gating and X injection that
  the original hand-written code did not have, so Gen SV is not a like-for-like baseline (p531).
- Asynchronous reset is outside the scope of timing-abstract modeling (p529).
- The eliminated conceptual bug may not have been reachable in the full-chip model (p531).

chunks.heading: 05. The two foundational TL-Verilog papers (Makerchip LEARN menu) > Paper 1: Timing-Abstract Circuit Design in Transaction-Level Verilog > Future work and open threads
chunks.text:
### Future work and open threads
- Phase-granular, latch-based timing augmentation is described as possible but deferred (p528).
- Real-world IP modification data is explicitly missing and needed (p531).

---

## Paper 2: Top-Down Transaction-Level Design with TL-Verilog

### Citation (as printed)
- Title: "Top-Down Transaction-Level Design with TL-Verilog".
- Authors: Steven Hoover (Redwood EDA, Shrewsbury, MA, USA) and Ahmed Salman (Alexandria,
  Egypt) (p1).
- Venue and year: NOT printed anywhere in the PDF. There is no copyright block, no DOI, and no
  page numbers. The most recent references are dated "Last edited 2 Sept. 2018" and "Last edited
  12 Oct. 2018" and the TL-X spec is cited as 2018 (p5), so the paper is 2018 or later. Cite it
  as an unpublished or self-published Redwood EDA paper distributed via Makerchip's LEARN menu
  unless a venue is confirmed elsewhere.

### Thesis in two sentences
- Transaction-level design extends timing abstraction from pipelines to arbitrary "flow
  elements" (FIFOs, arbiters, queues) so that combinational transaction logic can be written
  anywhere along a flow and tools generate the staging and steering (p1).
- Combined with a scoping property called lexical reentrance, this makes a top-down flow
  possible: instantiate library flow components, add transaction logic, verify and evaluate
  performance early, then reposition the logic to obtain a quality RTL implementation (p1).

chunks.heading: 05. The two foundational TL-Verilog papers (Makerchip LEARN menu) > Paper 2: Top-Down Transaction-Level Design with TL-Verilog > Problem framing
chunks.text:
### Problem framing
- Circuit complexity scales exponentially but team size and project duration cannot; RTL "has
  remained the norm for over 30 years and 1/25,000 transistor scaling" and "The industry is at
  its breaking point" (p1).
- Adoption of high-level methods is slow because "high-level modeling languages are failing to
  offer sufficient simplification to justify the loss of direct control over details" (p1).
- Top-down design "has long been explored, but it is, today, generally understood to be
  infeasible. We show that it is not." (p1)
- The authors are careful about scope: "We study a top-down approach not to imply that
  transaction-level design is a top-down methodology, but rather to demonstrate that a top-down
  approach is, indeed, possible." (p1)

chunks.heading: 05. The two foundational TL-Verilog papers (Makerchip LEARN menu) > Paper 2: Top-Down Transaction-Level Design with TL-Verilog > Problem framing
chunks.text:
### Key concepts with the paper's definitions
- Transaction: "A transaction, in this methodology, is an entity that moves through structures
  like pipelines, arbiters, and queues. A transaction might be a machine instruction, a flit of
  a packet, or a memory read/write." (p1, abstract)
- Transaction logic: "Transaction logic, like packet header decode or instruction execution,
  that operates on the transaction can be placed anywhere along the transaction's flow. Tools
  produce the logic to carry signals through their flows to stitch the transaction logic." (p1)
- Recap of timing abstraction from [1]: "All logic belongs to a pipeline and exists within a
  pipeline stage. The stage of a logic expression is purely a physical implementation attribute.
  It has no impact on behavior, so timing details can be refined safely without impacting
  behavior. While the resulting expression of the design contains identical detail, it is
  simpler, smaller, and both easier and safer to manipulate." (p1)
- Transaction-level design "builds upon timing-abstract design. It extends the notion of
  transactions flowing through pipelines to transactions flowing through arbitrary 'flow
  elements,' such as FIFOs, arbiters, and queues." (p1)
- Fields and flow: "A transaction is a collection of signals, or fields. The transaction flow
  defines the path by which these fields travel through the machine. Unlike structures,
  transactions 'change shape' as their fields are operated upon by transaction logic. Each field
  travels along its flow from the point at which is is produced to the downstream locations in
  which it is consumed." (p2; the doubled "is is" is the paper's typo)
- $ANY and flow expression: "$ANY can be used in a logic expression in place of an output signal
  and one or more input signals. The expression must be one that transfers an $ANY input to the
  $ANY outputs, unaltered." A ternary mux `$ANY = $select ? /in1$ANY : /in2$ANY;` is the example
  (p2, Fig. 2).
- Flow graph: "Flow expressions can be chained to form a directed graph that defines a flow";
  fields "can be assigned anywhere along the flow and consumed anywhere downstream in the flow"
  (p2).
- Flow logic versus transaction logic: "This creates a decoupling of flow logic and transaction
  logic, depicted in Fig. 4, similar to the decoupling of timing and behavior in timing-abstract
  design." Expressions move along the flow "by cutting and pasting", implementation may change

chunks.heading: 05. The two foundational TL-Verilog papers (Makerchip LEARN menu) > Paper 2: Top-Down Transaction-Level Design with TL-Verilog > Problem framing
chunks.text:
"dramatically" while "overall behavior remains unchanged", subject to not moving upstream of
  producers or downstream of consumers (p2 to p3).
- "The flow takes care of the sequential staging and steering of the fields, and the
  transaction logic is merely combinational." (p3)
- Lexical reentrance: "the ability to define content in a scope, change scope (in program
  order), then reenter the earlier scope to define more content. This simple property provides
  an important ability to separate concerns, similar in some respects to aspect-oriented
  programming." (p3)
- Why it matters for libraries: library components "provide generic aspects of functionality"
  and the instantiating context adds "more-detailed logic into the context established by the
  library components"; WARP-V uses this to keep microarchitectural components ISA-independent
  (p3).
- Bug locality argument: "most bugs, particularly difficult bugs, tend to relate to sequencing
  and flow control. Combinational logic bugs are less common and are generally easier to verify
  and debug." Lexical reentrance therefore lets "complex, bug-prone flow logic to be defined in
  pre-verified library components" (p3). This is asserted from experience, no data is given.
- Ready/valid: components use a "ready/valid" interface where upstream signals validity and
  downstream signals readiness; "there is no need for glue logic to stitch one interface to
  another. The components fit together like pieces of a jigsaw puzzle." (p3)
- Library contents: combinational flow components (arbiters), pipelines with varying
  backpressure mechanisms including phase-based backpressure, FIFOs, routing components (ring)
  plus a testbench macro (p3).

chunks.heading: 05. The two foundational TL-Verilog papers (Makerchip LEARN menu) > Paper 2: Top-Down Transaction-Level Design with TL-Verilog > Top-down design steps as the paper presents them
chunks.text:
### Top-down design steps as the paper presents them
- Step 1: construct the microarchitecture "simply by instantiating components" from the flow
  library; the showcase is four ports on a ring, each with a pipeline, a FIFO, a back-pressured
  pipeline, ring transit, arbitration with local traffic, another pipeline, and another FIFO
  (p1, p2, Fig. 1).
- Step 2: with only flow, the model is already "sufficient for performance studies" (for example
  how often arbitration forces local traffic onto the ring) and for early verification models,
  and the library includes a testbench (p3).
- Step 3: add combinational transaction logic "first into the beginning of the flow, enabling
  functional verification activities to verify the computations now performed by each
  transaction" (p4).
- Step 4: "Then the statements can be properly positioned along the flow to support the physical
  implementation" (p4, Fig. 7), where the Pythagorean logic is split across the stall pipeline,
  the back-pressured pipeline in the sending port, and the second free-flowing pipeline in the
  receiving port, using lexical reentrance to enter the library-created scopes.

chunks.heading: 05. The two foundational TL-Verilog papers (Makerchip LEARN menu) > Paper 2: Top-Down Transaction-Level Design with TL-Verilog > Methodology (Section V, p4 to p5)
chunks.text:
### Methodology (Section V, p4 to p5)
- Single showcase design (Fig. 1 ring) with the Pythagorean calculation from [1] reused as the
  transaction logic "in the interest of consistency" (p4).
- Code size in characters excluding comments and whitespace, at three levels: Source (with M4
  macros), Expanded TL-V (after macro substitution, pure TL-Verilog), and SystemVerilog (after
  SandPiper) (p4, Fig. 8).
- Fig. 9 isolates the transaction-logic addition alone, with no macro expansion involved (p5).
- The SystemVerilog baseline is machine-generated; the authors note this "is not a perfect
  comparison versus a hand-coded SystemVerilog model, however the generated SystemVerilog
  conforms to an industry-recommended coding methodology with strong focus on readability" (p4).

### Quantitative claims (exact numbers as printed)
- The Fig. 1 flow plus its testbench was implemented "in just 13 lines of code" (Fig. 5): eight
  macro instantiations, four scope lines (replication, pipeline, pipestage), one logic
  expression (p3).
- Flow example: "Transaction-level design, therefore, enables a substantial portion of the 6.8x
  code reduction from modularity, and it can reasonably be credited with the additional 4.0x
  reduction versus SystemVerilog." (p4) Here 6.8x is Expanded TL-V over Source (the macro
  library effect) and 4.0x is SystemVerilog over Expanded TL-V.
- Fig. 8 (chart reading, approximate): Source about 1,000 characters, Expanded TL-V about
  7,000, SystemVerilog about 29,000, with the SystemVerilog split across Staging, Declarations,
  Logic, Misc, and Untouched (p4).
- Transaction logic alone (the four Pythagorean statements placed into the flow): "It generates
  73x the SystemVerilog code, including signal declarations, staging logic, and steering logic
  (in flow expressions)." (p5)
- Fig. 9 (chart reading, approximate): Source and Expanded TL-V both around 150 characters,
  SystemVerilog about 11,000 (p5).

chunks.heading: 05. The two foundational TL-Verilog papers (Makerchip LEARN menu) > Paper 2: Top-Down Transaction-Level Design with TL-Verilog > Comparisons made
chunks.text:
### Comparisons made
- Against RTL/SystemVerilog only. Pass-through components (ring, FIFOs, arbiter) "could be
  implemented in SystemVerilog" and SystemVerilog components can be used inside TL-Verilog with
  the steer/stage/pack/unpack at the boundaries eliminated; but components meant to contain
  transaction logic (pipelines) "cannot be implemented generically without lexical reentrance"
  (p4).
- No comparison to HLS, Chisel, or Bluespec is made in this paper.

### Limitations the authors state
- "Though we believe this showcase to be reflective of real-world use, we leave real-world
  examples to future research." (p1)
- The 6.8x and 4.0x figures are on one hypothetical ring design with trivial transaction logic;
  the authors note a router "might include transaction logic to decode packet headers" instead
  (p4).
- The SystemVerilog comparison is machine-generated, not hand-coded (p4).
- Modularity relies on an M4 plus Perl proof-of-concept because the language lacks native
  library features; the work is "being used to aid in the specification of proper language
  features" (p3).
- The paper is "an early view" of the methodology (p1).

chunks.heading: 05. The two foundational TL-Verilog papers (Makerchip LEARN menu) > Paper 2: Top-Down Transaction-Level Design with TL-Verilog > Future work
chunks.text:
### Future work
- Real-world examples of top-down transaction-level design (p1).
- Proper language features for modularity and reuse to replace the M4 framework (p3).
- Transaction logic beyond a toy computation, such as packet header decode (p4).

---

## Arguments to reuse (paraphrased, with page refs)

Why TL-Verilog reduces code:
- A pipesignal stands for a signal and every staged copy of it, so per-stage signal names and
  their declarations disappear (ICCD p527).
- Flip-flops are implied at pipestage boundaries, so the always_ff blocks that only copy a
  signal from one stage to the next are generated rather than written (ICCD p527, Table I p530).
- Types live in the assignment and assign/always_comb keywords are dropped, which the author
  classifies as a "syntactic" saving separate from timing abstraction (ICCD p527, p530).
- On the divider, almost everything that remains in TL-Verilog is assignment statements; the
  pipeline and pipestage scopes "account for very little code" (ICCD p530).
- Clock gating and validity checking are derived from a single ?$valid scope rather than hand
  written per flop (ICCD p529, Table I p530).
- In transaction-level design, $ANY flow expressions replace the per-field steer, stage, pack,
  and unpack logic at every component boundary (Top-Down p2, p4).
- The three real-world conversions show the TL-Verilog bar visibly below the original
  SystemVerilog bar in every case, with the smallest gain on the 250MHz FPGA design (ICCD Fig.
  13, p531; chart reading only).

chunks.heading: 05. The two foundational TL-Verilog papers (Makerchip LEARN menu) > Paper 2: Top-Down Transaction-Level Design with TL-Verilog > Future work
chunks.text:
Why TL-Verilog reduces errors:
- Staging is an implementation attribute with no effect on behavior, so a retiming edit cannot
  change the waveform of a timed output and "does not carry the risk of introducing bugs" (ICCD
  p527).
- Relative alignment (>>n, <<n) is what keeps retiming safe when pipelines interact, and it makes
  the interaction explicit in the source (ICCD p528).
- Moving the operand mux one stage in RTL requires adding and removing 64-bit flops, signals, and
  renaming, which is "non-trivial and rather bug prone"; in TL-Verilog it is a one-token change
  from @3 to @4 (ICCD p528).
- Repipelining the divider touched 7 lines and 30 characters in TL-Verilog versus 34 lines and
  1122 characters in the generated SystemVerilog (ICCD Table II, p531).
- "Regression testing is unnecessary if timing changes can be shown at the source-code level to
  have no impact on behavior." (ICCD p528)
- A consumed-before-produced reference is an infeasible implementation, not a behavioral bug, so
  it is caught as a timing issue rather than silently mis-simulated (ICCD p527).
- Validity information allows X injection or assertions that expose consumption of invalid
  values and makes traces readable (ICCD p529).
- The hardest bugs are in sequencing and flow control, and transaction-level design moves that
  logic into pre-verified library components while user code stays combinational (Top-Down p3).
- One real conceptual bug was eliminated during hand conversion as a side effect of cleaner
  pipeline expression (ICCD p531, with the author's caveat that it may not have been reachable).
- Smaller code correlates with fewer bugs per Brooks [15] (ICCD p530; a citation, not a
  measurement in this paper).

Why reuse improves:
- IP written at RTL bakes in the logic depth per clock period; timing-augmented IP lets the stage
  assignment be changed without rewriting behavior (ICCD p525, p527).
- "Safe and easy retiming results in fewer builds, fewer simulations, fewer bugs, and less debug
  effort." (ICCD p528)
- Physical designers or tools can be empowered to change timing in the source "with minimal or
  no involvement from the logic designer" (ICCD p528).
- Had the divider been written with the two-cycle scenario in mind, the alignment could have
  been parameterized, so one source could target both timing contexts (ICCD p531).
- After conversion, one real design lost a pipeline stage that would have been "impractical" to
  remove in the Verilog source (ICCD p531).

---

chunks.heading: 05. The two foundational TL-Verilog papers (Makerchip LEARN menu) > What the papers do NOT claim (guard against overclaiming)
chunks.text:
- Neither paper prints a "50 percent" or "2x" figure for directly translated designs. The ICCD
  paper's printed ratios are 3.4 (divider, versus generated SystemVerilog), 3.0 (divider, timing
  abstraction only), and 6.4 (two-cycle divider, versus generated SystemVerilog). The Top-Down
  paper's printed ratios are 6.8x, 4.0x, and 73x on a hypothetical ring with toy logic. All of
  these are against machine-generated SystemVerilog, not hand-written code (ICCD p530 to p531;
  Top-Down p4 to p5).
- The only hand-written-Verilog baseline is ICCD Fig. 13 (three industry modules), and the paper
  prints no ratio for it. Reading the bars gives roughly 17k to 7k, 18k to 6k, and 28k to 16k
  characters (Orig SV to TLV), which is roughly a 40 to 65 percent size reduction depending on
  the design. Steve's "about 50 percent when directly translated" is consistent with the
  middle of that range but is not a number either paper states, and the sample is three designs
  with module interfaces excluded (ICCD p531). If citing it, attribute it to Steve's statement,
  not to the papers.
- The papers measure characters and lines, not gate count, area, timing, power, or simulation
  speed. Synthesis was run on two real designs only to check "consistency with the original
  code" (ICCD p531).
- Bug reduction is not measured. The evidence is one anecdotal conceptual bug found during
  conversion (ICCD p531), a cited correlation from Brooks (ICCD p530), and an argument from
  experience that flow-control bugs dominate (Top-Down p3).
- Reuse across timing constraints, the stated primary goal, is demonstrated only on the
  contrived divider; "No data is currently available to analyze real-world IP block
  modifications" (ICCD p531).
- Neither paper claims TL-Verilog is a high-level synthesis approach; the ICCD paper positions it
  as keeping RTL-level detail while abstracting timing, and it explicitly keeps the designer in
  charge of microarchitecture (ICCD p525 to p526).
- The ICCD paper does not claim automatic retiming by SandPiper; retiming is a designer edit of
  the augmentation, and whether synthesis is allowed to retime is a separate flow decision (ICCD
  p528).
- The ICCD paper does not cover back-pressure, FIFOs, or arbiters; its pipelines are
  "free-flowing without back-pressure" (p527). Those come only in the Top-Down paper.
- The Top-Down paper does not claim transaction-level design is inherently top-down, only that a
  top-down flow is possible with it (p1), and it does not claim real-world validation (p1).

chunks.heading: 05. The two foundational TL-Verilog papers (Makerchip LEARN menu) > What the papers do NOT claim (guard against overclaiming)
chunks.text:
- The Top-Down paper does not claim native library support in TL-Verilog; modularity came from an
  M4 plus Perl framework outside the language (p3).
- Neither paper reports designer productivity in time (hours or days), and neither reports a
  controlled comparison with human RTL authors.
- The generated SystemVerilog in ICCD Fig. 13 is larger than the original hand-written
  SystemVerilog in all three cases, partly because it adds clock gating and X injection; this
  should not be read as TL-Verilog producing bloated RTL without that context (p531).

chunks.heading: 3. Idiom index
chunks.text:
## 3. Idiom index

For each idiom: the best 1 to 3 examples, `file:line`, verbatim snippet. Entries marked (tutorial) are from the teaching files and should be preferred as the canonical form; entries marked (lib) or (warp-v) show the same idiom at production scale. Longer per-batch candidate lists follow in 3.22.

### 3.1 State register: `>>1` recirculation, `$State <=`, and `<<1$State =`

Three equivalent ways to hold a value across cycles. Tutorials present the first two side by side.

(tutorial) `tutorial/fibonacci_example.tlv:14`, plain pipesignal reading its own past via `>>1`/`>>2`:
```tlv
   $val[15:0] = $reset ? 1 : >>1$val + >>2$val;
```
(tutorial) `tutorial/fibonacci_state_example.tlv:14`, explicit state signal (capitalized) assigned with `<=`; `$Val` on the right is the current (pre-update) value:
```tlv
   $Val[15:0] <= $reset ? 1 : $Val + >>1$Val;
```
(tutorial) `tutorial/makerchip_tutorial.tlv:186-196`, next-state assignment through `<<1$State`, allowed inside a concatenation on the left-hand side:
```tlv
      @2
         // Remember the purpose of the memory operation: fetch, load, or store.
         {<<1$FetchPending,
          <<1$LoadPending,
          $next_store_pending} =
            $reset || $mem_resp        ? 3'b000 :
            /top|fetch<>0$instr_valid  ? 3'b100 :
            /top|exe>>4$valid_ld       ? 3'b010 :
            /top|exe>>5$valid_st       ? 3'b001 :
                                         {$FetchPending, $LoadPending, $StorePending};  // $RETAIN
         <<1$StorePending = $next_store_pending;
```

### 3.21 Sibling-scope reference rule (path starts at an ancestor, never at a sibling)

Every hierarchical reference in the corpus starts from an ancestor of the current scope: `/top` (or the macro's `/_top` argument), an enclosing `|pipeline` name, or an enclosing `/scope` (which may be re-indexed). A sibling is reached by naming the common ancestor and descending. No file writes a bare `/sibling|pipe$sig` or `/sibling$sig` from inside another scope.

This matches the rule derived from the language spec in `notes/01_tlv_spec.md:361-362` (the first path element jumps to any ancestor by name, which works because ancestor names are unique along a chain, spec section 10; there is no `..`).

(tutorial) `tutorial/makerchip_tutorial.tlv:72`, from `|fetch @0` to sibling pipeline `|exe`:
```tlv
         $valid_br_taken = /top|exe>>6$valid_br_taken;
```
(example) `makerchip_examples/elevator.tlv:291`, from top-level `|ctrl` to the sibling scope's pipeline `/version2|ctrl`:
```tlv
         $Error <= $reset ? 1'b0 : !((*floor_mask == /top/version2|ctrl$floor_mask) && ((3'b1 << $Floor) == /top/version2|ctrl$floor_mask)) || $Error;
```
(tutorial) `tutorial/array2d_example.tlv:136-140`, from `|rd/mismatch` to siblings `/trans2`, `/trans3` via the enclosing pipeline `|rd`:
```tlv
            /mismatch
               // A vector pulled through $ANY, with bits asserted for any mismatches between read data for
               // different implementations.
               $ANY = (|rd/trans2$ANY ^ |rd/trans3$ANY) |
                      (|rd/trans2$ANY ^ |rd/trans4$ANY);
```
More forms of the same rule:
- `tutorial/speculative_adder.tlv:46-47`, from `|in_pipe/pred_trans/digit[*]` to sibling `/trans` via `|in_pipe`: `|in_pipe/trans/in[0]$value[#digit:#digit-2]`.
- `tutorial/mini_cpu_1_cyc.tlv:227`, from `/instr/src[*]` to sibling `/reg[...]` via `/instr`: `$reg_value[11:0] = /instr/reg[$reg]$Value;`.
- `tutorial/dac_2020_ring.tlv:29`, from `/port[*]|ring/upstream` to another element of the same replicated scope: `/port[(#port + #_size - 1) % #_size]|ring>>1$ANY` (re-index the enclosing scope, then descend).
- `warp-v/warp-v.tlv:3790`, child scope reading its parent pipeline: `$reset = |fetch$reset;`; `makerchip_examples/elevator.tlv:269` from `/floor[*]`: `|ctrl$reset`.
- `warp-v/warp-v.tlv:6560-6562`, from `|done` to `|fetch` through `/top` and a hierarchy argument: `*passed = & /top/_hier|fetch/instr>>m5_REG_WR_STAGE$passed;`.
- Inside a library macro, `/_top` stands in for the common ancestor: `makerchip_examples/ring_viz.tlv:42` `/_top/tb/ring_stop|send<>0$accepted`, `tlv_flow_lib/pipeflow_lib.tlv:218` `/_top|_out>>m4_align(@_out, @_in1)$blocked`.

- `\viz_js` references follow the same rule but indices are JavaScript: `makerchip_examples/viz_demo.tlv:187-194` (quoted in 3.20).

| `makerchip_examples/snakes_and_ladders.tlv` + `snakes_and_ladders_tlv.tlv` | same game in SV and in TLV | full | Second before/after pair. Header rule quoted below. |
| `tutorial/verilog_pyth_example.tlv` + `tutorial/pythagorean_example.tlv` | SandPiper's own SV output vs the TLV source | full | The ground truth for stage flops to `@N`. |
| `makerchip_examples/tiny_tapeout_examples/tt_um_AES.tlv` | student Verilog AES rewritten as TLV macros | full | Real conversion, single-stage; residue noted below. |
| `makerchip_examples/memory_instantiation_examples.tlv` | how to keep a Verilog memory and wrap it | full | The rule statement for wrapping RAMs. |

So: for "how does an idiomatic Verilog-to-TLV conversion look", read `elevator.tlv` (versions 2 and 3), `snakes_and_ladders_tlv.tlv`, `verilog_pyth_example.tlv` against `pythagorean_example.tlv`, `memory_instantiation_examples.tlv`, and `tt_um_AES.tlv`. Do not model on `serv.tlv` or the two LLM Verilog files; they never convert anything.

chunks.text:
### 4.3 Verilog stage flops become `@N` (SandPiper's own output)

`tutorial/verilog_pyth_example.tlv:49-61` is what SandPiper emits for `tutorial/pythagorean_example.tlv:16-25`. Reading them together gives the mapping: a signal `x` computed at stage N is `x_aN`; every `always_ff @(posedge clk) x_a2 <= x_a1;` is the implicit flop between `@1` and `@2`; the TLV source has no flops at all, only the `@` labels. Conversely, when converting Verilog, every `always_ff` that only copies a value (`a_a2 <= a_a1`) should disappear and the consumer moves to a later `@`; only `always_ff` blocks with feedback (a `reg` that reads itself) become state (`$Sig <=`) or `>>1` self-references.

### 4.4 Patterns in the LLM-written TLV files that are idiomatic

- State via `>>1` self-reference (`claude_booth_multiplier.tlv:17-41`, `claude_1shot_clock.tlv:9`, `claude_chess_clock.tlv:20-29`, `claude_posit_pipeline.tlv:51`, `snakes_and_ladders_tlv.tlv:31-37`) matches `tutorial/fibonacci_example.tlv:14`. State via capitalized `$Sig <=` (`claude_uart.tlv:61-119`) matches `tutorial/fibonacci_state_example.tlv:14`. None of the LLM TLV files fall back to an SV `always_ff` for state.
- `*reset` used directly inside macro bodies (`claude_uart.tlv:61,74,79,98`) matches library practice (`DAC_ring_example.tlv:45`, `tutorial/incrementer_example.tlv:20`).
- Cross-pipeline `$ANY` transfer through `/top` (`claude_pyth_viz.tlv:37-38` `$ANY = /top|compute>>2$ANY;`) and a recirculating hold scope (`claude_pyth_viz.tlv:39-40` `/held $ANY = ... ? ... : >>1$ANY;`) match `tutorial/stall_example.tlv:10` and `warp-v/warp-v.tlv:2283-2287`.
- Design in its own SV module with an SV `top` testbench (`claude_pyth_viz.tlv:6-16`, `claude_fpu.tlv:1069-1084`) matches `tutorial/sv_tb_example.tlv`.
- M5 `var(...)` plus `if_defined_as(MAKERCHIP, ...)` to shrink dividers in simulation (`claude_uart.tlv:7-17`) matches `tt10_project.tlv:20-25`.

chunks.text:
### 4.5 Patterns in the LLM-written TLV files that are not idiomatic

- No `?$valid` gating: `claude_posit_pipeline.tlv:64-182` computes every stage unconditionally; `claude_booth_multiplier.tlv` computes `$busy`/`$done` but never uses `?$busy`. The tutorials wrap DUT logic in `?$valid` (`tutorial/pythagorean_example.tlv:17`, `tutorial/fpga_mult_example.tlv:13`) and `tutorial/makerchip_tutorial.tlv:110` says why: `// Condition on valid instruction if pipelined implementation.`
- Everything in one stage: `tt_um_AES.tlv:866-867` (`|encrypt @0` for a 10-round loop), `SAFEcore.tlv` (no `|pipe`, no `@`, twelve `$rf_rN` signals each recirculated with `>>1` at lines 305-316 instead of a `/regs[11:0]` scope), `pong.tlv` (`|pong @0`). Legal, but the timing abstraction is unused; `tutorial/mini_cpu_parameterized.tlv:156-164` shows the parameterized-stage alternative.
- Missing `*passed`/`*failed`: `claude_1shot_analog_clock.tlv`, `claude_1shot_clock.tlv`, `claude_booth_multiplier.tlv`, `claude_posit_pipeline.tlv`, `claude_SERV_VIZ.tlv`. `tutorial/default.tlv:19-21` requires them.
- Hardcoded stimulus instead of `m4_rand` (`claude_booth_multiplier.tlv:10-11`, `claude_chess_clock.tlv:16-17`) and cycle-number-hardcoded checks (`claude_verilog_pyth.tlv:225-303`, `claude_pyth_viz.tlv:506-511`).
- Unused `/_top` macro argument on every macro in `claude_fpu.tlv:64-500` (macros hardcode `|fpu_pipe`); compare `warp-v/warp-v.tlv:3517-3520` where `/_top` is where inputs are read from.
- Version-line drift: `claude_pyth_viz.tlv:1` `\TLV_version 1d: tl-x.org` (no `m4_`/`m5_` prefix); `claude_1shot_clock.tlv` mixes `\m5_TLV_version` with `m4_makerchip_module`; `viz.tlv:1` has `tlx.org`. Tutorials pair `\m5_TLV_version 1d: tl-x.org` with `m5_makerchip_module` or `\m4_TLV_version` with `m4_makerchip_module`.
- Debug residue: `claude_booth_multiplier.tlv:121` contains `debugger;`; `serv.tlv:708-740` references nine undeclared `*_string` JS variables.
- Bare SV identifiers inside a `\TLV` region: `serv.tlv:97` and `WIP_SERV_ALU.tlv:97` `*passed = *cyc_cnt > 500 || finished;`, `smith_waterman.tlv` `*passed` uses bare `cyc_cnt`, `warp-v/formal/verilog/pseudo_rand.tlv:61` `$reset = reset;` (1b-era). The reference card form is `*finished`.

chunks.heading: 3. Idiom index > 4. Conversion-relevant observations > 4.7 Tutorial rules vs `serv.tlv`
chunks.text:
### 4.7 Tutorial rules vs `serv.tlv`

- `tutorial/reference_card.tlv:19` defines `*SV_signal` as the way to reference an SV signal from TLV; `serv.tlv:97` writes `finished` bare. It compiles (SandPiper passes unknown identifiers through to Verilog) but it is not the documented form and it hides an SV dependency from NAV-TLV.
- `tutorial/default.tlv:14-15` and every tutorial start with `$reset = *reset;`; `serv.tlv` has no `$reset` and no `$` signal at all. Its `|default @1 /dummy` (`serv.tlv:100-102`) exists only so a `\viz_js` block has a scope to hang from. `|default` is otherwise used in the corpus as an explicit name for the implicit top-level pipeline (`life_viz.tlv:39`, `pseudo_rand.tlv:59`, `pipeflow_lib.tlv:1209`).
- `tutorial/sv_tb_example.tlv:12-15` prescribes "TL-Verilog for the DUT, Verilog testbench module instantiates it"; `serv.tlv` inverts this (Verilog DUT under a TLV-flavored top). That is consistent with the Examples pane calling it an import, not a conversion.
- The tutorials always pass `*passed` from design state or a cycle count; `serv.tlv:97` ORs a cycle limit with an SV wire, so it "passes" at cycle 500 regardless of whether `blinky` did anything.
- `serv.tlv:593-596` reads SV signals in VIZ with `this.svSigRef(\`servant_sim.dut....\`)` (no `top.` prefix) while `claude_SERV_VIZ.tlv:554` uses `this.svSigRef("top.servant_sim.dut....")` and `chatgpt5_verilog_uart.tlv:196` uses `this.sigVal("uart_inst.tx_busy")`; the corpus does not settle on one path root. `viz_demo.tlv:187-194` documents only the TLV-reference form `'$sig'`.

chunks.text:
### 4.8 Checklist distilled from the corpus for a Verilog-to-TLV conversion

1. Keep the Makerchip top interface (`module top(input logic clk, input logic reset, input logic [31:0] cyc_cnt, output logic passed, output logic failed)`, `tutorial/verilog_pyth_example.tlv:13`) or use `m5_makerchip_module`; put the design in its own module with a `\TLV` region as in `tutorial/sv_tb_example.tlv:46-60`.
2. First lines of the `\TLV` region: `$reset = *reset;` and one `$in = *in;` per input; last lines: `*out = $out;` (`tutorial/sv_tb_example.tlv:50-58`, `tt10_project.tlv:134-139` for the `\SV_plus assign *out =` variant).
3. Each `always_ff` with pure staging (`x_a2 <= x_a1`) is deleted; the consumer moves to a later `@N` (`tutorial/verilog_pyth_example.tlv:53-59` vs `tutorial/pythagorean_example.tlv:19-25`).
4. Each `always_ff` with feedback becomes either `$x = $reset ? init : cond ? next : >>1$x;` or `$X <= $reset ? init : cond ? next : $RETAIN;` (`snakes_and_ladders_tlv.tlv:31-37`, `elevator.tlv:267-279`). A concatenated `{$A, $B} <=` is fine (`tt_um_padlock.tlv:34-38`); a concatenated `<<1$A` LHS is fine (`makerchip_tutorial.tlv:188-190`).
5. `if/else` chains and `case` become nested `? :` (`tutorial/mini_cpu_1_cyc.tlv:238-258`) or, when a literal `case` is wanted, `\always_comb` + `casez` with `$$` on the first assignment (`tutorial/makerchip_tutorial.tlv:121-127`).
6. `valid`/`enable` conditions become `?$valid` blocks around the stages they gate (`tutorial/pythagorean_example.tlv:17`); do not condition the condition signal itself (`warp-v/warp-v.tlv:2090`).
7. Per-element `reg` arrays become `/name[N-1:0]` scopes with `#name` (`RISC-V_MYTH_Workshop/tlv_lib/risc-v_shell_lib.tlv:75-79`); indexed writes go through `\always_comb`/`\SV_plus` with `<<1$$Sig` (`tutorial/mini_cpu_1_cyc.tlv:303-313`) or stay as an instantiated SV memory with `<<N`/`>>N` port alignment (`makerchip_examples/memory_instantiation_examples.tlv:117-132`).
8. Sub-modules stay as SV and are instantiated inside the stage that drives their inputs, with `$$` on outputs and `>>N$$out` when the module has latency (`tutorial/makerchip_tutorial.tlv:134-152`, `warp-v/warp-v.tlv:3535-3547`); never inside a `?$when` (`warp-v/warp-v.tlv:2152`).
9. Ready/valid interfaces map to `$avail`/`$blocked`/`$accepted` if flow-library macros will be used (`tlv_flow_lib/pipeflow_lib.tlv:40-73`, `makerchip_examples/1st-claas_template_with_macros.tlv:64-78`).
10. Cross-module references become `/top|pipe>>N$sig` from a common ancestor (`tutorial/makerchip_tutorial.tlv:72`); parameters become `\m5 var(...)` or `m4_define` with `@m5_STAGE` stage names (`tt10_project.tlv:10-27`, `tutorial/mini_cpu_parameterized.tlv:156-171`).
11. Finish with `*passed`/`*failed` derived from design state plus a cycle bound, random stimulus via `m4_rand`, and `` `BOGUS_USE `` for outputs nobody reads (`tutorial/incrementer_example.tlv:28-35`, `tlv_flow_lib/macro_tests/flop_fifo_v2_test.tlv:57-58`).

chunks.heading: 3. Idiom index > 4. Conversion-relevant observations > 4.9 Additional conversion observations from the per-batch passes
chunks.text:
- **`>>1` self-reference vs `$State <=`:** `claude_booth_multiplier.tlv:17-41`, `claude_1shot_clock.tlv:9`, `claude_chess_clock.tlv:20-29`, `claude_posit_pipeline.tlv:51` all keep state as plain `$sig = ... >>1$sig ...`. This matches the tutorial `fibonacci_example.tlv` form and is idiomatic. `claude_uart.tlv:61-119` instead uses PascalCase `$Sig <=` state signals throughout (the `fibonacci_state_example.tlv` form), also idiomatic. Mixing both in one file is fine; none of the claude files do the unidiomatic thing of an SV `always_ff` for state.
- **Reset in the reset term:** `claude_uart.tlv:61,74,79,98` use `*reset` directly inside the macro rather than a `$reset` pipesignal, which the DAC ring macro also does (`DAC_ring_example.tlv:45`). `claude_booth_multiplier.tlv:13` assigns `$reset = *reset;` at `@0` and consumes it at `@1` (fine, SandPiper aligns it).
- **Missing `?$valid` gating:** `claude_posit_pipeline.tlv:64-182` computes every stage unconditionally with no `?$valid`; the tutorials (`pythagorean_example.tlv:17`, `fpga_mult_example.tlv:13`) always wrap DUT stages in `?$valid`. `claude_booth_multiplier.tlv` has `$busy`/`$done` but never uses them as `?$busy`. `claude_fpu.tlv` does gate (`?$valid_input`, `?$addsub_enable`) at every stage.
- **Redundant width/sign juggling:** `claude_1shot_analog_clock.tlv:23-26` allocates `[31:0]` for a value bounded by 16 bits and uses `/` and `%` by 60/3600, which synthesizes dividers; `claude_1shot_clock.tlv:12` has a pointless copy `$total_seconds[31:0] = $seconds;`. Tutorials avoid `/` except in `div_example.tlv` where it is the point.
- **TLV inside a non-top module with a separate SV testbench:** `claude_pyth_viz.tlv:6-16,463-518` and `claude_fpu.tlv:1069-1084,1405-1470` put the design in its own SV module and test it from an SV `top`. This matches `sv_tb_example.tlv` and is the recommended shape for a real conversion; the checks are cycle-number-hardcoded (`claude_pyth_viz.tlv:506-511`), which is fragile.
- **`\SV_plus` use is limited to `$display` debugging** in the claude files (`claude_fpu.tlv:1290-1310`); no LLM file instantiates SV modules from TLV. `claude_fpu.tlv:1183-1185` declares `**real` typed signals (`**real $check_real_a;`), a rarely seen but legal form.
- **Macro discipline:** `claude_fpu.tlv:64-500` takes a `/_top` argument on every macro but never uses it (the macros hardcode `|fpu_pipe`). `claude_uart.tlv:24` defines `uart_with_viz()` with no args and expects the caller to be inside a pipeline; it uses `m4+` to call an m5-era macro (line 315), which the tutorials also do.
- **Version line drift:** `claude_pyth_viz.tlv:1` is `\TLV_version 1d: tl-x.org` (no m4/m5 prefix), `claude_1shot_clock.tlv` mixes `\m5_TLV_version` with `m4_makerchip_module`. Both compile but are inconsistent with the tutorials, which pair `\m5_TLV_version` with `m5_makerchip_module`.
- **No end-of-sim assertion:** `claude_1shot_analog_clock.tlv`, `claude_1shot_clock.tlv`, `claude_booth_multiplier.tlv`, `claude_posit_pipeline.tlv`, `claude_SERV_VIZ.tlv` omit `*passed`/`*failed`; `default.tlv:19-21` asks for them.
- **Hardcoded stimulus instead of `m4_rand`:** `claude_booth_multiplier.tlv:10-11` fixes the operands (`8'sd13`, `8'sd11`); `claude_chess_clock.tlv:16-17` fakes button presses from a counter. Tutorials use `m4_rand($sig, hi, lo)`.
- **Stray debug artifact:** `claude_booth_multiplier.tlv:121` contains `debugger;` inside `render()`.

#### 4.9.2 tt_um_AES, uw_ece755, WIP_SERV_ALU, snakes_and_ladders, memory_instantiation_examples, mandelbrot, tt_um_calculator/padlock

##### `tiny_tapeout_examples/tt_um_AES.tlv` (student Verilog rewritten as TLV)
- Idiomatic: the AES data-path modules became `\TLV` macros over 2-D scopes (`subbytes`, `mixcolumn` at lines 781-835), so bit-slicing loops turned into `#xx`/`#yy` index math and `[*]`-style concatenations; the 10-round loop is a `$round` counter recirculated with `>>1` (lines 923-926) with round-dependent work gated by `?$not_round0` / `?$do_mixcolumn` (942-950); the key schedule ripple is `/word[(#word - 1) % 4]$next_word` (859).
- Less idiomatic / conversion residue: everything sits in one stage `|encrypt@0` (line 866-867), so the "pipeline" is a single-cycle loop with no timing abstraction exploited; `$reset = *reset;` is assigned mid-block at line 910 after `$blk_counter` already used `$reset` at 905 (legal in TLV but reads out of order); comments say "Can't clean this up because of a Yosys limitation" (line 802) about byte reversal; the `check` macro compares against hard-coded ciphertexts (809-813). Roughly 70 percent of the file is VIZ (`aes_viz()` lines 49-779).
- Wrapper pattern (lines 973-1036): SV `top` testbench instantiates `m5_user_module_name tt(.*);`, then the TT module opens a `\TLV` region and calls `m5+tt_connections()` and `m5+board(/top, /fpga, 7, $, , calc)` (1028-1031). `passed` is assigned in SV as `assign passed = top.cyc_cnt > 60;` (996), not via `*passed`.

##### `uw_ece755.tlv` (course neural node)
- Not a Verilog conversion but reads like one: dot products are written out term by term (lines 18-21, 27-30) instead of a replicated scope with a reduction; weights use `$random[4:0]`, an undeclared pipesignal that Makerchip randomizes (an implicit-random idiom also used in `memory_instantiation_examples.tlv:20-22`). State capture uses `$RETAIN` on a rising-edge detect (line 10-12), which is the idiomatic replacement for an `always_ff` with an enable.

##### `WIP_SERV_ALU.tlv` (SERV imported by URL)
- Zero conversion: all SERV sources are fetched with `m4_sv_get_url(...)` (lines 12-65) and the core is instantiated in `\SV` (line 91). TLV is used only for `*passed = *cyc_cnt > 500 || finished;` (97) mixing a `*` SV reference with a bare SV wire, and a `/dummy` VIZ scope that reads Verilog hierarchy via `this.svSigRef("servant_sim.dut.cpu.cpu.alu.i_rs1")` (224-229). This is the "wrap, do not convert" end of the spectrum, and is what the Examples pane means by "Importing TL-Verilog/SystemVerilog/Verilog by URL".

chunks.text:
##### `snakes_and_ladders.tlv` vs `snakes_and_ladders_tlv.tlv` (the cleanest before/after pair)
- The Verilog version keeps all state in one `always_ff` with a reset branch (lines 94-137) and attaches VIZ via `this.svSigRef("p0_pos", 0)` (254-265).
- The TLV version maps each `reg` to a `$sig = $reset ? init : cond ? next : >>1$sig;` line (71-81); `if (do_move) ... turn <= ~turn;` becomes `$turn = $reset ? 1'b0 : ($do_move ? !$turn_now : $turn_now);` (79); the `<=`/blocking distinction disappears because "previous value" is spelled `>>1$x` and "this cycle's value" is `$x`. Note the author introduced `$p0_prev`/`$turn_now` aliases for `>>1$p0_pos`/`>>1$turn` (31, 36-37) to keep expressions readable, and did not use capitalized `$State <=` signals at all.

##### `memory_instantiation_examples.tlv` (rule statements for wrapping Verilog memories)
- Lines 3-22 are an explicit instruction block: place the instance "in the context of the primary WRITE inputs", reach reads with `<<N` (earlier stage) or `>>N` (later stage), and "$$ marks module OUTPUTS". Lines 20-22: "read/write inputs are left undriven so Makerchip randomizes them, and explicit bit ranges on each use supply the signal widths. Outputs are consumed with `BOGUS_USE."

##### `mandelbrot_synthesizable.tlv` and `mandelbrot_wip.tlv` (SV helper functions rather than conversion)
- Fixed-point math stays in SV `function`s (`fixed_add`, `fixed_mul`, `real_to_fixed`) called from TLV expressions; `mandelbrot_wip.tlv:1` shows the export flags `--fmtFlatSignals --bestsv --noline` and line 3 says "For exporting the kernel, use --bestsv --noline, and cut debug sigs statements from _gen file."

##### `tiny_tapeout_examples/tt_um_calculator.tlv` and `tt_um_padlock.tlv` (Makerchip-only testbench guards)
- Two different guard styles for the same purpose ("Only because Yosys chokes on $urandom"): `tt_um_calculator.tlv:55` and `:72` wrap the `top` module in `/* */` emitted by `m5_if_defined_as(MAKERCHIP, 1, [''], ['/']['*'])`, while `tt_um_padlock.tlv:60` uses `m4_ifelse_block(m5_if_defined_as(MAKERCHIP, 1, 1, 0), 1, ['...'], ['...'])`. `tt_um_calculator.tlv:43-44` also hoists `RW_rand_vect` and `cyc_cnt` into the design module via hierarchical reference so `m4_rand`/`*cyc_cnt` work inside a non-top module:
```tlv
   \SV_plus
      m5_if_defined_as(MAKERCHIP, 1, ['logic [256:0] RW_rand_vect = tt_um_calculator.RW_rand_vect;'])
      m5_if_defined_as(MAKERCHIP, 1, ['logic [31:0] cyc_cnt = tt_um_calculator.cyc_cnt;'])
```
